Homage to Caṇḍavajrapāṇi!

Now, therefore, the Blessed One was dwelling in the city named Vipulaprabhāsa. There, surrounded by a great assembly of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, as well as by great ṛṣis and a vast multitude of beings, he delivered a discourse on the great teaching of the Dharma.
The scribe’s hand is very thick... mistaking the letter *makāra* for the initial *ikāra*!

Now, moreover, in that assembly there was a guild-president named Vijayaprabhāsa, who was abundant in wealth and gold, rivalling even Vaiśravaṇa, accompanied by his wife, a great lay follower (*upāsaka*), faithful, and one whose refuge was virtuous. He had been harassed by King Caṇḍapradyota and informed upon by an assassin; terrified, he approached the presence of the Blessed One.
Then the merchant Vijayaprabhāśa and the lay disciples rose from their seats and, lamenting most piteously before the Blessed One while weeping, spoke as follows:

"Blessed One, my king, overcome by rage, has issued an order to the executioners; therefore, for the sake of my life, I am filled with extreme fear. Blessed One, what should I do? How should I conduct myself? Blessed One, be my protector and my refuge."

Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni, having comforted Vijayaprabhāsa, emitted great rays of light from the circle of hair between his eyebrows (*ūrṇākośa*). After circumambulating him three times, they entered through the Blessed One’s mouth. As soon as they had entered, water like pearls began to flow from the Blessed One’s forehead. The Blessed One extended his right hand, stroked his forehead, and struck the surface of the earth. Immediately upon being struck, the surface of the earth began to tremble in six ways. Piercing through this earth, the Great Rākṣasī Vidyujvālākarālī emerged. She had eyes like heaps of glowing coals; she was lightning-like, pot-bellied, and terrifying with her fangs. She was adorned with a crown of tawny-brown matted locks, her body was blue-black, and she possessed eighteen arms bearing various weapons. Fierce and wrathful, she had twelve heads and wore human skin. She was garlanded with skulls, her hands were filled with bowls of marrow, blood, and fat, and she blazed with fire. She was clothed in a lion’s skin, and her sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) was made of black serpents. She held a sword, a hook, a discus, a mace, a trident, a banner, a staff, a spear, a horizontal javelin, and a skull-cup. She also held a bow, an arrow, a club, a noose, and an axe. All her hands held blazing weapons. With high shoulders and adorned with every ornament, she stood before the Blessed One in a terrifying manner and spoke thus:
[... *vidyu* likely equals *vidyujjihvā* (Lightning-Tongue), as seen in the first *vidyā*: [... *vidyujjihvā mahodari* [...
"Tell us!
Then the Blessed One, the Great Rākṣasī Vidyujvālākarālī, spoke thus:
"Go, O Rākṣasī! Repel all adversaries and enemies; ward off all the wicked and the malicious. Restrain all bonds, strife, quarrels, tumults, death, fear, and calamities.
Then the great Rākṣasī Vidyujvālākarālī, having prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, bowed her heads in homage, circumambulated him, and addressed the Blessed One as follows:

“Blessed One, I have a heart-mantra named *Raudrajvālā*, which is formidable, the destroyer of all enemies, and the repeller of all yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, apasmāras, and kaṭapūtanas; it is the crusher of all Māras. Therefore, I shall recite it before the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
“Speak, O great rākṣasī! Then it was authorized by me.
Then the rākṣasī was terrified by this spell.

Homage to all the Tathāgatas of the three times! Oṃ, Raudriṇī! You who possess fierce and great speed; you whose tongue is like lightning; O Mahodari! O Raudrī, wearer of a garland of skulls! Adorned with a crown of matted hair, bearer of various weapons! Hūṃ! Sphaṭaḥ 2! Remember the pledge (*samaya*) of the Tathāgata! Huru 2! Hūṃ! Crush all enemies! Drink their blood! O bearer of fierce speed! Cook them! Burn them! Hūṃ! Scatter them 2! Strike them 2! Strike them 2! All enemies, all wicked ones—cut them down! Appease [them]! Hūṃ! O bearer of great speed, Kālakā! Hūṃ phaṭ 2! Bring such-and-such a person under my control! Svāhā!
[Sphuṭaḥ]— perhaps a misreading of *phaṭ*—
O Blessed One, by this [mantra], fierce rites (*raudrakarmāṇi*) are to be performed.

Having drawn the great rākṣasī with red ochre on a cloth, a birch-bark leaf, or a wooden board, while burning guggulu incense, one should recite the vidyā one hundred and eight times. Red flowers should be offered, and [the drawing] should be buried in a cemetery. Having consecrated mustard seeds one hundred and eight times, they should be scattered over it, and the name [of the enemy] should be taken up; as soon as it is buried, all adversaries, enemies, and evil beings will become terrified and paralyzed.
Having fashioned an image of a maiden with charcoal from a cremation ground and placing a finger in her vulva, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times; they will become submissive.
Having fashioned an image out of wax and offering silver as the sacrificial fee, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times; then one becomes a *vasa*.
Or, if one recites over that very effigy eight hundred *karavīra* flowers and offers them into the vulva, she will become submissive.
Furthermore, if one buries it at the site of the Mothers (*mātṛsthāna*), all the enemies will die.

Having offered a blood-sacrifice for seven nights, one should seize and give over all wicked animals wherever they are being presented; within fourteen days, it will bring about the destruction of the entire lineage.
If he does not return within twenty-one days, his house, along with his village and the walls of his enclosure, shall perish.

Having fashioned an image of the enemy out of human bone, one should smear it with blood. One should place the syllable *Hrīḥ* at the location of the navel; one should place the syllable *Oṃ* on the forehead; the syllable *Dhrīḥ* on the right arm; the syllable *Hūṃ* on the left arm; the syllable *Pāṭ* on the back of the right foot; and the syllable *Dha* on the back of the left foot. Taking that image, one should wrap it in a shroud from a cemetery and bury it in a cemetery. Upon it, one should throw mustard seeds consecrated eight times with the root mantra, saying, "Kill so-and-so! To release him, one must extract [the image].
-bāhūṃ attracted by hūṃ-;
yāṭ- is a misreading of phaṭ; -cīrena read as -cīvareṇa.

Having fashioned a six-finger-high image of Vināyaka for the king, one should place a *vajra* on its head. On the sixteen joints, a trident; on the tooth-socket, an axe. On the right arm, the syllable *Dhrīḥ*; on the left arm, the syllable *Dhrī*. On the back of the right foot, the syllable *Ca*; on the back of the left foot, the syllable *I*. On the back of the middle of the arm, a hook (*aṅkuśa*). To the right of the *vajra*, a line at the tip of the needle, a bubble arising from blood. In the middle of that left needle, likewise, having taken its likeness, soaked in blood, one should bury it in a prepared spot of ground. Upon it, one should scatter mustard seeds soaked in blood and consecrated with mantras. One who wishes [to harm] should be told: "If he transgresses, Vināyaka himself will seize his house. By all these—lizard, jackal, cat, pig, crow, and so forth—which resemble Vināyaka, the city, kingdom, and countryside are seized, and pestilence breaks out. One must not bring them back oneself. Having extracted those likenesses, one should wash away all the placements with milk. Incense, flowers, perfumes, curd, and boiled rice should be offered, and they should be kept in a pleasant place. There will be great pacification. This excellent mantra should be performed in secret.

Having fashioned an image out of wood from a hollow tree, one should smear that image with red sandalwood. One should place the syllable *hrīḥ* at the location of the navel. Taking it, one should cast it into a river flowing to the ocean while saying, "Kill so-and-so! Then, one should again prepare that image and place it in a vessel of milk; thus there will be pacification.

During a lunar eclipse or a solar eclipse, one should place *māṣa* beans in the mouth until the sun is released from the eclipse. Observing the sprouts of those *māṣa* beans, one should rinse them and then wash them again with scented water by those who are pure and devoted to these rites. In the house of a Brāhmaṇa, having adorned a maiden with all ornaments and drawn a mandala, one should have the maiden stand within that mandala facing east and offer the aforementioned *māṣa* beans using the maiden’s hand. Taking that substance, one should form it into pills (*guḷikā*). Having hidden the pill, one should let it dry in the shade; then, one should consume seven pills together with honey. One will become a possessor of the Vedas, intelligent, free from wrinkles and gray hair, and the body will possess a radiance like that of the *karṇikāra* flower.

Having taken that pill (*guḍikā*), one should wrap it with cloth of excellent color. Having taken a well-blessed jar, having smeared its location with sandalwood paste, one should wrap it with a thread spun by a maiden. Then, having placed the pill inside the jar, one should wrap it with new cloth. One should then decorate that jar and, having taken it, bury it in the center; wealth and grain will not diminish, and one’s prosperity will increase.
-karttika- = -karttita- is obvious;
ghaṭo = ghaṭe is a misreading of the archaic ṭ;
naca- = nava-.

One who desires to bring [another] under control should fashion an image out of *sindhaka* wood, representing either a woman or a man. For the purpose of subduing a *śravaṇa*, a Brāhmaṇa, or a king, one must perform the ritual of seizing [the essence]. A single pellet from that ocean [of substances] should be placed [within the image]. Having recited the mantra eight thousand times over mustard seeds and *sumukha* seeds, one should place them upon that image facing east. In a copper vessel, at the three junctions of the day (*trisandhya*), one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times over water mixed with those seeds and strike the image with it. Incense of *guggulu* should be offered. Within one night, [the person] becomes submissive; within ten *yojanas*, he will become a servant. By practicing for two nights, that woman becomes greatly submissive through her husband. By practicing for three nights, the *śravaṇa* Brāhmaṇas will become submissive. By practicing for seven nights, the king, along with his inner apartments and retinue, together with his wealth, gold, and silver, becomes submissive. He remains a slave for as long as he lives. By practicing for fourteen days, all fears, bonds, beatings, and accusations, and so forth, shall be completely removed; and all women, men, boys, girls, and others will become servants, whatever they may be. If they do not come quickly, then, O Blessed One, I shall take away the life-breath of all of them with a single exhalation; I shall drink their blood and marrow; I shall cast a great fever into their bodies.

Insofar as one desires to perform the subjugation of all malevolent beings, one should take mustard seeds and recite this *hṛdaya* over them. Then, having consecrated a stake of *khadira* wood seven times with a five-colored thread wrapped around it, it should be driven into the ground at the threshold. By the mere act of driving it in, the binding of the senses (*indriyabandha*) is accomplished for the one who has been paralyzed (*jambhita*), together with his retinue. As long as it remains there, the binding of the senses persists; when it is extracted, there is liberation.

One should wrap a stake made of human bone, measuring six finger-breadths in length, with a five-colored thread. Having consecrated it seven times with mantras, one should strike a woman who has arrived at a single location while she is mixed with mustard seeds. This is for her benefit. By extracting [the stake], there is liberation.

Having consecrated a stake made from the bone of a deer or a jackal, measuring four finger-breadths in length, one hundred and eight times with mantras; and having fashioned an image of a maiden using charcoal from a cremation ground on a milk-tree, that stake should be driven into the vulva. At the mere moment of striking, she is seized by a great fever. Upon its extraction, there is release.

One should fashion a stake made of tiger bone measuring one finger-breadth in length; one should place the syllable *ṭha* in the middle of the stake, and then wrap it again with tiger skin. By whose name [this is buried] in a cemetery, upon merely being buried, he causes [that person] to cry out; by lifting up the tiger [skin], there is liberation.

Having ground together the bones of a cow, buffalo, donkey, dog, horse, and human, and having kneaded them with blood and mustard seeds, one should fashion an image of the enemy. This should be placed facing east at the feet of the Great Rākṣasī Svedāmbujā. One should recite the Heart Mantra over the mustard seeds eight hundred times. As soon as the name of the enemy is uttered while holding the image, [the enemy] will be seized by a great fever and will perish. For a man, [this rite] brings about his destruction.
Oṃ {Caṇḍatharāpari pracura 2 phaṭ hūṃ} ||

{All rites are to be performed with this mantra.} Having {prepared it}, {measuring eight finger-breadths, one should offer it}. {It is to be destroyed}. {Having recited this mantra one hundred and eight times, one should bury it in a cremation ground}. For whomever it is buried by name, that person’s power of merit and vigor {will be destroyed}. He will become loathsome, and wherever he goes, people will avoid him. Great hatred is thereby produced. {By digging it up, there is liberation}.
Sa + + [3] + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + + Caṇḍavegadhara, strike all the wicked! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!

With this mantra, one should bury mustard seeds at the four corners around the perimeter of the house. As soon as [the person] enters that house, they will fall down; immediately, they will come under one's control. Enraged with great wrath, he speaks these words: "Eight... [if one digs them up, there is liberation].
Having empowered a wooden stake one hundred and eight times with the mantra, it is buried in a temple. By whose name [it is buried], if one digs it up, there is liberation.
If one buries a hideous form in front of a female companion, it becomes a heavy burden; one is hated by all attendants and is despised by everyone.

[With] skulls, blood, and mustard seeds... [omitted] ...for either a woman or a man, it becomes effective against all classes of beings. One should offer eight hundred oblations with the mantra of mustard-seed milk, and one will be liberated.

Having recited the mantra eight thousand times over powdered skull, one should mix it with mustard seeds, *vacā*, and *kuṣṭha*, and consecrate it with cow’s urine; one should then perfume it with *argada*. Having recited it another eight thousand times, one should offer oblations while uttering the [target’s] name. Having recited it twenty-one times, one attracts [the target] from within a distance of a *yojana*; they become submissive and remain like slaves for as long as they live.
If one buries it at the threshold, merely by stepping over it, one is seized by a great disease; one should bathe with milk and mustard seeds, and liberation occurs.
One should give that very pill together with food and drink; once given, it remains always like a living being.

One should bind [the mantra] on the arm after reciting it eight thousand times. Victory is attained wherever one goes; one becomes possessed of great heroism and prowess; one’s enemies are subdued; all sentient beings remain under one's control, and they will all become like servants. If one places it in the mouth, one becomes an unimpeded speaker regarding all strife, quarrels, conflicts, and disputes.

One should wrap eight hundred pills in red cloth, tie them with a five-colored thread, and bury them at the base of a Buddha’s feet; they should be consecrated one hundred and eight times. All sentient beings will become like servants. All wicked ones, all adversaries, and all enemies, as well as all yakṣas and rākṣasas, will become like friends and will protect [the practitioner] as if he were their only son.

One should offer a hundred oblations of pills mixed with ghee while reciting the mantra; one is then liberated from great fear. One becomes the master of the king, his inner apartments, and his retinue, as well as of one's own person and wealth. Having consecrated eight hundred [offerings] mixed with *guggulu* resin, one should offer them in the name of someone; that person will become doubly hated and the king will fall into captivity.

Take *bālatuṣanarandatta*, *kuṣṭha*, *vacā*, *gorocanā*, and *rocanī*, as well as *akṣa*, peacock, *sasa*, and *ullaka*. Having combined whatever is there with ashes, one should apply it to the body with smoke. One should steep it in bitter oil (*kaṭukataila*). Having mixed boiled rice (*sithakalūka*) with *sālyodana* placed in a skull-cup (*kapāla*), one should fashion an image of the head with red sandalwood (*raktacandana*) and smear it so that it is soaked in blood. Having quickly prepared it in a certain spot on the ground, one should stand facing south and bury it while employing the six-faced mudrā. Accompanied by the heart-mantra, one should perform three circumambulations and depart to the left, turning one's back. Even when one has gone not too far, even if one has traveled a distance, no voice is heard. Regarding him, the procedure for observation must be performed; to turn him back, he should be raised up and released.

Taking funeral ashes, one should recite the mantra seven thousand times over them and scatter them on the path in the name of whoever is the target; by the mere act of treading upon them, that person will be seized by a great disease. For the counter-measure, one should recite it seven times. Taking those ashes mixed with mustard seeds and consecrated eight hundred times, one should bury them in a single spot; by the mere act of burying them, the city will fall into pieces, bit by bit.

Having prepared three stakes made from the bones of a cat, each measuring three finger-breadths in length, and having consecrated them one hundred and eight times with mustard seeds mixed together, one should bury two of them at the site of the [enemy's] house to a depth of ten finger-breadths; thus one causes [the enemy] to be tormented by *kuṇḍa* (fever/disease). He becomes hated by all people.

Take *bhallātaka* wood, the bones of a cow, buffalo, dog, donkey, and human, as well as *pataṅga*, *upaku*, safflower (*kusumbha*), sandalwood (*candana*), saffron (*kuṅkuma*), *madayantikā*, *kiṃśuka*, *rocanā*, vermilion (*sindūra*), realgar (*hiṅgula*), collyrium (*añjana*), *manaḥśilā*, and *kūryaviṣa*. Having combined all these five parts of gold together, one should grind them with blood. Taking the powder once, mixed with mustard seeds and consecrated eight hundred times, one should fumigate the houses of the enemies. By the mere act of fumigating, within a great distance of a single *sarpa-pātra*, humans fall down due to severe headaches and eye diseases; walls of wood and stone appear to be made of gold, and the earth is dug up. They wander about like madmen. To reverse this, one should fumigate the houses of the enemies at the three times of day with milk, mustard seeds, and water mixed together, consecrated eight hundred times with the *Hṛdaya-mantra*, and have [the patient] drink it. Immediately upon its disappearance, one should cover [the area] with the hand while reciting the *Ṣaṇmukha-mudrā-mantra* and sweep the ten directions.

Then that great rākṣasī said this to the Blessed One:

"I shall, with a great outbreath in a form of wrath, fear, and terror, subdue those wicked beings who harm the Three Jewels, who stand ready to strike down, who destroy images, who break idols, who reject the true Dharma, and who speak words of falsehood, emptiness, and base attachment—those beings who are truly poisonous."
Then the Blessed One said this to him:

“Let all the yakṣas and rākṣasas hear me—those of evil mind, those who are fierce and of fierce mind, and those who are gentle and of gentle mind; one should employ these three types of beings in the sequence of their respective actions. Then that great rākṣasī, having circumambulated the Blessed One three times and having bowed her head with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Blessed One as follows:

I shall devour the flesh, blood, fish, and fat of those who transgress the truth of the Buddha, those who transgress the truth of the Dharma, those who transgress the truth of the Saṅgha, and those who cause the loss of the Saṅgha’s gains. Having seized by the foot even one who is excessively exerted—a man who harasses men devoted to the Three Jewels—I shall seize his tongue. Why do humans, who have no fear, terrify those dwelling in the abodes of the Thirty-three? (Note:

Note for Sociography: Regarding those who have fallen away from gains within the Saṅgha as targets, then the Blessed One said this to him:
"Go, O Great Rākṣasī! You who possess the knowledge of falling [from grace], you are empowered and favored."

Then, in the midst of that great assembly, the Great King Vaiśravaṇa—along with a vast multitude of gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, siddhas, and vidyādharas; Hari, Hara, Hiraṇyagarbha, and others; the rākṣasī Vidyujjvālāsvedāmbujā; and the merchant Vijayaprabhāsa—all spoke these words with a single, resonant voice:

Alas, alas! In the future time, in the final age, there will be those who hold wicked and fierce mantras, who delight in gain and honor, and are full of envy and avarice. They will act with calamity, through worldly existence, or through habitual practice; they will teach without having seen [the truth], without having performed the ritual acts, and without skill. This must be done [by such persons].
Then that rākṣasī said this to the Blessed One:
"Neither the lunar day nor the constellation, nor the fast,
is prescribed."
Guhyasiddhi 1.66ab: The yoginī who is well-versed in the secret mantra, And who is skilled in the application of the mudrās, [is the consort].

No ritual means (*sādhana*) is required; one achieves success through mere recitation alone. By offering a white or yellow *bali* oblation, I shall perform all rites. Blessed One, if I should speak otherwise, may the Tathāgatas split my body asunder; may my body become foul-smelling and putrid, and may it likewise crumble from my head. Furthermore, Blessed One, all rites must be performed by a clearly manifest disciple who is pure, well-bathed, and undisturbed; they must be performed by the practitioner (*sādhaka*) while holding [the mantra]. I myself, the Great Rākṣasī, stand here with a vow of truth.

II. The Chapter on the Characteristics of the Path and its Fruit (Mārgaphalalakṣaṇapariccheda) [The text begins with the following verses: Just as a lamp, when placed within a jar, does not illuminate the objects outside, so too the mind, when obscured by ignorance, does not perceive the nature of reality. When the jar is broken, the light shines forth; likewise, when ignorance is destroyed, the wisdom of the Tathāgata illuminates all things. The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has taught that there are two kinds of emptiness: the emptiness of phenomena and the emptiness of the person. All conditioned things are like a dream or an illusion; they have no self-nature and are devoid of inherent existence. By practicing the path of non-attachment and cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness, one attains the fruit of Arhatship. Thus, through the power of wisdom, one transcends the three realms of existence and realizes the state of Nirvana, which is peaceful and free from all suffering.
Homage to you, O supreme Vajra-granter of boons!
She who possesses the great ferocity of the single hero Hūṃkāra with his preeminent arms, whose tongue is terrifying,
whose prowess resembles lightning, and who is the sovereign of the Sugata and the protector of the teachings;

Having bowed my head to the Blessed One, the Lord, who holds a vajra and a full skull-cup, who drinks human blood, whose gaze is blazing, who is formidable, and who wields a sword while threatening the wicked with his upraised index finger.
[3] Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling in the great charnel ground of Naraka-raṅka-ruṇire.
Retinue: five *mahābhautikī* goddesses.

The great protectress of beings, the great Ḍākinī Mahābhūtautikā—namely, the Vajraḍākinī named Sarvapriyavādā; the night-wandering Vajraḍākinī named Māṃsamedavasāhārā, who is dark blue and emits great smoke, the remover of great siddhis, stationed on the path, the one named Saṃpādanakarī; the Great Vajraḍākinī named Sarvaojohāriṇī; the thousand-armed Great Vajraḍākinī named Prahlādanī; [and those] with faces like external and internal messengers and female messengers, like a ruru deer, an elephant, a lion, a tiger, a dog, a jackal, a monkey, and a crow, who create by means of [their] power.
Through the yoga of the great maṇḍala, the goddess Ghūrmī, having attained extreme wonder at the assembly of the five ḍākinīs, speaks:
"One who desires the siddhi of Mahāmatola should meditate upon the mantra-casket conjoined with the mudrās."
Established upon the earth as a treasury of virtue, desiring the knowledge that accomplishes these goals,
one should [practice] in a secluded, beautiful place crowded with great wrathful deities,
on a pure spot of ground.
In the great place of the garland of bones, where blood and sweat are the lotuses,
pervaded by hair, teeth, and nails, and filled with jackals of various tastes;
In a place filled with various [beings], where various [kinds of] grasses grow,
this delightful great ground belongs to the deities of the great maṇḍala.
Having invoked these [deities] into that adorned place by means of speech, [one should proceed].
O you who have attained supreme steadfastness, look upon me;
O yoginī, grant me success, for that is what you have said.
Let Maṇicandra speak; let him abandon his wager. May he obtain liberation as his reward.
The first nidāna in Apabhraṃśa.

[2] Then Sarvamahāvajraḍākinī, composed of the five great elements, with a face blooming with joy from extreme wonder and delight, her eyes like blossoming lotuses, fierce and terrifying in her playful movements, consuming flesh, fat, and marrow, chewing the heart, uttering the *hā-hā* and *hī-hī* loud laughter, and performing the dance of great transformation through the play of her arched brows, having formed the assembly (*samāja*), again requested the meditation (*bhāvanā*).
Speak, O Blessed One, O Protector who acts for the benefit of all sentient beings!
What are the afflictions of all the Buddhas? Ignorance is the destroyer of evil. All cultivation is non-existence; cultivation is that which is free from anger.
Due to the conceptualization of existence and non-existence, intrinsic nature is not apprehended.
In the absence [of existence], there is an absence of cultivation; cultivation is indeed not cultivation.
Thus, existence would not be existence, and cultivation is not apprehended. (GST 2.3)
First, by means of the syllable *la* alone, it is filled with the resonance of the syllable *oṃ*;

On his right side is Vajrapāṇi with four arms: in the upper right hand a vajra, in the second a *kaṇapa*; in the upper left hand a hook (*aṅkuśa*), and in the second hand the gesture of fear (*bhayamudrā*). One should place red sandalwood, red flowers, and red food offerings before Bhavatī. A white vajra and a white *bali* offering should be established in this same manner.

One should perform the invocation together with the six-faced mudrā and mantra: "Come, come! You who are situated in the east, south, west, and north, quickly accomplish my purpose! Thus it should be said. Then, one should cover the four doors with a washed cloth. Between the Vajra and the Vajrāntara, one should apply the heart-mudrā of the Bhagavatī.

Gold powder, silver powder, and likewise the paste of bricks and rice flour—this liquid mixture of rice flour, divided into five colors, should be employed for the powder-maṇḍala. One should apply the colors of the maṇḍala in the eight directions.

The mantra-holder, endowed with the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), should proclaim the *bodhicitta* in the midst of the entire assembly circle. Afterwards, one should offer a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) and cause the flower consecrated by that mantra to be sounded with a bell. Having observed the three families (*trayaḥ kulāḥ*) and the peerless family (*asamasamaṃ kulaṃ*), the mantra and mudrā should be bestowed. Taking that person, one should seat him facing the *vijākumbha* at the western gate. One should cause the remainder to enter. Some have taken up the triple refuge (*trisaraṇya*); some have received the commitment-mantra and mudrā (*samayamantramudrā*); and some have been favored by the tantras.

May those who have entered this maṇḍala behold the gateway to the City of Immortality; may they behold the lineage that is equal to the unequaled, the sovereignty of the City of Immortality; may they become vessels for the City of Immortality and all proceed toward the state of Blessed Buddhahood, remaining for hundreds of millions of billions of aeons without exhaustion. Through the three incalculable aeons that I spent attaining the unsurpassed state, may the one who constructs this maṇḍala obtain, by means of a single karma, the state of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.

All the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, the Cāturmahārājakāyikas, Vijayaprabha, and so forth, having departed, one should take the flowers, the offering of bali, and the dust from that maṇḍala and cast them into a river or a well; or, having thoroughly burnt them with fire, they should be thrown away, so that they do not tread upon it. Crows, jackals, and dogs shall not devour them. One should smear that maṇḍala with earth and cow dung, so that it is not known what was done there.

2. The Second Chapter: On the Refutation of the Self (Ātman) as a Substance. [The opponent] says: If the self does not exist, then who is it that experiences pleasure and pain? Furthermore, if there were no self, then the teachings regarding "my eye," "my form," and so forth would be untenable. Moreover, since it is said, "I see forms with my eye," the self must exist as the agent of seeing. Also, because it is said, "I am born," the self must exist as the agent of birth. Furthermore, since it is said, "The self is permanent," the self must exist as something eternal. Therefore, the self exists. [The Master] replies: This is not so. Why? Because the self is merely a conventional designation and does not exist as a substantial entity. It is like the case where one speaks of "the chariot" based on the collection of its parts such as the wheels and axles; yet, apart from those parts, no chariot can be found. Likewise, based on the collection of the aggregates (skandhas), we conventionally designate "the self," but apart from the aggregates, no self can be found. Furthermore, if the self were a substance, it would have to be either identical to the aggregates or different from them. If it were identical to the aggregates, then since the aggregates are impermanent, the self would also be impermanent. If it were different from the aggregates, then the self would be something other than form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; however, such a thing is never perceived. Therefore, the self does not exist as a substance. As for the statement, "I experience pleasure and pain," this refers to the continuity of the aggregates, which are subject to change and transformation, and is spoken of metaphorically. The teachings regarding "my eye" and so forth are likewise established through the power of worldly convention. As for the statement, "I see forms with my eye," this is a conventional expression used by people in the world; it does not imply the existence of a real agent. The statement, "I am born," is also a conventional designation applied to the arising of the aggregates. And as for the statement, "The self is permanent," this is a teaching given in accordance with the specific dispositions of certain beings to whom it was taught that the self is permanent. Therefore, the self does not exist as a substantial entity.
Now, therefore, I shall explain the meditation on the wheel of the hurling of the Bhagavatī.

Having formed the *vajramuṣṭi* with both thumbs, one should extend the index finger of the left fist and place it in the armpit. One should place the right fist in the armpit of the left arm in its original position. Having stepped upon the left foot with the right and the right foot with the left, one should gaze upward and recite the mantra seven times internally. This is the *ākṣepa-mantra*: *thuru thuru ājjharu ājjharu hūṃ hūṃ*. This is the *mahākṣepa*. Whether in a village, a city, or amidst a great conflagration, by reciting this mantra, one should employ it; even the fire will be paralyzed as if by an axe. At the site of any maṇḍala, at the time of protection, one should grasp what was previously mentioned and gaze into the sky. By the mere act of gazing, the sky is paralyzed. This is the *raudrakarmavijayoddharaṇamahākṣepa*.

Forming two fists with both hands while seated in the *utkaṭāsana* posture, one should extend the left fist toward the private parts and place it upon the back of the right foot; likewise, one should place the right fist upon the back of the left foot. The mantra for this hurling [gesture] is: *oṃ dhuru 2 vajratuṇḍa garuḍavijṛmbhita hūṃ phaṭ*. Merely by employing this, one pierces sixty thousand *yojanas* and overcomes eighty thousand *nāgas* dwelling in the seven netherworlds (*pātāla*). This is the Great Hurling of the Vajra-Garuḍa’s Speed and Expansion.

During a time of drought, one should cause a stream of water to fall. During a time of drought, one should cause a stream of water to fall. Vidyujjvālākarālī, whose great eyes are like perspiring lotuses, shall preside over the previously mentioned maṇḍala of the pledge (*samaya*). In the eastern direction, everywhere, the great Nāga King named Karacchatraparikara should be stationed with nine heads, using cow-dung from a tawny-colored bull. In the south is the great Nāga King Airāvaṇa with seven heads. In the west is the great Nāga King Napla with three heads. In the fourth [direction] is the Nāga King named Sāgara with eight heads. In the four directions are the great Nāgas, as previously described, with the great display of the Vajra-Garuḍa’s expansion. One should employ each individual Nāga seven times; as soon as they are employed together, they cause a great rain to fall all around for three hundred *yojanas*.

Then, for the "Throwing" (ākṣepa) [posture]: having smeared both hands with sandalwood paste, one should contract the thumbs and little fingers and extend the root-mudrā of the left fist, placing it in the position of the right arm. One should extend the root-mudrā of the right fist like a vajra and place it in the position of the left arm. As for the two feet: one should hold the tips of the toes of the left foot against the other with a single cord. Extending them by the measure of a cubit, the mantra for the "Uneven Throwing" is: *oṃ hrīḥ hūṃ phaṭ*. *Hūṃ phaḥ*, O Vaisvānara, *hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ*, stay! Stay! Do not move! Whatever one desires, that should be spoken. Having performed this "Throwing," one should recite the mantra. Whether in a triangular maṇḍala of fierce-formed pretas, or in a maṇḍala of four mudrās, or in any location of a maṇḍala, or in the sacrificial pit (*āhutikuṇḍa*), one should apply the previously mentioned "Throwing" seven times, seven times. Merely by its application, Vaisvānara becomes present; whatever success (*siddhi*) one desires, the young practitioners (*māṇava*) shall request from him.

I shall now explain the fourfold *ākṣepa* (the casting-off gesture). With the hand, one should apply the *hasta-gandhā* (hand-fragrance) and say "ciṭi 2. Having joined the two fists and placed them against each other at the heart-position, one should extend the index fingers (*tarjanī*) so that the middle fingers act as needles and rest upon the backs of the two ring fingers (*anāmikā*). The thumbs and little fingers (*kaniṣṭhā*) should press against each other. One should step forward with the tips of the feet in front of the left foot. Placing the left fist right there at the ankle of the foot, one should extend the needle-like middle and index fingers against each other. Extending the right arm along the spine, one should pull back the left index finger. With a fixed gaze, brows knit, and eyes rigid, one should stare with the right eye and hold the right arm in a fist while reciting the mantra. This is the *ākṣepa-mantra*: *Oṃ hūṃ oṃ huṃ payadeva hūṃ kha kha hūṃ | vighaṭitaraudrī hūṃ ā svāhā*. When this *ākṣepa-mantra* is employed during the time of accomplishing *siddhi*, obstacles appear in terrifying and fearsome forms. Having bound the previously mentioned *ākṣepa* mudrā and recited the mantra, one should direct it toward the obstacle. As soon as it is applied, one becomes free from obstacles. One should perform a circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*) of ten million times in every location. Even one who has committed the five sins of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*) will see, within a dream, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Great Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, Padmadhara, and the great Rākṣasī Svedāmbuja in a state of fearlessness. These three families are to be honored: the lineage of the Mother, Śākyamuni, and the fourfold *ākṣepa*.
In the *Vidyotama-mahāmantra*, the fourth [chapter], consisting of the Great Rākṣasī Svedāmbuja who is formidable with flashes of lightning, is completed. O ||
The Section on the Characteristics of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga-lakṣaṇa*)
Now, O Blessed One, I shall explain the meditation on the wheels (*cakra*) for pacifying, enriching, and subjugating.
First, I shall explain the wheel of pacification.

One should expand a thousand-spoked wheel situated upon a lotus; in the center of its eight spokes, one should place twenty-four syllables: *hūṃ svāhā | hūṃ ṭha ṭha hūṃ ṭha ṭha hūṃ ṭha ṭha hūṃ ṭha ṭha hūṃ ṭha ṭha*. This is the placement (*nyāsa*) in the middle of the hub: *oṃ hūṃ oṃ*. One should perform the placement of the wheel’s projection. First, the syllable *hūṃ* is placed; to its right, the syllable *oṃ*; to its left, the syllable *oṃ*. Afterwards, having circumambulated three times with this king of syllables, there are twenty-four syllables in the middle of the hub: *hūṃ ṭha 2 hūṃ ṭha ṭha*. One should say, "May peace (*śānti*) be mine," whether for oneself or for another. The ritual service (*upacāra*) of the wheel is performed on cloth or a wooden board; it should be drawn with non-fading pigments. The wheel should be white, like moonstone or white flowers; then, having offered oblations right there while burning *guggulu* incense, the mantra-holder should meditate on the wheel three times a day for the sake of pacification (*śāntika*). He should meditate on these characteristics for the purpose of pacification. He should observe the signs of success in pacification: the syllable *hūṃ* appears within the syllable *oṃ*; the syllable *oṃ* appears within the syllable *hūṃ*. With an unperverted mind, undeluded and clear-sighted, he should remain standing as before and meditate on the three kings of syllables. Through dreams, the mantra-holder sees the auspicious and inauspicious. They see black food and drink, chaff, hair, charcoal, a black snake, a donkey, a camel, a monkey, a black dog, or a cat; they see turbid water. By all these, one should meditate on the unfavorable sign of failure. There, the signs of success are seen in dreams: black food, drink, hair, chaff, and charcoal—these are seen under the guise of bad dreams as the dwarf-form (*vāmana*). They eat white food and drink, curd, milk, honey, and ghee. They see a grove of white and red lotuses. They see themselves climbing a mountain or a milk-tree laden with fruit, unsoiled and ascending. Such are the signs of success. Regarding "those whose mantras are successful," one should say to another: "May there be success! Whatever merit has been produced even momentarily, may that be dedicated to the multitude of all beings. By this merit, may they attain Buddhahood and remain for inconceivable eons, teaching the Dharma that leads to the state of immortality. May all those beings take hold of the multitude of beings."

The *Śāntikacakra* is completed. || o ||

3.2. The Section on the Characteristics of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga-lakṣaṇa*) The path of seeing is the direct realization of the four noble truths. It consists of fifteen moments of mind: the four moments of patience (*kṣānti*) and the eleven moments of knowledge (*jñāna*). These are as follows: 1. Patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).

2. Dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*). 3. Subsequent patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*anvayajñānakṣānti*). 4. Subsequent knowledge of suffering (*anvayajñāna*). 5. Patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaye dharmajñānakṣānti*). 6. Dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaye dharmajñāna*). 7. Subsequent patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of origin (*anvayajñānakṣānti*). 8. Subsequent knowledge of origin (*anvayajñāna*). 9. Patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodhe dharmajñānakṣānti*). 10. Dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodhe dharmajñāna*). 11. Subsequent patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*anvayajñānakṣānti*). 12. Subsequent knowledge of cessation (*anvayajñāna*). 13. Patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārge dharmajñānakṣānti*). 14. Dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārge dharmajñāna*). 15. Subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārge anvayajñāna*). Among these, the first moment is the supreme worldly dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), which serves as the immediate precursor to the path of seeing. From the second moment through the fifteenth, one enters the state of a "stream-enterer" (*srotāpanna*) and realizes the fruit of stream-entry. During this process, one abandons the afflictions associated with the desire realm and the higher realms, thereby attaining the vision of reality as it truly is. This is the path of seeing, characterized by the direct, non-conceptual intuition of the four noble truths.

Now, therefore, follows the ritual procedure for the cultivation of the wheel (*cakrabhāvanopacāra*) for the purpose of prosperity (*pauṣṭika*). One should visualize a thousand-spoked wheel drawn in yellow pigment with unguents (*aśleṣaka*). The practitioner of the wheel should contemplate the syllable *oṃ* situated in the center of the lotus, the syllable *ā* on the left, and the syllable *hūṃ* at the top. In the second [position] between the spokes, one should place: *oṃ dhare hūṃ dhare hūṃ dhare dhare dhare dhare*. In the second, in the middle of the support (*ādhāra*), one should place forty syllables: *hūṃ dhare svāhā | hūṃ vare ṭha ṭha | hūṃ dhare svāhā | hūṃ dhare svāhā hūṃ dhare svāhā hūṃ dhare svāhā*. First, this King of Four Syllables (*caturakṣararāja*) should be circumambulated; the syllable *oṃ* is first, and at its head is the syllable *hūṃ*. There, at the foot of the banner (*picapāda*), is the syllable *hūṃ*, and in the middle of the spokes are sixty syllables. One should say: "May there be prosperity, beginning with the syllable *oṃ* and ending with the sound *svāhā*. The wise mantra-holder should meditate upon these characteristics. If the characteristics are contrary, he should meditate with a clear mind upon the King of Syllables. For the sake of prosperity, the signs of success appear: the flame of the lamp increases, and the wheel is seen to be composed of the seven jewels. The mantra-holder sees his own body free from old age and disease, endowed with long life, strength, vigor, fortune, and power. He beholds the Great Rākṣasī, whose eyes are like great lotuses, terrifying with flashes of lightning and perspiration.
The cycle of meditations for enrichment is completed. || o ||
The Section on the Threefold Training (Śikṣātraya)

Now, therefore, I shall explain the wheel of malevolent rites (*abhicāracakra*) for the purpose of killing, withering, and eradicating, which pertains to the funeral ground rituals. This secret [teaching], whose instruction has been received and whose initiation has been obtained through the lineage of gurus—[this is for one who has received the teaching and initiation through a succession of masters].

In the secret place, one should place the thousand-spoked wheel; in the east, the vajra named Raudravijṛmbhana; in the south, the great vajra Trikoṇakavidhvaṃsanavikrama; in the west, the great vajra Vidyottamatejas; and in the north, the vajra named Merukuṃbha. To the north of the *kuliśa*, one should place the syllable *hrīḥ*—that is, *hrīkāra*, *hrīkāra*, *hrīkāra*, *hrīkāra*, *hrīraḥ*, and *hrīkāra*. In the center of the water, one should place the eight-spoked [wheel], the two skull-cups (*kapāla*) marked with the syllable *oṃ* (the two *oṃ*-skull-cups), and the *oṃ*-vajra. One should place the two skull-cups and the two *oṃ*-skull-cups in the center of the *ā* [spoke]. On the left side of the central needle, one should place the letter *pha*; there, on the right, one should place *phaṭaṅkāra*, *phaṭaṅkāra*, and *phaṭaṅkāra*. On the axle of the wheel, one should place the syllables *oṃ* and *hrī*. From all sides of the wheel, garlands of flames emerge. In the center of the *ā*, one should place a skull-cup filled with blood, and around it, the eight skull-cups.

On the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having fasted for a full day and night, one should have it painted by artists who are mantra-holders, free from attachment, and skilled in colors. It should be drawn upon a vessel made of a skull, or on a board of root-wood or fruit-wood, using the blood of a young boy mixed with fresh ink, on a black or dark-colored surface, or on a cloth hidden at a distance. Having offered a blood-oblation (*rudhirabali*) to the wheel, one should place the Great Vajra named *Raudravijṛmbhaṇa* in the east; in the south, the Great Vajra *Trailokyavidhvansanavikrama*; and in that same place, the four vajras: *Vajrārcis*, *Vajradṛṣṭi*, *Vajravāyu*, and *Vajrāsani*; as well as *Vajrolka*, *Vajravidyut*, *Vajrabāla*, and *Vajramegha*. Together with all these—whether they belong to a district, a kingdom, a province, a town, a city, or a village—the mantra-holder must remain with a mind that is wrathful and fierce toward the wheel. Why is this so? Because it was previously stated that it brings down [all things] consisting of vajra. What is it that is thus understood?

In the great city of Śūyāraka, on the excellent slopes of Mount Meru, not far from Jvālāvati, there was a king named Suvarṇabhujendra. [There were also] the Rākṣasīs Vidyujjvālākarālī and Svedāmbujamahārākṣī. Then that king, by means of the spells of those who propound supramundane knowledge, was meditated upon through a wheel of malevolent magic (*abhicāracakra*). He did not utter even a single word; Jambudvīpa was scorched by those terrifying and fearsome manifestations of the thunderbolt, those terrifying and fearsome manifestations of the destruction of the three worlds, those terrifying and fearsome manifestations of the splendor of supreme lightning, and those terrifying and fearsome manifestations of the pot of Mount Meru. They were enraged solely against the proponent in Jambudvīpa. Even the gods belonging to the Four Great Kings, as well as those dwelling in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven and the continent of Kuru—all those who dwell in their own abodes—came to the house of the one called Suvarṇabhujendra. "What do the enraged proponents say, O gods? [He asked]. The gods said to the proponent: "Welcome, Blessed One! What is it that you, who dwell in another state of existence, have said? All the seats have become made of diamond (*vajramaya*). Because of the terrifying fear of the diamond-wheel, the hosts of gods were destroyed. The carpenter-proponent said: "The diamond-wheels should be withdrawn. All the deities have been suffused with loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and are surrounded by happiness. Thus, having transcended the path of the sky, he passed over the previous wheel of malevolent magic.

The Great Vajra Ritual Procedure named *Vajravijṛmbhaṇa*: Having drawn [the mandala] with the previously mentioned colors and pigments, while burning red sandalwood, red *karavīra* flowers, and *guggulu* incense, one should fashion a triangular fire-pit (*agnikuṇḍa*) eight finger-breadths deep and three-cornered. Within an interval of eight finger-breadths from the pit, one should depict the Great King Dhṛtarāṣṭra with palms joined in reverence, adorned with pearl ornaments and having his hair loosened. While burning red *karavīra* flowers, red sandalwood, and *guggulu* incense, one should worship the thirty-two syllables within the interior of the thunderbolt (*kuliśa*). At the center of the wheel, one should place the *sūcī-mantra* ending in *phaṭ*. At the axle of the wheel, [one recites] *Oṃ Hrīḥ*. Having bound the previously mentioned fierce root-mudrā and visualized the left and right wheels, one should place [the mantra] three times upon the Great Vajra of Fierce Expansion in the east. One should place the Vajra-hook (*vajrāṅkuśa*) on the back of Kumāṇḍa. In the south, one should place the Great Vajra of the Destruction of the Three Worlds; at the tip of the middle needle, eight finger-breadths away, is a triangular fire-pit. Eight finger-breadths from that is the Great King Virūḍhaka, adorned with pearl ornaments, with palms joined and hair loosened. On his back, one should paint the Vajra-noose (*vajrapāśa*) with the previously mentioned colors. While visualizing the left wheel and binding the Lord’s root-mudrā, one should burn incense mixed with fragrant flowers, red sandalwood, mustard seeds, and resin, and place the syllable *Bhrūṃ* with the middle needle of the vajra. In the north, one should paint the Great Vajra named Merukumbha with the previously mentioned colors. At the tip of the middle needle, eight finger-breadths away, is a triangular fire-pit. Eight finger-breadths from that is the Great King Vaiśravaṇa, resting his left foot on the earth, adorned with pearl ornaments, with palms joined. Behind him, at the end of the vajra, is a mallet (*mudgara*) measuring eight finger-breadths. In the northeast corner, one should draw a platform (*vedikā*) of equal proportions; likewise in the southeast; likewise in the southwest and northwest. In the four corners, one should show four stakes (*sūla*) fixed in the ground. On each stake, one should depict three pretas standing on the earth—some appearing terrified, some showing flesh, some floating in blood, their bodies covered in ashes, holding clubs and skulls in their hands. In this same manner, one should paint the four directions with the previously mentioned black and red earth-colors. On all sides of the eastern platform, in the three places, one should show a heap of wood, a corpse being cremated, smoke, and fire; in the intervals between them, one should show jackals. In this same manner, one should show the great cremation grounds in the east, south, west, and north. In the center of the eastern goddess, one should paint eight skull-cups filled with beautiful liquid, with forms emitting garlands of flames. In the center of the southern platform, one should paint eight skull-cups filled with blood. In this same manner, it should be done in the west and north. Around the entire wheel, with garlands of flames emerging, one should paint two lamps placed in skull-cups for each of the four vajras. Each day, in three places around the wheel, one should paint great flesh situated on hides. One should offer an oblation (*bali*) mixed with sesame seeds, rice, mustard seeds, and beans, accompanied by the previously mentioned mudrās and mantras, in front of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. One should paint [an offering] filled with liquor and accompanied by fish and meat in front of Virūḍhaka. One should paint [an offering] mixed with parched grain, mustard seeds, honey, and water in front of Virūpākṣa. One should paint [an offering] mixed with *jambu* fruit and curds on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in front of Kuvera. With all these items arranged together, one should paint according to the previously mentioned procedure. One should surround [the area] with various colored flowers, red and black, and red sandalwood mixed with oil and mustard seeds. If the actual substances are unavailable, one should burn *guggulu* incense and, having offered it around the cloth painting of the wheel (*cakrapaṭa*), bind the root-mudrā and mantras of the Blessed Lady and apply them to the four vajras. Again, having performed the casting of the four [mantras], one should apply them to the four vajras along with the mantras. Again, having offered the previously mentioned perfumes, flowers, and oblations, one should conclude the rite and seal it firmly with lac.

The painting should be shown to men in a secluded, unconfused, and clean place—on a mountain peak, in a mountain cave, in an empty temple, in an uninhabited village, or on one’s own private grounds. It should be kept in a single location, a four-cubit square with four doors. That wise man, having smeared the ground with cow dung and prepared it well with properly joined timber, should have the house built so that sounds emerge from within. Having cleared the ground by four finger-breadths, it should again be leveled with the earth. With auspicious signs, well-secured door-fastenings, and door-mechanisms fixed with stakes, the house should be fully adorned. In the four corners, one should drive stakes of *khadira* wood measuring sixteen finger-breadths. With one-pointed concentration, the practitioner should place the syllable *hrīḥ* upon each stake. Taking hold of the stake in the northeast corner while facing south, the mantra-holders should bind it with the previously mentioned stake-seal (*kīlamudrā*) together with the mantra; after applying it seven times to the stake, it should be driven in quickly. At the southeast corner, having again bound the stake-seal and applied it seven times to the stake, it should be driven in quickly at the southeast corner. In this very same manner, it should be driven in at the southwest corner, and likewise applied at the northwest corner. The surrounding area of the house should be sprinkled with black and red various flowers while burning *guggulu* incense. At the four corners, the stake should be smeared with blood, mixed with water and mustard seeds. One should bathe the stake in lac-resin; having placed the hand over the stake, one should bathe it. Day after day, one should apply the ritual according to the Dharma.
% NB here the practitioner is a mantra-holder (mantradhara)

On the eighth or the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having fasted for a full day and night and entered the house, one should apply [the mudrā] seven times at each of the four corners to the Great Rākṣasī named Vidyujjvālākarālī-svedāmbuja. At the Brahma-position (the center), facing south, one should form the root-mudrā together with the mantra and visualize the Great Rākṣasī Vidyujjvālākarālī-svedāmbuja as having twelve heads and eighteen arms. Thereafter, one should place the painted cloth (*paṭa*) facing north. Having offered the previously mentioned perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings to the cloth according to the prescribed ritual, one should exit the house and perform the binding of the directions (*diśābandha*) together with its mantra and mudrā. One should apply the boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*), the enclosure-wall (*prākāra*), the cage-stake (*pañjarakīla*), and the earth-binding (*dharaṇibandha*) throughout the ten directions, joining each pair with their respective previously mentioned mantras and mudrās. Without confusion, one should offer flowers with the perfume-mudrā and mantra, and likewise the flower-mudrā, the food offering, the lamp, the incense, and the sacrificial oblation (*bali*) of fish, meat, and blood in all ten directions around the house. Then, having washed one's hands and feet and re-entered the house, one should face the cloth and, assuming the fierce stride (*raudravikrama*), the victory (*vijaya*), the support (*dhāraṇa*), and the great casting (*mahākṣepa*) mudrās, recite the mantra. First, one should apply the Great King Dhṛtarāṣṭra seven times to the east of the cloth. Assuming the great casting of the "Lightning-Stride" (*vidyuvikrānta-mahākṣepa*) together with the mantra, one should apply the Great King named Virūḍhaka seven times to the southern direction of the circle, while reciting the mantra of the "Great Ocean of Yawning" (*vijṛmbhana-mahāsamudra*). Assuming the great casting of the "Vajra-Garuḍa-Yawning" (*vajragaruḍavijṛmbhaṇa-mahākṣepa*) and reciting the mantra, one should apply the Great King named Virūpākṣa seven times to the western side of the circle. Assuming the great casting of the "Delighting in the Thirty-three Gods" (*trāyastriṃśavigalita-priyadeva-mahākṣepa*) and reciting the mantra, one should apply Kuvera seven times to the north. Facing these four Great Kings, one should recite the white "Yawning" (*svetavijṛmbhaṇa*) great mudrā and mantra, and apply them seven times behind the Great King Dhṛtarāṣṭra in the east. Then, thinking "I nail you down with the Buddha-eye; perform my task," one should assume the great mudrā of the "Lightning-Vajra" (*vidyuvajrī-mahāmudrā*), recite the mantra, and apply it seven times behind the Great King Virūḍhaka in the south. Thinking "I nail you down with the Buddha-victory-lightning; perform my task," one should assume the great mudrā of the "Great Yawning" (*mahāvijṛmbhaṇa-mahāmudrā*), recite the mantra, and apply it seven times behind the Great King Virūpākṣa in the west, thinking "perform my task. Assuming the six-faced great mudrā (*ṣaṭmukha-mahāmudrā*) and reciting the mantra, one should apply it seven times behind Kuvera in the north, thinking "perform my task."

In front of the cloth [painting], one should prepare four triangular fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*) with excellent characteristics and straight lines. In the first pit to the east, within the space of the cloth, there should be a vajra-hook made of clay or wood, resting upon a lotus. In the second pit, within the space of the cloth, there should be a vajra-spade made of wood or clay, resting upon a lotus. In the third pit, on the side within the space of the cloth, there should be a sword made of *tṛṇarāja* grass or red cloth, resting upon a lotus. In the fourth pit, within the space of the cloth, there should be a vajra-mallet made of *khadira* wood, resting upon a lotus. All of these should be dyed with lac.

A wrathful vajra (*krodhavajra*) made from cemetery wood, eight finger-breadths in length, five-pronged, mixed with *rājikā* mustard seeds, and placed within a skull-cup, should be positioned inside the eastern fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) between the practitioner and the deity. A vajra made of cemetery wood, six finger-breadths in length, five-pronged, with rays of light emanating forth, mixed with *rājikā* mustard seeds, and placed within a skull-cup, should be positioned inside the second fire-pit between the practitioner and the deity. A wrathful vajra made from *khadira* wood of the cemetery, eight finger-breadths in length, five-pronged, with rays of light emanating forth, accompanied by *rājikā* mustard seeds, and placed within a skull-cup, should be positioned inside the third fire-pit between the practitioner and the deity. All these thunderbolt-like implements (*kuliśa*) should be sprinkled with lac-dye.

In the first eastern pit (*kuṇḍa*), having performed the *raudravikramavijayoddhāraṇamahākṣepa* mudrā and recited the mantra, one should apply the Vajra and the Vajrāṅkuśa to the first eastern pit. One should gaze with a wrathful look. On the cloth (*paṭa*), having performed the *dhṛtarāṣṭravidyuvikrāntamahākṣepa* mudrā and recited the mantra, one should apply the Vajra and the Vajraparaśu to the second eastern pit. [On the cloth] to the south, the Great King Virūḍhaka should be applied with a wrathful look. Having performed the *vajragaruḍavijṛmbhanamahākṣepa* mudrā and recited the mantra, one should apply the Vajra and the Vajrapāśa to the third pit. On the cloth to the west, the Great King Virūpākṣa should be applied with a wrathful look. Having performed the *trayastrimśavigalitapriyadevamahākṣepa* mudrā and recited the mantra, one should apply the Vajra, the Vajramudgara, and the Varṇakuṇṭha to the western pit. On the cloth to the north, the Great King Kubera should be applied with a wrathful look. The mantra-holder, having offered the previously mentioned perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, garlands, and offerings, and having formed the root-mudrā of the Blessed Lady, should apply the Great Vajra-Krodhas to the four directions of the cloth. Having formed the seat-mudrā, one should apply them to the seats. Having produced the *vajrapadmagarbha*, remaining in the bound posture on a lotus seat, one should hold a wheel in the left hand; at the end, it is said to be like Meru, and the needle of existence (*bhavāmasūcī*) is first placed right there, and the needle on the right in that very manner. Having thus presented perfumes, flowers, incense, offerings, and lamps, together with the previously mentioned mantras and mudrās, one should subsequently recite the wheel (*cakra*) mantra one hundred thousand times day by day. If two hundred thousand or half a hundred thousand are recited, the kings of syllables (*akṣararāja*) proceed in reverse order. Having formed the six-faced mudrā and mantra together, one should recite the four Great Kings while looking at the king of syllables; one should strike again. Established in the station of the syllables, having observed, one should meditate on the wheel according to the previously mentioned rule. If it shows an obstacle within the range of the target, one should give one to each family: the Aśoka tree, the Mango tree, the Viṃvṛkṣa tree, and the Bhakṣa tree. The four obstacles belonging to the Cāturmahārājakāyikas are the protectors and non-protectors of the Blessed One. In this very manner, the Vidyādhara should complete one hundred thousand recitations. Having given perfumes, flowers, incense, and blood-offerings (*bali*)—including fish and meat—to the ten directions all around, one should give one *kulisa* (thunderbolt) to each *kulisa*; for each *kulisa*, one should give double the previously mentioned perfumes, flowers, incense, and offerings, and lamps. For each *kulisa*, one should perform great worship and honor, and likewise conclude the worship and honor of the perfected cloth. Having smeared the house with clay and cow-dung, one should offer the previously mentioned perfumes, flowers, incense, blood, fish, and meat to the ten directions all around the cloth. Day by day, one should meditate on the wheel until the dark fortnight days have arrived—that is, on the eighth or the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight. Having fasted for a day and night, the mantra-holder, having formed the six-faced mudrā together with the mantra and consecrated the cloth (*adhivāsya*), should contemplate it for one night. In the first eastern pit, having kindled a fire with funeral-pyre wood (*smasānakāṣṭha*), one should meditate on the wheel seven times. One should take seven oblations of black mustard seeds (*rājikā*) while grasping the name of the enemy; as soon as it is grasped, Indra’s thunderbolt falls, and he is likewise destroyed.
Note: Here, the practitioner is a *vidyādhara* or *mantradhara*.

Taking together all these—salt, a needle, poison, and the *phālguna* plant—and having fashioned an image of the enemy with them, one should contemplate it once upon the wheel-paṭa. Having made a likeness of that [enemy], one should take a vajra in one hand and take the name of that likeness; as soon as it is struck, the enemy of the king, the destroyer of cities, will perish instantly, just like one fallen into a vajra-fire.

If the practitioner desires to bring [the deceased] back, he should take a *vajra* previously offered and bathe it with milk mixed with mustard seeds. Reciting the root mudrā-mantra of the Blessed One together with the mantra-mudrā seven times, he should say: "O Blessed One, let such-and-such a person be at peace."

Among the four previously mentioned sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*), the first is the hook-pit (*aṅkuśakuṇḍa*); the second is the vajra-axe pit (*vajraparaśukuṇḍa*); likewise, the third is the vajra-noose pit (*vajrapāśakuṇḍa*); and the fourth is the vajra-mallet pit (*vajramudgara*). The gods belonging to the retinue of the Four Great Kings, having offered oblations in these four distinct pits, do not employ mind or mental factors, nor fire, nor fuel-sticks; neither with clarified butter, nor with oil, honey, or sugar; nor with sesame, nor with the three white substances. One should instead meditate solely upon the wheel-banner (*cakrapaṭa*). At the conclusion, taking mustard seeds, one should perform the meditation seven times before Dhṛtarāṣṭra at the front of the cloth-painting (*paṭa*). Having performed the meditation, one should offer an oblation, saying: "Kill so-and-so! There is no recovery from this; it must be thoroughly examined.

There is no reversal; the killing is final. Taking a black sesame seed (*kṛṣṇatila*), one should visualize it as a distinguishing [object]. Dried [seeds] are to be offered seven times into the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) located to the south of the *cakrapaṭa* and in front of the sprouted [seeds], while visualizing the *cakra* as previously described. Taking the sesame seeds, one should offer them. As soon as the name of the enemy is grasped, all enemies within a radius of seven hundred *yojanas* will be overcome. Furthermore, peace (*sānti*) shall prevail once again.

Having combined mustard seeds and the ashes of a cremation ground, and having ground them into a powder, one should fashion pills the size of jujube fruits (*kālāva*) soaked in blood. Taking that pill, one should perform seven recitations over the *cakrapaṭa* in a fire-pit before the great king Virūpākṣa at the western side of the cloth painting; one should offer oblations while grasping the name of the enemy. As soon as it is grasped, the enemies will be driven to the ends of the quarters. Furthermore, there is a method for bringing them back. One should consecrate a very auspicious seed with blood. Having taken those seeds when they are dry, one should perform seven recitations and offer oblations over the *cakra* in a fire-pit before Kubera at the northern side. The name of the enemy must be grasped; one should never do this with other people.

The Lokottaravādins establish a *liṅga* in place of a stūpa; they are proponents who intend to install [the image] in the place of a portrait-holding shrine within another temple, being envious of the monastery. Having observed their Lokottara-doctrine, one should apply the previously mentioned meditations on the four [sides] of the cloth, and at the end of the first day, having employed the Six-faced One and the Four Great Kings with their respective substances in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the Lokottara-vidyādhara must cause the Lokika-vādin to be killed.

% NB: The supramundane vidyādhara should slay those who establish *liṅgas* where stūpas once stood, consecrate other deities where [Buddhist] images were located, and speak with envy regarding monasteries, implying that they are mundane.

Now, therefore, follows the rite of killing (*māraṇa*) in four fire-pits (*agnikuṇḍa*). [It concerns] a Kṣatriya or a Kṣatriya woman, a king, a minister, or his wife; a Brāhmaṇa or a Brāhmaṇa woman; a Vaiśya or a Vaiśya woman; a Śūdra (*vṛṣala*) or a Śūdra woman; or any other various wicked person. One should employ these most fierce rites for all of them: threatening, beating, killing, driving away (*uccāṭana*), parching (*soṣaṇa*), cutting, splitting, pinning down (*kīlaṇa*), causing hatred (*dveṣaṇa*), suffocating, inducing vomiting, making blood flow, binding the senses, severing, causing flight, causing another to step over [the victim], and blocking the door. One should apply these through all of them as the most terrible rites.

First, for the killing of a Kṣatriya: take kuṇaṭī, guggulu, powdered human bone, and poison produced from the sea—these in equal parts. Having written the name of the king upon the heart of an image of that king adorned with all ornaments, one should kindle a fire in the previously mentioned *vajrāṅkuśa* hearth using golden wood. Standing over that image and becoming one with the *cakrapaṭa*, one should perform the oblation (*juhuyāt*). Vajrapāṇi must grasp the name of the enemy; as soon as it is grasped, the king, together with his inner court and his seven attendants, is killed. If the practitioner does not wish for the restoration of life, then one should take the ashes of the oblation and, mixed with guggulu, form pills. Again, having kindled a fire with golden wood, one should take seven pills and, having empowered the cloth (*paṭa*) seven times, write the name of the person upon each pill and offer them as an oblation. Vajrapāṇi must grasp the name of the enemy. As soon as it is grasped, the sound "Seven women are dead" is heard; then the restoration of life must be performed. Beginning with great worship and honor of the *cakrapaṭa*, one should bathe the four *vajras* with milk. The Four Great Kings should offer the previously mentioned perfumes, flowers, incense, garlands, and offerings, and with *goṣīrṣa-candana*, they should fashion an image of the king or the king’s consort. Having offered white flowers and fragrant incense to the Blessed One and bound the previously mentioned root-mudrā, one should apply it to that image seven times. Likewise, having empowered the four *vajras* and the *cakrapaṭa* seven times with the right hand, one should wipe the image [with the mantra] "May there be peace," saying "Oṃ mārjaya. Peace shall prevail. Taking one of those aforementioned pills, dividing it into seven parts, and having kindled a fire with the previously mentioned golden wood, one should empower the left side of the *cakrapaṭa* seven times and offer the oblation while grasping the name of the enemy. As soon as the name is grasped, they will die; then the restoration of life must be performed. One should offer an oblation mixed with rice, honey, and mustard seeds, and peace shall prevail.
% Note: Magic for use against kings.

Taking that ash, along with bone powder, snake-scented poison (*bhujaṅgagandhacaṃviṣa*), mongoose skin, cat fangs, the whole muskrat, as well as mice, and likewise the sinews of peacock, cow, donkey, and camel; the bones of a lizard and a *turaga*; *lāṅgalī*, *khajarīṭa*, female elephant, owl, and crow feathers—all these in equal parts combined with the previously mentioned ash—one should kindle a fire in a funeral-pot (*śmaśānaghaṭikā*) using funeral-wood and cook it over a fire of oil and clay until the cloth is finished. Having ground it in a skull-bowl (*kapāla*), one should fill four skull-bowls and, having kindled a fire in four pits (*kuṇḍa*) with funeral-wood, one should offer oblations seven times into each pit, mixing together in equal parts *mahānīla*, *ābhyaṅga*, tiger skin, elephant skin, and *rājabalā* skin. Taking the ash from the four pits while the embers have subsided, one should pour that ash into the oil remaining in the four skull-bowls and cover each bowl with a leaf of *sairṇṇa*. It should be placed before the cloth. At the end of seven days, on the seventh day, one should take the oil, mix it together, place it in an iron vessel, and add camphor, *kakkola*, and *trikaṭu*—these in equal parts—having made them into a dry powder. Having thrown this into the midst of that oil, one should seal it well. This is the "Enemy-Terrible Hatred-Oil," renowned throughout the three worlds; by it, the body is shattered like a diamond (*vajra*).

Having fashioned an effigy out of human bone, one should insert a single-finger-width vessel into the Brahma-hole [of the head]. Pouring a single drop of the previously mentioned oil into each pore, and having properly prepared the wheel with the previously mentioned *mayiṇa* cloth, one should take the name of the person who has been meditated upon as being of one essence and bury it in a cremation ground. Merely by being buried together, it causes great enmity; by digging it up, there is liberation.

Having fashioned an image out of *sittha* (wax) and having written his name upon its heart, one should take the aforementioned oil, fashion that image, and roast it. Having kindled a fire with *khadira* wood, one should heat that image slowly, twice over. Once heated together with the cloth consecrated by the mantra, he becomes seized by a great disease of consumption (*jārāroga*) and is rendered hostile. Upon its removal, there is liberation.

Having fashioned an image made of that [substance], one should place it in milk mixed with mustard seeds. Having formed the *mūlamudrā* of the Bhagavatī and applied the mantra seven times while saying, "May there be peace," one should offer a thunderbolt (*kulisa*), incense, flowers, and perfumes during the four watches of the day according to the previously mentioned rite. In this way, the gods of the Four Great Kings' realm shall likewise be liberated from suffering.

Taking earth from a cremation ground and mixing it with salt and mustard seeds, one should drink it. Then, having made an image of anyone toward whom one feels envy, one should prick the location of the vital organs with a needle heated to the color of fire while uttering the person's name. Having extracted the needle and placed it into the aforementioned hollow, one should kindle a fire with wood from a cremation ground and heat that image. As soon as the cloth painting (*paṭa*) is thus visualized—visualized together with [the victim]—he becomes a great instigator of enmity. To bring about a reversal, one should make an image of the same material, bind the root mudrā of the Blessed Lady as previously described, and offer the aforementioned perfumes, flowers, and incense along with the mantra to the *cakrapaṭa*. Likewise for the gods of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārajikāyika*). Then, having offered the aforementioned perfumes, flowers, and incense at the four vajra-crests (*kuliśa*), one should subsequently bind the Six-Faced Mudrā (*Ṣaṭmukhamudrā*) and, accompanied by the mantra, apply it to the back of that image, saying, "May there be peace for him. As soon as it is applied, great peace (*mahāśānti*) ensues.
One who hates this through unseen secret means becomes one whose hatred is directed toward [the victim's] tactile sensations.

Whether it be a king, a queen, a royal minister, a Brahmin, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra—one should anoint and smear the head or the limbs with the aforementioned oil. If the oil falls upon the feet or even just the back of a person while they are receiving flowers, great enmity arises; [however], there is a means for its reversal. One should prepare an offering to the Blessed Lady by combining all types of poison, milk, mustard seeds, equal amounts of ashes, and a portion of oil. Having kindled a fire with wood from the *udumbara* tree, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of milk and mustard seeds. All who are malicious will be liberated.

Having smeared a stake made of human bone measuring eight finger-breadths with the previously mentioned oil, and having written the name of the enemy upon it, one should take that name and strike it at a crossroads while visualizing the painted wheel-mantra. Merely by striking it, great enmity arises; by uprooting it, there is release.

One should take a stake made of *khadira* wood measuring eight finger-breadths (*aṣṭāṅgula*). Having written the person's name upon that stake and smeared it with the aforementioned oil, one should empower it and bury it at the place where the bed is located. As soon as it is buried, the bed shakes and that house becomes greatly agitated. By extracting it, there is release.

Taking four stakes made of human bone, each measuring six finger-breadths in length, one should draw four stakes [on the cloth], smear them with the previously mentioned oil, and having consecrated the cloth seven times, it should be struck at the four corners together with the image. As soon as it is struck, the *brahmarākṣasa* will be seen throughout the house; upon a great gasp, they will exit the house and flee. For a thousand years, humans will have no power over that house, and peace will prevail. This must be performed after careful examination.

Having kindled a fire with *madana* wood, one should offer one hundred and eight drops of the previously mentioned oil as an oblation (*juhuyāt*). Taking those ashes and mixing them with the aforementioned oil, one should recite the mantra over it and cast it into a pond or a well. Then, as soon as the water in that well or pond is touched, the people—including those of the city and the village—will meet their destruction through great mutual hatred. If the practitioner desires to bring about a reversal [of this effect], he should place the five jars filled with milk, as previously described, within the city. These should be situated in the four corners and the fifth in the central mandala of the *Svedāmbujamahārākṣasī-samayamaṇḍala*, which is presided over by Vidyujjvālākarālī. Having offered the previously mentioned perfumes, flowers, and garlands all around the mandala toward the ten directions, he should begin a grand worship and hospitality for seven days. He should cause the cry of "Victory! Victory! (*jayajaya*) to be proclaimed there for the Blessed Lady, starting from the worlds of *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*. Then, taking the milk from the five jars and casting it into the well or the pond, he should subsequently apply the six-faced mudrā along with the mantra seven times to the well or the pond. Afterwards, he should say, "The water has become nectar" (*amṛtodakam bhavati*). Thus, the one who caused the great enmity shall be liberated.

Regarding the previous wheel-paṭa, in the ritual called *Vajravijṛmbhana*, when a great vajra has been cast and the cloth is covered, one should paint an effigy of the enemy upon the wheel-paṭa using red pigment. Upon its body, at the station of Brahmā, one should display the three-pronged thunderbolt (*triśūla*) of the wrathful deity Vajrahūṃkāra as previously described; one should show the middle prong, place the syllable *hrīṃ* there, the syllable *phaṭ* on the left side, and likewise on the right side.
