Meditating seven times upon the wheel-paṭa with the thought, "I seize the enemy," one should wrap that paṭa in a triangle and bury it in a cremation ground or a spot of ground where a corpse has long been processed. As soon as it is buried, a king or a royal minister will die, and no peace shall prevail. This must be performed after thorough examination.
% NB: There is an injunction to carefully examine the situation where there is no counter-magic.

Having drawn an image of the enemy upon the previously mentioned cloth, one should display five needles—pierced from the thunderbolt (kuliśa) that has struck the head of the Great Vajra of Power which destroys the three worlds—at his head. On the middle needle, one should place the syllable *hrīḥ*; on the left side, the syllable *phaṭ*; and likewise on the right. Having encircled that cloth with a triangular border, one should take the name of the enemy and, having empowered it with the mantra *satya* and so forth, bury it at a [specific] location. As soon as it is buried, the king, or the king’s wife, or the king’s minister, will die; furthermore, peace is restored.

Having drawn an image of the enemy according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should display the great blazing vajra upon its head; [on the head] the form of a slain [victim], a three-pronged [vajra], and show the middle prong as the syllable *hrīṃ*, the syllable *phaṭ* on the left side, and likewise on the right side. Taking that cloth-painting and having folded it into a triangle, one should offer it. Having bound the root-mudrā, the cloth should be meditated upon seven times and buried in a cremation ground. The name of the enemy must be taken; as soon as it is taken, whether he be a king or a royal minister, he dies instantly, and peace is attained.

In that very place, having drawn an image of the enemy upon cloth of appropriate color, one with outstretched arms and loosened top-knot should display a great five-pronged vajra—shaped like a hammer—at the location of his head. On the middle prong, one should write the syllable *hrīḥ*; on its left side, the syllable *phaṭ*, and likewise on the right side. Having enclosed it within a triangle on that cloth, the cloth should be meditated upon seven times. Having bound the root mudrā and taken the name of the enemy, it should be buried in a cemetery. Merely by the act of burying it, any wicked king or royal minister shall die. Peace will ensue. This should be performed after careful observation; for each of the Four Great Kings, one should employ their respective specific mudrās and mantras. As soon as they are employed, they will swiftly accomplish their respective tasks. Om.

Henceforth, one should place *añjana*—specifically *srotāñjana*—in a skull-bowl before the cloth-painting (*paṭa*). One should meditate upon the wheel-cloth-painting (*cakrapaṭa*) one hundred and eight times and apply the collyrium to the eyes. One becomes invisible; while invisible, one will attain [the goal]. Taking one part from the portion of the *pūtiṣya* [constellation], and having consumed it, the hope of the Blessed Lady (*bhagavatī*) must be granted.

Having combined yellow orpiment and *gorocanā*, one should remain before a cloth painting (*paṭa*) placed upon a skull-cup, visualizing the eye of the *cakrapaṭa*. Having combined that substance with brown ghee, one should take the name [of the practitioner] during the four great *vajras* and likewise for the four great kings. Having offered the previously mentioned perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, garlands, and oblations to the *cakrapaṭa*, and without giving [the substance], having bound the root-mudrā, one should again visualize the *cakrapaṭa* ten million times. If it does not emit heat, one should bind the six-faced mudrā and, accompanied by the mantra, threaten the four great kings. If it still does not emit heat even after being visualized as before, one should take that substance and apply it to one's feet; having traveled three hundred *yojanas*, one returns once more. Having traveled seven hundred *yojanas* in one day, one returns on the second day.

Having fashioned an image of a Nāga maiden from *nāga*-wood and placed it before the *cakrapaṭa*, one should kindle a fire with *nāga*-wood. Into the previously mentioned *vajrāṅkuśa* hearth, one should offer seven hundred and eight oblations of *nāgakeśara* mixed with *guggulu*, while visualizing the cloth-painting (*paṭa*). Having smeared that image with the ashes of those oblations mixed with sour gruel (*kañjika*), one should bury it at the feet of the Blessed One. As soon as it is buried, all wicked *nāgas* are expelled, and all *nāga* maidens become submissive. If someone delivers a wicked poison to another by means of a wicked [agent], by extracting [the image], there is liberation for the disputant.
% Note: Opponent = the proponents (vādinaḥ)

Having fashioned an image of a deity from *devadāru* wood, one should stand before a painted mandala (*cakrapaṭa*). Having kindled a fire in the previously described *vajraparasu* pit using *devadāru* wood, one should offer oblations into it one hundred and eight times while visualizing the mandala, using mustard seeds mixed with poison. Taking those ashes and mixing them with sour gruel (*kañjika*), one should smear the image with it and bury it in a cremation ground. Having bound the six-faced mudrā and recited the mantra, one should bathe [the image] over it with water mixed with red sandalwood. The entire host of deities goes to destruction; this is the rite of expulsion (*uccāṭana*). Once [the image] is extracted, all the deities are restored to happiness.

Regarding the worship and honor of the great *cakrapaṭa* of the Bhagavatī, one should likewise [proceed] with the deities belonging to the Four Great Kings (*cāturmahārājakāyika*). Having offered the previously mentioned perfumes, incense, and flowers to each individual *kuliśa*, and subsequently having formed the root-mudrā (*mūlamudrā*) of the Bhagavatī, one should recite the mantra with a smiling face. Thus, the gods who were previously pinned down shall be conquered; all the gods will become subject to her control.

During the summer season, one should consecrate the *cakrapaṭa* (the wheel-painting) seven times. Then, standing on one leg upon a cloth that has not been seen before, one should gaze at the sun. At the moment when the sun appears as a single mark (*ekalakṣaṇa*), whatever object one desires is accomplished instantly. If tears fall from the eyes of the person being gazed upon, one should catch those tears with lotus petals and float them away. Having lit a lamp with sesame oil in a dry whirlpool, one places a skull-cup (*kapāla*) therein; then, taking the soot (*kajjala*) produced above the skull-cup, one places it in a leaf of the *asvattha* tree. Again, having consecrated the *cakrapaṭa* seven times, one should meditate for a single moment or a *muhūrta* on the state of being absorbed (*tanmayī*) while gazing at the solar disc (*ravimaṇḍala*) unseen. Standing on one leg, the mantra-holder should contemplate the oneness of the sun in the sky. By the mere thought of it, success (*siddhi*) occurs; the stars become visible in the sky. As before, having personally observed a star, one should perform the consecration (*adhivāsana*). Having bound the great mudrā of the Six-Faced One (*Ṣaṇmukha-mahāmudrā*), one lives for a thousand years, freed from old age, disease, and death, protected by the stars day and night. The aforementioned soot should be applied to both eyes in all places of subjugation (*vaśya*). Having ascended a mountain peak or a cremation ground, one should fashion an image of the enemy using charcoal mixed with golden ochre. Standing facing the east, pressing the heart-center with the left foot, and gazing at the sun, one should consecrate the *cakrapaṭa* seven times. One should strike the image of the enemy in the mouth with mustard seeds. By the mere act of striking, the enemy dies. To bring him back to life, one should draw that image in front of the *cakrapaṭa*. Having filled three handfuls of milk mixed with mustard seeds, one should wash that image with the previously mentioned perfumes, flowers, incense, and the *cakracakra* (wheel-circle), together with the *kulisa-kulisa* (thunderbolt-thunderbolt) root mudrā and mantra of the Blessed Lady. Facing the sun, one should say: "May such-and-such a person attain peace."
Henceforth, what are the *gulikās*?

Taking the corpse of a child who died in the womb or as an infant, one should place it before a cloth painting (*paṭa*). Having kindled a fire in four sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) with funeral-wood (*smasānakāṣṭha*), one should offer oblations (*juhuyāt*) one hundred and eight times. When the rite is completed, one should take the ashes from the four pits, mix them with *guggulu* resin, and form them into pills. For the purposes of killing (*māraṇa*), parching (*soṣaṇa*), driving away (*ucāṭana*), or causing enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*), they should be buried at every location; merely by being buried together, those subjected to the ritual act go to their destruction. That house, that wall, that enclosure, and that village [are destroyed]; for their restoration, they must be dug up, and then there is liberation.

Having made an image of the enemy twenty-four finger-breadths in size, one should meditate upon the cloth painting during the dark fortnight while roaming at night; one pill should be buried in its belly, and as soon as it is buried, the person is seized by a great disease; by extracting it, there is liberation.

Having taken seven *gulikā* pills, they should be buried in the place of the Mother (*mātṛsthāna*). As soon as they are buried together, all enemies within a radius of seven hundred *yojanas* will go toward the inner apartments with great panting; by digging them up, there is liberation.

Note: Taking one pill from the previously mentioned *mātṛsthāna* pills, one should visualize the wheel-paṭa eight hundred times and bury it before Vināyaka; it should be buried before Vināyaka. Having formed the six-faced mudrā, one should employ it for Vināyaka together with the mantra. As soon as it is employed, all the enemies within one's own group will die, and thereafter there will be peace.

Having taken the three previously mentioned pills, one should consecrate them one hundred and eight times over the cloth and bury them in the house of Mahādeva. Having formed the six-faced mudrā along with the mantra, one should employ it for Mahādeva. As soon as it is employed together [with him], his enemies will perish upon entering his retinue, and peace will prevail.

[Note: At the house of Mahādeva (the Gaṇas being Śaivas?), one should place the previously mentioned pill—one pill—into the mouth of Mahākāla while reciting the six-faced mudrā along with the mantra. Having directed it toward the ten directions, one should say, "Seize so-and-so! As soon as this is said, he causes [the victim] to be seized by a great fever. By removing the pill from his mouth, there is release.]
% NB: Regarding Mahākāla:

having taken the three previously mentioned pills, one should visualize them seven times over a painted image of the wheel (*cakrapaṭa*) and bury them in the house of the sun. As soon as they are buried together, one should seize the name of the enemy; then, having formed the root-mudrā of the Blessed Lady, one should apply it to him. All enemies will die, and peace will prevail.

At the time of crossing a river, one should throw seven pills into the water; as soon as they are thrown, within a range of a hundred *yojanas* from the riverbank, no crocodiles, *kumbhīras*, *makaras*, frogs, turtles, one-faced or two-faced water-snakes, nor any species of wicked aquatic creatures, shall have power over it.

Taking seven of the previously mentioned pills, one should place them before the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) while meditating on the painting for seven days. Taking one pill from among them, it should be buried under a fruit-bearing tree; as soon as it is buried, [the tree] becomes fruitless. When it is extracted, it becomes endowed with fruit.
Taking eight pills together, one should bury them in the middle of a field; as the branch of Indra’s throne falls, so should they be extracted.

By taking five *gulikās* together and burying them at once in the place where the serpent-offering (*nāgabalisthāna*) is made, the knots break apart as soon as they are buried; having extracted them, there is liberation.
Taking four [of these] as a single pellet, one should bury it in an elephant stable; at the very moment it is buried, the elephant dies.
Note: Contrary to [the case of] elephant stables, if one takes three pellets together and buries them in a horse stable, the horses will die.
% NB: Contrary to [the practice in] horse-stables, one should take a second pill at one time and bury it in the middle of a picture-gallery; as soon as it is buried, a line of wealth appears.
Taking one pill, one should bury it at the place where one lies down; by the mere act of burying it, sleep occurs. By digging it up, one awakens.

On the previously mentioned *siddhapaṭa*, behind the four Great Kings (*mahārāja*) and the attendant deities, there are four installations (*nyāsa*). I shall describe the ritual service (*upacāra*) first for Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and then the ritual service for Vajrāṅkuśa. Having offered the previously mentioned perfumes, flowers, incense, and food offerings to the *siddhapaṭa*, one should bind the root mudrā, recite the mantra, and contemplate: "I shall accomplish the *aṅkuśavajra*. Thereafter, having offered a handful of flowers to the Blessed Lady, one should visualize the wheel-paṭa alone on the right side. With mustard seeds, one should accomplish the *vajramudgara* behind Dhṛtarāṣṭra; thus one should accomplish these in the four locations. Each should be visualized ten million times (*nayuta*), and one should strike with mustard seeds. As soon as they are struck—[behind Dhṛtarāṣṭra]—tears fall from his eyes. Having seen this, the practitioner should offer the aforementioned perfumes, flowers, incense, garlands, and food, as well as peacock-ghee mixed with beans and *kuśa* grass, and even twice that amount. Then, having washed his hands and feet, and having anointed his hands with perfume, he releases his hands. Having formed the *cakravikramacakra* or the *mahākṣepa* mudrā and recited the mantra, he should apply it to the four thunderbolts (*kuliśa*). Then the four Great Kings, residing in all the maṇḍalas, will bring about accomplishment (*siddhi*).

The previously described *cakrapaṭa* should be installed in secret at the location of the asura-cavern according to the prescribed rite; one should offer the aforementioned perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, garlands, and oblations. One should meditate upon the *cakrapaṭa* for seven days. If [the deity] does not arrive on the eighth day, one should employ the "Great Summoning of the Thirty-three Beloved Deities" together with the mantra into the asura-cavern. As soon as it is employed, an asura maiden will arrive, seize the practitioner, and lead him into the asura-cavern. One must not harbor any desire for the mortal world.

Having installed the wheel-paṭa in the location of the treasure according to the previously stated procedure, one should offer perfumes, flowers, incense, food offerings, lamps, garlands, and other presents. Having placed these all around the paṭa together with the previously mentioned mudrās and mantras, one should meditate upon the wheel-paṭa for one night. Having applied the face-seal (mukhamudrā) at the locations of the treasures, one should leave it there; as soon as it has been installed, the treasure becomes visible and may be taken and enjoyed at will.

Delighting in giving toward the Three Jewels, with a mind of loving-kindness and compassion, and delighting in the construction of images, the copying, reading, recitation, and worship of the True Dharma—having abandoned envy, stinginess, malice, and defilement—the mantra-holder should fulfill the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*). Just as the lotus born from mud remains unsullied by the sun, the moon, or the sky, so too can the wise mantra-holder, while aspiring for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, fulfill this practice.
[The Procedure for the Sadhana of Vajrāṅkuśa begins.]

On the previously described mandala-cloth (*cakrapaṭa*), in the first of the four fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*) located in the east, one should fashion a golden *vajrāṅkuśa* (thunderbolt-hook) and a *viśvavajra* (double thunderbolt), each measuring one cubit in length. With well-proportioned handles made of gold, eight-finger-width hooks, and eight-finger-width bases, one should place the syllable *ka* at the tip of the hook in the position of the hook-base. [5] One should place the syllable *ā* in the center; right there, at the root-joint of the hook, one should place the syllable *śī*. At the tip of the handle, one should place a five-pronged *vajra*; in the middle prong of the wrathful *vajra*, the syllable *bhrūṃ*; and in that same [prong], on the second prong, one should place the syllable *hrīḥ*. In that same [prong], on the third prong, one should place the syllable *oṃ*; and in that same [prong], on the fourth prong, one should place the syllable *āḥ*. On the middle joint of the prongs pointing toward the four directions, one should place the syllable *hūṃ*; on the second prong, the syllable *hūṃ*; on the third prong, likewise the syllable *hūṃ*; and on the fourth prong, the syllable *hūṃ*. One should place a *vajra* at the three positions of the handles, measuring four finger-widths. One should place a three-pronged *vajra* measuring four finger-widths at the end of the eight-finger-width handle, positioning it right there in the middle of the handle. Right there in the middle of the handle, one should place a *viśvavajra*. Having completed this with all these [syllables] at intervals of one finger-width, one should bathe the *vajrāṅkuśa* with water mixed with red sandalwood and ghee. Having placed it in the secret location according to the previously mentioned procedure for the cloth of accomplishment (*siddhipaṭa*), and having offered the previously mentioned perfumes, flowers, and incense, one should place the *vajrāṅkuśa* before the cloth with leaves of the *asvattha* tree. Again, having offered perfumes, flowers, and incense, and having formed the root-mudrā of the Blessed Lady, one should recite the mantra and display the mudrā and mantra for each of the twelve spokes. Furthermore, one should empower the eighteen weapons together with the mudrās and mantras. Afterwards, having offered white *hiṅgu*, white sandalwood, white food-offerings (*naivedya*), clarified butter, lamps, and a *vajra*, and likewise having offered to the Blessed Lady’s *vajrāṅkuśa*, one should subsequently accomplish the *vajrāṅkuśa*. Belonging to the three families, one should apply oneself to the four great mudrās.
% NB three *kula*s, four "great" *mudrā*s (which are not the same, but as given below)

First, having bound the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of the Six-Faced One and recited the mantra, one should place it on the forehead seven times. Second, having bound the White Vajra-Yawn Great Seal and recited the mantra, one should remain at the tip of the right ear for seven repetitions. Third, having bound the Vajra-Fist Great Seal and recited the mantra, one should apply it seven times to the region of the back of the head. Fourth, having bound the seal and recited the mantra, one should place it at the tip of the left ear for seven times. One should visualize the previously mentioned Vajra-Hook (vajrāṅkuśa) cloth-painting (cakrapaṭa) alone and strike it with mustard seeds. One should visualize the Vajra-Hook in this very manner ten million times (*nayuta*). If the painting does not rise on a single day, then having bound the Six-Faced Seal of the Vajra-Hook and recited the mantra, one should strike each of the Four Great Kings (*cāturmahārāja*) once with a mustard seed. At the mere moment of being struck, the Vajra-Hook emerges garlanded with flames. Both [the practitioner and the deity] stand; the boon is accomplished. Having offered to the accomplished painting (*siddhapaṭa*) the aforementioned perfumes, flowers, incense, food offerings, lamps, and garlands with great and noble devotion, there is the previously mentioned "Vajra-Yawn" named Great Vajra, the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of all deities. To the south is the meditative absorption named "Destroyer of the Three Worlds. To the west is the meditative absorption named "Non-Abandonment of All Deity-Vidyās through Radiance. To the north is the meditative absorption named "The Meru-Pitcher," the Great Vajra that transcends the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*trāyastriṃśadbhavana*). With these four meditative absorptions, one should offer the aforementioned perfumes, flowers, and incense, visualizing each meditative absorption individually. Having given double or triple the aforementioned perfumes, flowers, and incense to the gods of the Realm of the Four Great Kings (*cāturmahārājakāyika*), and then having focused the mind on their departure together, one should wrap the accomplished painting tightly. That painting should be placed in a casket made from the shoots of the *nyagrodha* tree, wrapped in a well-marked red cloth. The previously accomplished painting should be kept in a single location by those who know the pledges (*samaya*) and wear the garments of existence, while the mantra-holder, recollecting the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, offers a handful of flowers and pays homage. By means of the Blessed Lady, the Buddha-painting, and the hook held in the armpit, the Vidyādhara enters the city of the Vidyādharas invisibly. Many hundreds of thousands of millions of Vidyādharas have arrived, and the Lord of Vidyādharas circumambulates him. With palms joined, he falls at the feet of the Lord of Vidyādharas. For that Lord of Vidyādharas, the Vidyādhara city possesses a lion-throne made of the seven jewels, and the Vajra-Hook is desired by the Vidyādhara maidens. The Lord of Vidyādharas has a thousand eyes, a thousand arms, is adorned with various ornaments, is garlanded with flames, and his body is composed of the seven jewels. Having conquered the senses, the Vajra-Hook is the accomplished Lord of Vidyādharas. Beginning with worship and honor for the Lord of Vidyādharas, the Vajra-Hook, many hundreds of thousands of millions of Vidyādharas will perform worship. The Vidyādhara maidens will do so: some with censers of jewels in their hands, some with censers of gold, some with censers of *karketana*, some with censers of great *karketana*, some with censers of sapphire (*indranīla*), some with censers of great sapphire, some with powdered *goṣīrṣa* sandalwood, some with powdered black aloe-wood (*kṛṣṇāguru*), some with powdered *vāyasantuṇḍa* aloe-wood, some with the powder of divine Gandharvas, and some with powders of many various kinds of fragrances. Some hold garlands of *parvata-kokila* flowers, some hold garlands of *māndārava* flowers. Many hundreds of thousands of millions of Vidyādhara maidens, with hundreds of various divine fragrant flowers, powders, jewels, and lamps burning, and with various musical instruments, drums, songs, and charming sounds, with various umbrellas, banners, and flags—these hundreds of thousands of millions of Vidyādharas will perform worship for the Lord of Vidyādharas, the Vajra-Hook, as he sits upon the lion-throne, and they will cry out "Well done! (*sādhukāra*).
% NB may become a chief of the *vidyādharas*, as well as a female *vidyādhara* % Note the peculiar break in continuity!

"Excellent, excellent, O Lord of Vidyādharas! Having paid homage, he stood to one side. Then the former sovereign of the Vidyādhara city, named Vidyātkṛtapaṭa, spoke to the Vidyādhara: "O Lord of Vidyādharas, in this Vidyādhara city there is the sublime nectar of the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañcakāmaguṇa*). O Vidyādhara Lord Vajrāṅkuśa, listen to what I have to say: through my lordship over the city of the Vidyādharas, I have experienced the strands of sensual pleasure throughout many births; I have enjoyed sovereignty like that of the kings Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha, as well as the state of Brahmā and Indra. Furthermore, for many hundreds of thousands of millions of eons, I have endured the fierce and bitter torments of the five destinies—among animals and hungry ghosts—experiencing inconceivable sufferings within saṃsāra. Having heard this, the lords of the Vidyādhara cities, Bodhisattvas who had attained the stage of *Ekabhūmi*, along with hundreds of thousands of millions of Vidyādharas and hundreds of thousands of millions of Vidyādhara maidens, all addressed him with a single, harmonious voice: "In this very life, you are the immortal one, consecrated with jewels, the transcendent speaker, the Vidyādhara Lord Vajrāṅkuśa! You are established in the Vidyādhara city. Seeing the Vidyādhara maidens playing and sporting amidst the five strands of sensual pleasure, and seeing that city, the Vidyādhara Lord Vajrāṅkuśa reflected: "It is unstable, a mere vessel for urine and excrement, a heap of worms, a dwelling place of bile, phlegm, and wind—a burden of filth. Once dead, it quickly becomes like wood in the cremation ground. Hearing this, the hundreds of thousands of millions of Vidyādharas spoke thus to the one who was rejoicing in his lordship over the Vidyādhara city:

The five sense objects appear as great beings (mahāsattvas) grasped by the vajrāṅkuśa. In a body possessing the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and a form endowed with the eighty minor characteristics, some call him the Tathāgata Śākyamuni; some call him the Tathāgata Dundubhisvara; some call him the Tathāgata Akṣobhya; and some call him the Tathāgata Amitābha. Having understood this, the Vidyādharas, having first placed it within a Nyagrodha-wooden casket, bring forth the cloth-painting (paṭa). The Vidyādhara, having established the cloth-painting within a palace made of the seven jewels in the center of the city, offers sovereignty over the city to the Vidyādharas. With hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of various Vidyādharas, amidst the sounds of various musical instruments and songs, and offering various perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, parasols, banners, and flags, he gives many jewel-filled offerings to the cloth-painting. Having circumambulated it three times, they are filled with great joy, satisfied, elated, and cheerful, and they perform a sublime and grand worship.

Immediately after the mention of the ancient Tathāgata Dundubhisvara, the Vidyādharendra Vajrāṅkuśa—having uttered the mantra that forms the Great Projection (*mahākṣepa*) which causes the thirty-three [gods] to dissolve their dear speech—was empowered by the Great Vajra named Vajravijṛmbhaṇa in the east. As soon as he was thus empowered, the Vidyādhara, dwelling in the city, became invisible; with his loincloth bound and holding a vajrāṅkuśa in his hand, he appeared before the four mudrā-maṇḍalas in the cultivation of the wheel of the four samādhis, as a Vidyādhara accomplished in the *sādhana* of the vajrāṅkuśa.
The procedure for the practice of the Vajrāṅkuśa, within the *Vidyottama-mahāmantra-uttamapiṇḍaka*, is completed. O ||
The ritual procedure for the sādhanā of Vajrāṅkuśa concludes.
The ritual procedure for the sādhanā of Vajraparaśu begins.

Now, therefore, I shall explain the ritual procedure for the practice (*sādhana*) of the Vajra-axe (*vajraparaśu*) on the aforementioned accomplished cloth-painting (*siddhapaṭa*). In a previously unoccupied place, having consecrated the house and smeared it with clay, one should, on the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, remain fasting for a day and night. Accompanied by a mantra-holder, one should offer perfumes, flowers, incense, food offerings, lamps, garlands, and other gifts, while assigning the respective mantras and mudrās to the ten directions. Then, one should perform the binding of the directions, the enclosure wall, the cage, the ritual stake (*kīla*), and the binding of the earth. Having properly consecrated one's own feet according to their respective rites, one should prepare a Vajra-axe made of "flower-metal" (*puṣpaloha*), measuring twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length, with a blade eight finger-breadths wide. On that very axe, there should be a long Vajra of eight finger-breadths; at the tip of the handle, there should be a three-pronged wrathful Vajra (*krodhavajra*) situated upon a lotus. The handle of the axe should be well-proportioned with the characteristics of a staff, and the Vajra-stake (*vajrakīla*) should be one finger-breadth thick. With all these parts, the placement (*nyāsa*) of *Oṃ Āḥ Hrīḥ* is to be performed upon the tongue of the axe. One should place the syllable *Vaṃ* on the chest at the tip of the handle, the syllable *Sṛ* on the middle prong, and the syllable *Sa* on the second prong. One should place the syllable *Kā* on the Vajra-stake. When finished, one should bathe the Vajra-axe with white sandalwood water mixed with fragrant flowers, and again smear the Vajra-axe with fragrant camphor. Having placed it in a casket of *vibhītaka* wood, one should set it before the aforementioned accomplished cloth-painting. After offering perfumes, flowers, and incense to the cloth-painting, one should form the four general mudrās of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*) and likewise the three families, recite the mantra, and station oneself in the four directions. Likewise, after forming the root mudrā of the Blessed Lady (*Bhagavatī*) and reciting the mantra, one should station the four Vajras. Then, one should form the mudrā of the Blessed Lady’s Vajra-axe and contemplate: "I shall accomplish the severing of the heads of all malevolent beings."

Furthermore, having offered perfumes, flowers, and incense to the *siddhapaṭa*, one should meditate on the perfected cloth (*siddhapaṭa*) alone. Then, while meditating with mustard seeds, one should strike the previously mentioned casket (*samudgaka*). In this very manner, one should perform the meditation for one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*). Now, if it becomes warm at the hundred-thousandth repetition, one should take yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), *asurī*, and *guggulu* mixed together, and fashion an image of Dhṛtarāṣṭra twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in size, adorned with all ornaments. Having placed the previously mentioned *vajrāṅkuśa* (vajra-hook) staff-vajra in front of the practitioner, facing the cloth, one should place there the powder of *kunaṭī* and *kūrpāsana* mixed with *sikṣaka*. Then, having fashioned an image of Virūḍhaka twelve finger-breadths in size, adorned with all ornaments, one should place the *vajraparaśu* (vajra-axe) staff-vajra in front of the practitioner, facing the cloth. Next, having fashioned an image of Virūpākṣa twelve finger-breadths in size, adorned with all ornaments, using the dung of a tawny cow (*kapilāgomaya*) mixed with earth from both banks of a river flowing to the ocean and *asurī-kagavita*, one should place the previously mentioned *vajrapāśa* (vajra-noose), along with the powder of nine types of resin (*phaṇita*) and jewels, in the northern part of the *kuṇḍa* in front of the practitioner. Then, having fashioned an image of Kubera twelve finger-breadths in size, adorned with all ornaments, using the powder of black *kapittha* fruit and *māṣa* beans mixed with curd-whey, one should place the previously mentioned *vajramudgara* (vajra-hammer) in the *kuṇḍa* in front of the practitioner. The placement of the heart-mantras (*hṛdaya-nyāsa*) is as follows: for sovereignty over the continent of Pūrvavideha, the placement is *dhruṃ* on the back; for sovereignty over Jambūdvīpa, the placement is *dhraiḥ*; for sovereignty over Aparagodānīya, the placement is *ṣṭreḥ*; for sovereignty over Uttarakuru, the placement is *pro*. With these placements, which are situated upon lotuses, one should apply the placement using *gorocanā* (cow-gallstone) according to whichever deity was specified. At that moment, the previously mentioned *vajraparaśu* casket will become warm. As long as it remains standing, the mantra-holder should maintain it. If the *vajraparaśu* stands on both sides, one should observe the two-fold nature of the action—whether it is possible or impossible. If it is possible, having examined it, one should employ the perfected rites. Afterwards, the gods of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*) appear. Having offered double the previously mentioned perfumes, flowers, incense, garlands, and offerings to the perfected cloth, one should take the four images mentioned before and place them in their respective directions and positions. If the rite is not to be successful, one should begin the fierce ritual (*raudrakarma*). Having bound the four great mudrās and recited the mantra, one should project oneself seven times toward each of the four directions. After that, having bound the "Great Casting of the Thirty-three Gods" (*Trayastriṃśavigalitamahākṣepa*) and recited the mantra with wrath, one should project the images of the gods of the Four Great Kings onto the backs [of the figures]. Then, one should meditate on the perfected cloth alone and strike each of the four images seven times with mustard seeds. If, day after day, they do not rise up despite thirty million recitations, one should begin the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) with the *vajraparaśu* in the four *kuṇḍas*. One should take one's own blood in three vessels placed in four skull-bowls (*kapāla*). There, having mixed the blood, one should kindle a fire in the eastern *kuṇḍa* circle with *karavīra* wood in front of the cloth of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Meditating on the perfected cloth, one should offer ten thousand oblations (*ayuta*) of mustard seeds mixed with the aforementioned blood. Having cut that image into pieces, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Great King, appears with his body ablaze. He says: "What shall I do? O practitioner, choose a boon! What must I do? The practitioner, visualizing the *vajraparaśu*, should bind that king with the great noose of the *vajrāsaṃkalā* mudrā. When he asks, "What must I do?", the practitioner, while the fire-ritual in the four *kuṇḍas* is still unfinished, should say: "At this very moment, the *vajraparaśu* emerges with a garland of flames; it stands on both sides. (As previously noted, one should observe the two-fold nature of the action—whether it is possible or impossible. If it is possible, having examined it, one should employ the perfected rites. Afterwards, the gods of the Four Great Kings appear. Having offered double the previously mentioned perfumes, flowers, incense, and garlands to the perfected cloth, one should take the four images mentioned before and place them in their respective directions and positions. If the rite is not to be successful, one should begin the fierce ritual. Having bound the four great mudrās and recited the mantra, one should project oneself seven times toward each of the four directions. After that, having bound the "Great Casting of the Thirty-three Gods" and recited the mantra with wrath, one should project the images of the gods of the Four Great Kings onto the backs. Then, one should meditate on the perfected cloth alone and strike each of the four images seven times with mustard seeds.)

Second, regarding Virūḍhaka: within the space of the *siddhapaṭa*, one should kindle a fire with *apāmārga* fuel-sticks. Having cut an effigy made of blood and mustard seeds placed in the previously mentioned skull-cup, one should offer it mixed with blood and mustard seeds into the *siddhapaṭa*, focusing the mind on it as one, and perform one hundred thousand (*nayuta*) oblations. At that very moment, the great king Virūḍhaka will arrive and say, "O practitioner, why are you angry? Choose a boon! The practitioner should say, "O Blessed One, I have been burnt, rendered fruitless, and have gone to ruin; what must I do now? Then the Vidyādhara should act. The deities, having formed the Great Seal of the Vajra-Noose (*vajrapāśamahāmudrā*), should recite the mantra and bind that king with the fivefold noose. Then, the Vajra-Axe situated in the eastern earth remains eight finger-breadths in the intermediate space above both [the king and the practitioner]. Furthermore, having washed one's hands and feet, one should offer perfumes, flowers, and incense to the Blessed Lady upon the *siddhapaṭa*, as well as to the Vajra-Axe.
Note: [This concerns] the river flowing toward the ocean.
Furthermore, in this ritual, one's own blood is used in four skull-cup vessels (*kapālabhājana*).
Then Dhṛtarāṣṭra appears and asks, "What is it? The same occurs with Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, and Kuvera. [The deity] Vajraparaśu becomes possessed (*āviṣṭa*) and trembles. (28v5)

In the third [section], within the cloth-painting of Virūpākṣa, one should kindle a fire drawn from the portions of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍabhāga*). Having placed the previously mentioned skull-cup (*kapāla*) there, one should offer oblations (*juhuyāt*) into it, having consecrated the perfected cloth-painting with a mixture of blood and mustard seeds. At that very moment, the great king Virūḍhaka will arrive and say: "What shall you do? O practitioner, choose a boon! O practitioner, what must I do? The deities say: "The mantra-holder, having bound the great mudrā of the Vajrāmoghapāśa and recited the mantra, should bind [the deity] with the five-fold noose. Virūpākṣa, at that very instant, stands eight finger-widths in the air in front; the Vajra-axe likewise stands sixteen finger-widths in the air, both remaining in the space before him. Having washed his hands and feet and offered the previously mentioned perfumes, flowers, and incense to the Blessed Lady, the perfected cloth-painting [is thus empowered]. Likewise, the gods belonging to the retinue of the Four Great Kings [are present].

In the fourth [section], within the space of the *siddhapaṭa* of Kuvera, one should kindle a fire in a pit using *devadāru* wood. Standing before an image of him, one should take blood and mustard seeds placed in the skull-cup as previously described, mix them together, and unify them with the *siddhapaṭa*. One should offer one hundred and eight oblations. As soon as he is struck by Vajrapāṇi, the great king Kuvera will cry out, "Alas! Alas! What misery! My body is being burned! O Vidyādhara, what shall I do? Ask a boon, O practitioner! The practitioner should wash the hands of the king, form the great mudrā of the distorted flame, and recite the mantra. He should bind the king of the Yakṣas with the five-fold noose. As soon as he is bound, he stands sixteen finger-breadths above the sky at both ends. Again, a vajra-axe, two finger-breadths in measure, stands in the sky at both ends. Possessed, he wanders about. The practitioner should direct the vajra-axe to a single spot. As soon as it is sent, it severs his head and quickly returns. At the original place where he stood, the practitioner's vajra-axe remains smeared with blood. Having seen the practitioner’s vajra-axe, he should wash his hands and feet, smear his hands with perfume, fill them with a handful of flowers, and present a jewel-casket upon a stūpa of the *Sarvabuddhasamāyoga*. After that, having formed the root-mudrā of the Blessed Lady and recited the mantra, he should empower the *kuliśa-kuliśa* on the *siddhapaṭa* of the Blessed Lady, as well as the gods of the Four Great Kings.
A certain mudrā called *sarvabuddhasamāyogastūparatnakaraṇḍaka*!

Furthermore, through further manipulations of the *vajraparaśu*, [the weapon] is hurled into the sky; it severs heads and is dispatched against enemies, such as kings and the various social classes (*varṇa*).

Having offered the previously mentioned perfumes, flowers, and incense according to the ritual procedure, one should then take the perfected *vajraparaśu* (adamantine axe) and bathe it with fragrant water mixed with mustard seeds. Having fumigated it with *agaru* (aloe wood), one should grind equal parts of *śīta*, *harītakī*, *kapūra*, *kola*, and *lavaṅga*. Having gone to a crossroads and anointed the perfected *vajraparaśu*, one should wrap it in a blue cloth and stand before the perfected painting (*siddhapaṭa*). During the dark fortnight, for the purpose of a malevolent rite (*mārakarma*), one should visualize the enemy, uttering his name, and meditate upon the perfected painting seven times. Then, taking the *vajraparaśu* in one’s hand, one should hurl the *vajraparaśu* into the sky, commanding: "Cut off the head—once, twice, or thrice! As soon as it is hurled, the *vidyādhara* who has been struck on the head will quickly return and stand in the sky above the forehead. The *vidyādhara* should then take that perfected *vajraparaśu*, pay homage a second time, bathe and anoint it according to the previously mentioned procedure, wrap it in the aforementioned cloth, and place it before the perfected painting. By means of this very *vajraprākāra* (adamantine enclosure), one should dispatch the *vajraparaśu* against all wicked beings—whether a king or a queen, a royal minister or a minister’s wife, a Brahmin or a Brahmin’s wife, a Vaiśya or a Vaiśya woman, or a Śūdra or a Śūdra woman; or any other wicked person of various kinds and many varieties. One should meditate upon the perfected painting seven times. Wherever it is dispatched, having accomplished the task assigned, it returns quickly. The *vidyādhara* stands in the sky above the forehead. Taking the perfected *vajraparaśu*, having bathed and anointed it with the aforementioned substances, and wrapped it in the aforementioned cloth, it should be placed before the perfected painting. This is the "visible dispatch" (*dṛṣṭapreṣaṇa*) which severs the head and enters all places of the wicked. I shall now describe the *vidyādhara-vajraparaśu-pāṇi* (the adamantine axe held in the hand of the Knowledge-Holder). One should meditate upon the perfected painting seven times according to the previously mentioned procedure. Holding the *vajraparaśu* in hand, one should invisibly hurl it at the enemy in the sky, bind the six-faced mudrā (*ṣaṭmukhamudrā*), cover it with a cloth, and recite the mantra. The king, together with his harem, becomes visible. Overcome by great wrath, they will be instantly paralyzed in their speech. One should take the aforementioned *vajraparaśu* into the sky as previously described and arrive with the axe in hand. The perfected *vajraparaśu* should be placed before the painting and reminded of daily with the previously mentioned perfumes and ointments.
The *Bhagavatī-ābhicāra-cakra*, the Vajra-Axe for the Severing of the Invisible Head, is completed. O ||
The ritual procedure for the *sādhana* of Vajraparaśu ends.
The ritual procedure for the *sādhana* of Vajrapāśa begins.

It is directed, among other things, against worldly deities and their followers; dreams play a role, revealing inauspicious things; even those who have committed the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantaryakāriṇaḥ*) are liberated [from their sin].

O three-pronged vajra! Now I shall explain the ritual procedure for the practice of the Vajrapāśa. All other worldly deities are of many kinds, distinguished by various diverse classifications; they say that beings are satisfied with their own respective [deities]. Having granted initiation through the holder of various worldly mantras, they say it is within the domain of beings. One who is deluded by worldly views [should act thus]: with the Vajrapāśa, one should pin all worldly and supramundane deities with the noose. Having performed the expulsion, [the victim] is turned toward the east; one should bind them with the Vajrapāśa.

Then, in front of the aforementioned *siddhapaṭa* (accomplished cloth-painting), one should first perform the following according to the previously stated ritual: having prepared a well-constructed house on ground endowed with auspicious marks, and having provided it with the aforementioned perfumes, flowers, and incense, one should establish the equality of the dwelling while employing the previously mentioned mantras and mudrās for the binding of the directions (*diśābandha*), the enclosure wall, the stakes, and the cage, as well as the seat. Thereafter, taking that *siddhapaṭa*, one should install it. Having offered perfumes, flowers, and incense to the Blessed Lady as prescribed, one should bind the three general family (*kula*) seals and the four great mudrās, recite them, and apply them to the four directions of oneself. With a five-colored thread thirty-two finger-breadths in length, one should place a vajra made of three-pronged flower-stalks, eight finger-breadths in size, in the middle of each section; the middle prong of the enclosure wall should be placed there. On that very middle prong, one should place the syllable *Oṃ*; on its left prong, the syllable *Hrīḥ*; and on its right prong, the syllable *Ṭha*. There, on the second middle prong of the enclosure wall, one should place the syllable *Hūṃ*; on its left prong, the syllable *Hūṃ*; and on its right prong, the syllable *Bhṛṃ*. When all these placements are completed, one should bathe the Vajrapāśa with fragrant water mixed with mustard seeds and fine perfumed flowers. Placing that Vajrapāśa in a box made of *aśvattha* wood measuring one cubit, and having set it before the aforementioned *siddhapaṭa*, one should strike the painting with mustard seeds while visualizing it as a single entity. In this same manner, one should meditate upon the box for ten million times (*nayuta*). If the box becomes warm, then one should again meditate for ten million times, visualizing the painting as a single entity, and strike the Cāturmahārājakāyika deities of the painting with mustard seeds. As soon as they are struck, they cause the aforementioned box to become warm. The mantra-holder must not touch that box. Again, having offered perfumes, flowers, and incense, one should strike the *siddhapaṭa* with mustard seeds while visualizing it as a single entity. When the ten million Victors have been reached, the Vajrapāśa will emerge surrounded by garlands of flames and stand on both sides. Seeing the accomplished Great Vajrapāśa, one should offer the aforementioned perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and garlands in a grand and noble manner to the ten directions. Then, having offered fragrant flowers, incense, and lamps to the Cāturmahārājakāyika deities of the *siddhapaṭa*, and likewise to the accomplished Vajrapāśa, one should cover it with a white cloth and place it before the *siddhapaṭa*. The accomplished Vajrapāśa possesses great supernatural power (*mahardhika*), great majesty (*mahānubhāva*), and great splendor (*mahātejas*). It is the noose of delusion in *saṃsāra* that binds many beings who are tormented. For the world, it brings about disease and mental distress. Those who are afflicted see white things as if asleep, biting their own teeth with their teeth, and experience untimely sleep. In dreams, they see terrible inauspiciousness; the fruits of agricultural labor do not come to pass; and spells and armor fail. Many rogues remain standing on both sides, and it is said that beings are seized by delusion and destroyed by obstacles. If such inauspicious signs are observed by the Vidyādhara, he should fashion an image of that person using a mixture of white sandalwood, *gorocana*, and mercury. Having placed that image before the *siddhapaṭa*, he should bind it with the previously mentioned Vajrapāśa. To the south of the *siddhapaṭa*, one should perform the binding; one should strike that image with mustard seeds. As soon as it is struck—even those who have committed the five sins of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*)—they become liberated from the noose and attain auspiciousness. That person should then give a teacher’s fee (*gurudakṣiṇā*) to the practitioner.

When the practitioner desires to bind one mantra with another, he should fashion an image of that person against whom he is intent in the tantra, facing eastward. Having fashioned an image of Mahādeva—either from *veliya* wood or *nimba* wood, measuring twenty finger-breadths in size, adorned with all ornaments, three-eyed, four-armed, with matted hair and a crown hanging down, his two upper hands joined in *añjali* mudrā, the second right hand holding a rosary, and the second left hand holding a trident—he should take that image and place it facing the *siddhapaṭa*. After offering perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps to the *siddhapaṭa*, he should invoke the deities of the Cāturmahārājakāyika realm, the *Siddhavajrapāśa*, and likewise the self-protection; then, having applied the *mahāmudrā*, he should take that single nose of the man intent on Mahādeva’s tantra and, thinking "I nail [him] with the mantra," take the previously mentioned *vajrapāśa* and bind that image with it. When the *siddhapaṭa* is focused as one, he should strike that person who is standing facing east with mustard seeds; at the very moment of being struck, together with the wrathful *Antaka*, he shall remain facing east for as long as he lives.

Having fashioned an image and placed it facing the practitioner, one should fix it and then drive it out. When focused with single-minded devotion upon the *siddhapaṭa*, Rudra becomes manifest before one’s face. Taking cremation ashes mixed with mustard seeds, one should draw an image of Mahādeva thirty-two finger-breadths in height in front of the *siddhapaṭa*. He should be depicted with matted hair bound in a crown, wearing a half-moon on his forehead, possessing three eyes and six arms, adorned with all ornaments. His first right hand performs a gesture of salutation (*namaskāra*); the second right hand holds a rosary; and the third right hand holds a trident. His second left hand holds a *kuṇḍī* water-pot; and the third left hand holds a skull-cup (*kapāla*). Having drawn him in this manner and offered perfumes, flowers, and incense to the *siddhapaṭa*, one should then bind the four great mudrās and recite the mantra. One should apply oneself to self-protection, thinking, "I shall bind the mantra of Mahādeva. Taking hold of a person named Ekatva, one should press down upon the image of Mahādeva with the left foot. The mantra-holders should bind the Great Seizure (*mahākṣepa*) of the thirty-three beloved gods and, with their arms, recite the mantra of the Vajrapāśa. Then, by means of the fifteen-fold concentration, having pressed down with the foot, one should strike that image once with mustard seeds while focusing on the *siddhapaṭa*. Both mantra-holders should say: "I am intent upon your tantra; I am striking the mantra of so-and-so who is intent [upon us]. Immediately, a great heat arises. If success is near, the heat will fade away. If it has come as cold, it is said: "The cold has arrived. If the body does not tremble when the cold has arrived, it is said: "The cold has arrived. [One asks: "Where has he gone? What is his destination? From where has fear come? By what form was he seized? When the mantra-holder looks with such a gaze, he is seized by the invisible. If the cold reaches a great body of water, such a person will [be reborn] for seven lifetimes from there. Then, taking the ashes of the image and wrapping them in red cloth, one should focus on the *siddhapaṭa* seven times and bury it at a crossroads. As soon as it is buried, the [possessing spirit] immediately disappears.

Regarding the counteracting of the mantras of others, such as *mahādevatantrābhiyuktaḥ* (in contrast to *yuṣmatantrābhiyuktaḥ*): here, for instance, an image of Mahādeva is employed and Rudra is to be manifested; one should take his ashes (*bhasma*). He has six arms, is adorned with the moon and a *kapāla*, displays the gesture of salutation (*namaskāra*), and holds a rosary (*akṣasūtra*), a trident (*triśūla*), a *kutsāśa* (?), and a *kapāla*; a doll is being trampled underfoot. (30v2ff.)
Then, likewise, in order to obstruct the Vaiṣṇava mantra (31r5ff.):

Alternatively, if the practitioner desires to bind a Vaiṣṇava mantra, he should fashion an image of that person out of *devadāru* wood, twelve finger-breadths in measure, adorned with all ornaments, with loose locks of hair, holding a discus in his right hand and a conch in his left. This image should be placed facing the entire painted cloth (*paṭa*). Four iron stakes, eight finger-breadths in length, should be driven into the cloth once; these four stakes should be driven at the four corners of the image, ending eight finger-breadths from its edges. Thereafter, having offered the previously mentioned perfumes, flowers, and incense to the perfected cloth, one should take the name of a single man among the gods of the Cāturmahārājakāyika realm who is devoted to that tantra. Taking the previously mentioned Vajrapāśa, one should visualize it seven times upon the cloth. One should bind the image with the Vajrapāśa at both ends of the stake. In the four directions, the image of the Vajra should face forward, bound before the tip of the Vajrapāśa. The practitioner should then visualize the six-faced deity. Afterward, one should visualize the Discus-cloth (*cakrapaṭa*) with mustard seeds. The image should be struck while saying, "Let such-and-such a person stand facing east," and it should be removed. If he does not come within one day, he will die. If the practitioner desires to lift [the spell], he should visualize the Discus-cloth seven times and strike the image with mustard seeds from the right side. The mantra-staked [image] of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, common to the three families, should be addressed by forming the four great mudrās and reciting the mantra. The image, bound in the four directions by the Vajrapāśa, should be touched with the hand bearing the Vajra-mudrā at the stake. Thereafter, one should say: "The knowledge goddesses residing on the Viṣṇu-cloth have been bound for him by my mantra; protect him according to his measure. By this rite, the application of binding with the mantra-stake for those included in the Viṣṇu host is accomplished. Having set forth two types of action, one should grasp the task in one place: removal and liberation.
Then, in the same manner, in order to obstruct the *gāyatrī* mantra and other mantras included within the *brahmagaṇa* (31v4ff.):

If the practitioner desires the pinning (*kīlana*) of the *gāyatrī* mantra included within the Brahma-group, he should fashion an image of a Brāhmaṇa out of *niṃba* wood, measuring twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), with four faces or six faces, wearing a crown of matted hair (*jaṭāmakuṭa*), and adorned with all ornaments. His right and left upper hands are in the gesture of saluting the *siddhapaṭa*; his second right hand holds *kulmāṣa* (sour gruel), his third right hand holds a *darbha*-cord, and in that same third hand a conch shell. Having placed these together before the *siddhapaṭa* according to the ritual for bathing, he should take an iron pin twelve finger-breadths long, place the syllable *hrīḥ* in the middle of the pin, and set it in a copper vessel. Then, having taken the name of the person [to be acted upon], and subsequently offering perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings, he should present them to the *siddhapaṭa* with undistracted mind, accompanied by the mantra and mudrā. Then, taking the previously mentioned four pins from the Cāturmahārājakāyika deities—the *Siddhavajrapāśa* and so forth—and accompanied by the pinning-mudrā and mantra, he should empower each pin seven times. Taking the image of Vajrapāṇi eight finger-breadths in length, he should drive those pins into the four directions, reciting: "I pin [the name of] such-and-such one with this mantra. Afterwards, [reciting] *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, *savituḥ vareṇyam*, and for the sake of subduing those twice-born ones who are compassionate by nature but hostile toward the assembly, he should take the previously described image and the *vajrapāśa*. Visualizing the image as the *paṭa* itself, he should fix the image in the four directions at the tips of both ends of the pins, facing the *vajra*-image and the *vajrapāśa*-bound practitioner. By this very method, engaged with his own mantra, he should face east; as many gods as there are, having been extracted, there is liberation.

Then, in the same manner, in order to obstruct the worldly deities (*laukikadevāḥ*), such as the *antarīkṣayakṣas* (32r2ff.), by this very procedure: the worldly deities and the *antarīkṣayakṣas* are to have their respective images fashioned according to the previously mentioned procedure within their own individual tantras; then, in front of the *siddhapaṭa*, the binding with mantra-stakes (*mantrakīlabandhana*) must be performed. || O ||
Likewise, for the purpose of obstructing Buddhist mantras and the like, one should employ the *pāśa* [noose] as before.

It is said that the practitioners are [to be visualized as] monks (*bhikṣu*), nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*), laymen (*upāsaka*), and laywomen (*upāsikā*); the counteraction is even more friendly, which is easily understood.

Now, therefore, follows the binding of supramundane mantras by means of a supramundane mantra; this is the pinning down of supramundane mantras by means of a supramundane mantra. This shall subdue even that mass of Māras which is otherwise impossible to overcome within the realms of existence until the end of becoming. One should bind the mantra with a mantra and pin it down; one must not allow it to turn away. If the practitioner desires the pinning down and binding of supramundane mantras by means of a supramundane mantra—even against the gods of knowledge (vidyādevas)—then I shall now explain the threefold division of family-mantras, the division of mudrās, and the division of invocations.

First, there is the classification of the mantras and mudrās of the Tathāgata family, which is the introduction. Likewise, there are three types of mantra: superior, middling, and inferior. Within that family, there are three types of mudrās: superior, middling, and inferior mudrās. The introduction therein is likewise threefold: superior, middling, and inferior. In that very context, the introduction of mantra and mudrā consists of three kinds of accomplishment: with a superior mantra, there is superior accomplishment; with a superior-middling [mantra], there is superior-middling accomplishment; with a superior-inferior [mantra], there is superior-inferior accomplishment; with a middling-superior [mantra], there is middling-superior accomplishment; with a middling-middling [mantra], there is middling-middling accomplishment; with a middling-inferior [mantra], there is middling-inferior accomplishment; with an inferior-superior [mantra], there is inferior-superior accomplishment; with an inferior-middling [mantra], there is inferior-middling accomplishment; with an inferior-inferior [mantra], there is inferior-inferior accomplishment. Thus, through the superior, middling, and inferior [mantras], there is the accomplishment of the superior, middling, and inferior.

One who has clearly received the instruction on the fruit of mantra-attainment in the single Tathāgata family, having discerned the various distinct categories of objects, being a holder of the mantra, should perform the rites of binding, pinning, piercing, and cleaving for the Tathāgata families and the vidyā-deities contained within those Tathāgata families, as well as for the heart-sons of the Jinas. Maitreya, Kumārabhṛta, and Ayakarma—one should begin the ritual. For the *samādhi*, one should fashion an image from white sandalwood wood, two-armed and twelve finger-breadths in measure, with a *caitya* situated upon its matted hair-crown (*jaṭāmakuṭa*), adorned with all ornaments, and with both right and left upper hands in the gesture of salutation to the Tathāgata. In this very same manner, Vajrahasta, Vajrapāṇi, Padmahasta, Padmadhara, likewise Ākāśagarbha with sword in hand, Māṇiradūpa, Cittāmaṇi with jewel in hand, Kṣitigarbha with earth in hand, likewise Viskambhin with various implements in hand, and Mañjuśrī with a manuscript of the *Prajñāpāramitā* in hand—by means of all these Bodhisattvas, in brief, two-armed, for whichever practitioner among monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen, their mantra-samaya should be clearly established through the previously mentioned procedure by Maitreya, Kumāra, and the others, in a single *samādhi*. Having fashioned it from the aforementioned wood, possessing good marks, unbroken, and free from flaws, seated upon a lotus, one should consecrate the heart-son of the Jina. At the conclusion, having mixed water prepared with white sandalwood, having bathed that image, and again having offered fragrant perfumes, flowers, and *agaru* incense to that image, having bound the three general Mahāmudrās of the Families together with their mantras, having directed oneself toward the ten directions, and afterwards having filled a handful of flowers and offered them to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, one should take that representation, wrap it in cloth scented with fragrant incense, and place it oneself in the location where the deity’s rite is performed. Until the day near the full moon, having prepared the house according to the previously mentioned procedure, having smeared it with clay, and having selected a ground endowed with excellent marks and free from all defects, one should perform the *ākṣepa* (summoning) of the Blessed Lady, recite the mantra, and cover it with those [materials], having consecrated it on the ground. Afterwards, having placed the previously mentioned *siddhapaṭa* facing east in the Brahmā-location of the house, having filled a handful of fragrant flowers, and having performed three circumambulations with prostrations, one should bind the "Great Summoning" (*mahākṣepa*) of the blazing weapon-energy, recite the mantra, and apply each of the eighteen weapons once, or a thousand weapons. Afterwards, having gone out of the house, the mantra-holder should perform the binding of the directions (*diśābandha*) fourfold; having applied the binding of the directions and the boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*), he should firmly recite the mantras for the fence and the stakes according to the stated procedure, remaining undeluded. Afterwards, having bound the house on all sides in the ten directions with offerings of perfume, flowers, incense, and garlands, together with mudrās and mantras, and having washed his hands and feet, he should enter the house. Facing both sides of the cloth, the mantra-holder should bind the "Great Summoning" of the Wheel-Turning Sovereign, the Lord of the Wheel’s Stride, recite the mantra, and apply each vajra once. He should think: "I shall bind such-and-such practitioner with the mantra. Again, having offered perfume, flowers, and incense to the Blessed Lady and the *siddhapaṭa*, and likewise to the Cāturmahārājakāyikas and the accomplished Vajrapāśa.

Having taken an image as previously described and placed it facing the cloth painting, and having taken a reliquary (*caitya*) containing relics, one should take that fourth image and, at a distance of eight finger-breadths, smear a white sandalwood mandala. In the center of that mandala, one should place a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*) four finger-breadths wide; in the middle of each of its prongs, one should place a syllable. In the middle of the first prong, one should place the syllable *bu*; in the middle of the second prong, one should place the syllable *bu*; in the middle of the third prong, one should place the syllable *bu*; and in the middle of the fourth prong, one should place the syllable *bu*. In this same manner, in the southeast corner, one should smear a mandala with white sandalwood at a distance of eight finger-breadths from the image. In that mandala, having smeared a crossed-vajra four finger-breadths wide with red sandalwood, one should place the syllable *oṃ* in the middle prong of the vajra; the syllable *kraṃ* in the middle prong of the second vajra; the syllable *buṃ* in the middle prong of the third vajra; and the syllable *thuṃ* in the middle prong of the fourth vajra. In this same manner, it should be stated for the southwest corner. This is the placement: one should place the syllable *suṃ* in the middle prong of the vajra; the syllable *dhvaṃ* in the middle prong of the second vajra; the syllable *laṃ* in the middle prong of the third vajra; and the syllable *kṣa* in the middle prong of the fourth vajra. In that very same way, in the northwest corner, one should place the vajra according to the previously mentioned rule. One should place the syllable *traṃ* in the middle prong of the vajra; the syllable *jṛṃ* in the middle prong of the second vajra; the syllable *proṃ* in the middle prong of the third vajra; and the syllable *rṇṇe* in the middle prong of the fourth vajra. Having offered incense, flowers, and perfumes to all those images with great and sublime devotion, the mantra-holder should visualize a person there, facing east, absorbed in his own practice. Afterwards, he should take a stake made of "flower-metal" (*puṣpaloha*), measuring eight finger-breadths, and a fourth stake whose two tips are like those of a stake. [The mantra is: *Oṃ traiḥ phaṃ*. *Oṃ*. *Note: The Sanskrit text provided contains several orthographic inconsistencies and abbreviations (e.g., *aṣṭāṃgulānte*, *visvavajraṃ*, *vajromadhyamāsūci*, *bukāraṃ*, etc.). The translation reflects the intended ritual sequence based on standard tantric iconography and liturgical conventions.*

Regarding this fourth stake, one should place the kings of single syllables upon it with a liquid prepared from fragrant substances. Having bathed the stake in a copper vessel containing the four aforementioned elements, the mantra-holder should place that vessel together with the stake upon the seat. He should place the *Hā* on his right side, and likewise visualize the *Siddhavajrapāśa* on his left side. Then, having offered fragrant flowers and incense to the Great Thousandfold One (Mahāsāhasra) and the perfected cloth (*siddhapaṭa*), the practitioner, facing the cloth, should visualize himself seated in the lotus posture, firmly clad in the previously mentioned garment. Taking the first stake from the copper vessel, he should strike it at the northeast corner—the site of Viśvavajra-Brahmā—while forming the *Aṅkuśa* (hook) mudrā with his hand and uttering the syllable *Hūṃ*. Taking the second stake, he should strike it in that same manner at the southeast corner—the site of Viśvavajra-Brahmā. Taking the third stake, while remaining in the *Avimukta* posture, he should strike it at the southwest corner—the site of Viśvavajra-Brahmā—accompanied by the previously mentioned mudrā and mantra. Taking the fourth stake, he should strike it at the northwest corner—the site of Viśvavajra-Brahmā—according to the previously mentioned rite. The mantra-holder, remaining in the *Avimukta* posture, should say: "This mantra, which was previously applied, has been driven in and properly established by me; it is non-deceptive, as spoken by the Buddha. Taking the four stakes together with the four vessels containing the elements that were placed in the copper vessel, he should hold them all at once with both hands and himself place them upon the head of Brahmā. Remaining in the *Avimukta* posture, he should visualize the *Pratītyasamutpāda* formula seven times. Visualizing the stake situated in the body of him who is struck by the great fire of Vajra, he should say: "I cause the terrifying fear of Vajra-fire to fall upon his head. Having visualized this in his body, he should place the vessel containing the elements within the stake at the northeast corner—the site of Viśvavajra-Brahmā—and visualize the previously selected cloth. Taking the second stupa with both hands, he should place it upon the head of Brahmā and remain in the *Avimukta* posture. Then, reciting the *Pratītyasamutpāda* seven times, he should say: "I cause it to fall upon his body. Remaining in the *Avimukta* posture, he should place it within the stake at the southeast corner—the site of Viśvavajra-Brahmā—and visualize the cross-vajra (*viśvavajra*) according to the previous method. In that same manner, taking the third stupa with both hands, he should place it upon the head and remain in the *Avimukta* posture. Reciting the *Pratītyasamutpāda* seven times, he should place the stupa within the stake at the southwest corner—the site of Viśvavajra-Brahmā—according to the previously mentioned rite, and then visualize the previously selected cloth. In this very manner, taking the fourth stupa, he should establish that stupa within the stake at the northwest corner—the site of Viśvavajra-Brahmā—according to the previously mentioned rite. The mantra-holder, remaining in the *Avimukta* posture with arms crossed in the *Vajrapāśa* gesture, should offer fragrant flowers and incense to the perfected cloth. Taking its name, he should form a fist containing the elements and, facing the Vajra image, bind the practitioner who faces the cross-vajra with the *Vajrapāśa* at the four corners of the stupa-pole, binding him at both ends. Afterwards, the mantra-holder, taking the name of the one previously engaged, should declare: "The mantra of that person has been pinned down, paralyzed, bound, and turned away!"

If the vajra-noose is unavailable, one should wash that thread—wound with a thread spun by a brahmin girl and treated with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) and scented water—and once it is dry, the nooses should be applied according to the previously mentioned procedure. Having filled an offering of fragrant flowers, while remaining seated without rising, the four practitioners should contemplate the *siddhapaṭa* as a single entity and touch the flower-offering; each [practitioner] is [to be visualized as] Vajradhara.
If no pāśa is available, then [use] a thread spun by a brahmin girl.

The lotus-holder, having been encircled from the east, should take the name of one person and slowly offer a handful of flowers; then, behind the image, he should gently strike [the ground]. Afterwards, with a truthful vow, he should say: "O so-and-so, stand facing the east! As soon as this is said, they shall stand facing the east for even a moment without transgressing. Through the awakening mind (*bodhicitta*), with great exertion of vigor, through the vows of silence, asceticism, and self-restraint, they may attain results difficult to achieve; yet at the time when the vajra-fire falls, everything from the realm of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of the Thirty-three and the Akaniṣṭha heaven is consumed by fire and rendered fruitless.

The remedy for this is found in the *Vidyottama* Great Mantra. For that reason, whatever mantra in this tantra is known by one skilled in its application, it may be pinned, paralyzed, and bound by a holder of the tantra. However, one who is devoted to the *Vidyottama* Great Mantra—having received initiation, being intent on service to the Guru, well-disciplined, and a god among gods—there is no one capable of unpinning him. Yet, even one whose mind is compassionate might at some time unpin him; if he is not released even for a single day, then [the deities] remain pinned, paralyzed, and bound, facing forward for seven years. If he is not released, then they will remain pinned, paralyzed, and bound, facing forward for three years. No one at all will be capable of turning them toward him, nor will such a person ever exist.
Perhaps the users of the *vidyot[t]amamahāmantra* are treated as a special case? (34v2ff.)

If it is not extracted on the second day, for twelve years the deity will remain pinned, bound, and turned away. If it is not extracted, then for seven years they will be well-consecrated. For seven hundred years, having been propitiated through the practice of painful vows and austerities, wearing garments of bark, having renounced great wealth and grain, and desiring the fruit of the mantra, he made this resolve: "I shall liberate [the one] who is a vessel of suffering. The place of the *cintāmaṇi*—the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system—is ablaze and set on fire; having attained the fruit of the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment of the single ocean of Dharma, he is near to the fruit of the mantra in order to turn the wheel of Dharma.
% NB: Among the fruits, [it is] *samyaksambodhi*!

If it is not extracted on the third day, then the adamantine fire (*vajrāgni*) falls upon the domain of the Buddha, and the fruit of the mantra comes to be unaccomplished and fruitless. In this very manner, for whichever practitioner of mantra the Tathāgata Śākyamuni has spoken of compassion—[compassion] which turns away from the pinning, the summoning, and the binding of mantras—[for them] there are the eight stages of enlightenment.

Then that great rākṣasī, having heard this, with a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand arms, surrounded by various mudrās and mantras, her body emerged from the abode of the Thirty-three Gods. Wearing a crown of matted hair, with a Tathāgata seated upon each individual lotus within the matted locks, she was directed: "O Blessed One, you who are the Wrathful Wrath, apply yourself to the rites of emptiness and gentleness."
He said: "Excellent, excellent, O great rākṣasī! Listen to the samādhi which I shall describe: the Wrathful One, Vajradhara, named 'The Radiance of Wrathful Loving-kindness'."

She asked: "What is the vajra like? He replied: "The wrathful king named Dṛḍhakrodharāja; the wrathful one holding a lotus named Vajrabhairava; the wrathful one named Ākāśagarbha, who hurls the wrath of space; the wrathful one named Māṇibhadra, who strides across the island of pride; the wrathful one named Viskaṃbhina, the lord of all islands; the great wrathful one named Mañjuśrīyamāntaka. [Then the rākṣasī asked: "Please teach the methods for countering these!"

Having heard this, the great *rākṣasī* was satisfied, elated, and joyful. She circumambulated the Blessed One three times and said this: "O Krodha, O Krodha, of whom else but the Blessed One shall I ask? Immediately thereafter, having looked toward the ten directions, he entered the Great Samādhi of the Radiant Pervasion (*mahāspharaṇaviparidīpta-mahāsamādhi*). At that moment, rays of light entered his eastern face and emerged as one, [manifesting] the wrathful deity named Maitrīspharaṇa-māra-hata. The wrathful king named Indra-avaṣṭabdha-pādahṛdaya-krodharāja was struck by Kiṃkirīṭa. The great deity Mahādeva-avaṣṭabdha-pādahṛdaya was struck by Vajrabhairava; [he is] the great wrathful deity named Vajramahābhairava. Ākāśanavikariṇa-hata was struck at the heart of his feet; [he is] the wrathful deity named Ākāśakrodhotkaṭa. Kṣiti-hata was struck by the goddess Pṛthivī.

The Omniscient One, residing upon each of his lotus-like arms, split the earth at the big toe of his right foot for sixty thousand *yojanas*. Having illuminated the jewel on his throat, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni spoke this before him: "O Blessed One, [it is] according to the inclinations of sentient beings, O Tathāgata Śākyamuni."

One should press the heart with the foot. One should press the heart with the foot against Kṣitigarbha, the wrathful one named Gambhīra, who has struck Viśvakarman. One should press the heart with the foot against the great wrathful one named Visvadīpa-krodha. One should press the heart with the foot against Mahābrahmā. One should press the heart with the foot against the wrathful one named Maṇiprajvalita-krodha, who has struck Yama. One should press the heart with the foot against the wrathful one named Yamāntaka-krodha.

For each single one there are eight wrathful deities (*krodha*), and for those eight wrathful deities there are incalculable wrathful deities. In that very place, the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of each individual Bodhisattva could be counted as many as the sands of the Ganges; yet the number of a Bodhisattva’s meditative absorptions cannot be known. One cannot attain the limit of a Bodhisattva’s meditative absorption, for it is exceedingly profound and exceedingly subtle—the domain of the Buddhas, peerless, inconceivable, and difficult to fathom.

Then that rākṣasī, having heard this, was satisfied, uplifted, and filled with joy, gladness, and mental well-being; she circumambulated the Tathāgata Śākyamuni three times to the right and, standing before him, said this: "O Blessed One, I ask about such wrathful mantras of anger as these: piercing, paralyzing, turning [the enemy] away, and interrogation. I am... [Blessed One].

Having heard this, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni said to her: "Listen, O Mahārākṣasī! I wish to perform the various kinds of wrathful rites—namely, the eight [rites] of wrath: the mantra-kīla (piercing), stambhana (paralyzing), bandhana (binding), and parāṅmukhīkaraṇa (turning away)—against those who are hostile. One should fashion an image of wrath out of red sandalwood according to the previously mentioned method, measuring ten finger-breadths. Whichever person is the object of the rite, one should depict that very person's wrath as four-armed, with matted hair resting upon a crown. One should mount the image upon the respective signs as previously described; in this very manner, the image is completed. Oṃ.
This does not appear to be a strong separator.

Having purified [the site] with fragrant water according to the previously mentioned ritual, one should place it before the accomplished cloth-painting (*siddhapaṭa*). Having performed the mantra-nailing, immobilizing, and binding according to the stated procedure, and having turned [the practitioner] toward the east, these should be applied to the four directions of the image. By the previously mentioned ritual, the ignorant one should form the three Family Universal Great Mudrās (*kulāsāmānyamahāmudrā*), recite the mantra, and assign [the deities] to the ten directions of oneself. Having offered fragrant flowers and incense to the *kuliśa* (thunderbolt) of the accomplished cloth-painting, [one addresses] the gods belonging to the Four Great Kings (*cāturmahārājakāyika*): likewise again, having offered fragrant flowers and incense, and having placed the four elements (*catuḥsadhātuka*) in copper vessels, the nails, the accomplished Vajrapāśa, and the images; then, having formed the "Great Summoning of the Thirty-three Gods" (*trayastrimśad-vigalita-priyadeva-mahākṣepa*) mudrā and recited the mantra, one should apply it seven times to that image, saying: "O you who are intent upon your own tantra, stand facing such-and-such person! Then, according to the previously mentioned ritual, the four nails should be struck in the four corners at the Brahma-station with the Wrathful Viśvavajra; one should visualize this. Next, taking each of the four practitioners, one should take them according to the previously mentioned ritual and station them oneself at the Brahma-station. With hands not released from their seats, in this very manner, one should establish the four elements in the four corners and the struck nail at the Viśvavajra-Brahma-station above, and visualize the second Bhayabhairava. Again, having offered fragrant flowers and incense to each *kuliśa* of the accomplished cloth-painting, [address] the gods belonging to the Four Great Kings.
