Again, having offered fragrant flowers and incense to the four elements, and likewise to the accomplished Vajrapāśa; with hands not released from their seats, grasping the Vajrapāśa, and with hands released from their seats, having visualized the third "fruitless action" (*nisphalakarma*) of this [practitioner], one should bind the Vajrapāśa to the four elements and the staff, fastening it at both ends. The practitioner, facing the image and facing the Vajrapāśa, should fill his cupped hands (*añjali*) with red Karavīra flowers while remaining with hands not released from their seats, and contemplate the accomplished cloth-painting seven times. He should slowly strike the back of that image with the handful of flowers, saying: "Such-and-such person, stand quickly with your back turned! As soon as this is said, he attains the great fruit of heat (*uṣmaphala*) and success; at that very moment, they go fruitless. Overwhelmed by the great power of the command and the great noose, their resolve is like a mind that has reached its end; this becomes fruitless. Just as a single day’s fire of the Great Vajra burns down a forest thicket, so that no one is able to cause even a sprout to grow—so too, the Mantradhara, whose mind is moist with compassion, joins [the practitioner] himself.
For example, in the case of one intent upon the *yuṣmat-tantra*, it should be said: "O so-and-so, stand facing the east... Having visualized that this ritual action shall be fruitless...

even upon hearing such a ritual action, the Great Rākṣasī—being pure, fearless, satisfied, exultant, and joyful—circumambulated the Blessed One three times with a mind full of gladness, and with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words: "I grant you the gift of fearlessness, O Blessed One; I ask a question of the Blessed One, I ask a question.
The Rākṣasī requests the gift of fearlessness (*abhayapradāna*).

"I grant fearlessness. Having obtained the empowerment, O one of heroic strength and great prowess, having attained the white victory that bestows fearlessness for those whose bodies remain within the elements, he spoke. "O Blessed One, there is the secret of the wrathful wrath; having heard the secret samādhi from the Lord of Jinas, he replied: 'Listen, O Great Rākṣasa! The secret of wrath is manifold. Regarding the rites of piercing, paralyzing, and binding, one should perform the application of the mantra-yantra facing eastward. With the two cords and the two stakes, the wrathful one pervades all directions and all activities. One must never reveal this to anyone who merely investigates the mantra.'"

Having heard this, the great Rākṣasī Satyapratijñā said to the Śākyamuni Tathāgata: “Listen, O Great Rākṣasī! For each of the eight Krodhas, there is a side-Krodha; for each of the eight Vidyādevis, there is likewise a Krodha. Through the meditative absorption (samādhi) of all the Tathāgatas, by means of the mantra and the excellent Yantra of the Lord of Tantras, according to the previously stated procedure, one should fashion a single image of a Krodha from the prescribed wood. It should have four arms, holding the aforementioned symbols. Whichever Krodha-tantra it belongs to, that specific Krodha’s image should be consecrated. Having bathed that image with red sandalwood mixed with ritual water and mustard seeds, and having offered black and red flowers and Guggulu incense to the image, one should wrap the image in a black cloth scented with that incense. Then, one should perform the eightfold rite. On the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should take a stake made of iron or wood, twelve finger-breadths in length—eight at the top and ten at the bottom—and perform its installation with the syllables: *Oṃ kraḥ dhruḥ bhaṃ yaḥ o*. Upon the completion of this stake-installation, having bathed the image according to the previously stated procedure and placed it within the womb of the Viśvavajra of the Krodha, one should recite: *Hrī hrī hrī hrī hrī hrī o*. This is the fourfold installation: *Oṃ pau rhūṃ dhaṃ hūṃ maṃ hūṃ he hūṃ tu hūṃ pra hūṃ ha bhūṃ te hūṃ sa hūṃ he hūṃ*. On the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having performed the previously mentioned purification of the house and having offered the five services (*pañcopacāra*) with nectar to the perfected painting (*siddhapaṭa*), one should then take up the perfected painting, place it facing east, and offer fragrant flowers and incense to the Blessed Lady upon the perfected painting. Having purified hand with hand, and having bound the Vikrama-cakra or the Mahākṣepa mudrā, one should recite the mantra and visualize the twenty-armed, thirty-two-armed, hundred-armed, or thousand-armed Krodhavajra-mahābhairava, empowering each individual weapon. Having bound the Mahāmudrā common to the three families and recited the mantra, one should direct oneself toward the ten directions and visualize the previously intended object. Then, placing the image of the Krodha in one spot before the perfected painting, with its hands turned toward the painting, the practitioner should take the previously mentioned stake, place it in a copper vessel, and hold it in his right hand. The practitioner, having bound the Mahānyāsa on the back of the image and the thirty-three-fold Mahākṣepa of the beloved deity, should recite the mantra and fix the image behind him. He should say: ‘By the power of the Krodha, stand facing east, directed toward such-and-such person who is devoted to your Tantra. As soon as this is said, the result will be like the flower of the Udumbara tree.”

Furthermore, with perfumes, flowers, and incense, the gods belonging to the retinue of the Four Great Kings [protect] the accomplished cloth-painting (*siddhapaṭa*), and likewise the accomplished Vajrapāśa. Again, having filled a handful of fragrant flowers and offered them to the image, one should bind it at the prescribed place while seated in the firm lotus posture (*sthirapadmāsana*). Visualizing oneself as the Wheel-Painting (*cakrapaṭa*), one should touch the stake (*kīla*) situated in the previous copper vessel, together with the stake-seal (*kīlamudrā*) and mantra, and contemplate.

In the fierce (*raudra*) sequence, one should prepare a replica as previously described, measuring eight finger-breadths (*aṣṭāṅgula*), each day making it a perfect square and smearing it with white sandalwood paste. Once that mandala is dry, one should place the replica upon it. At the location where the replica stands, one should fashion a circular seat of red sandalwood, four finger-breadths high, from which a garland of flames issues forth. To the east, at a distance of eight finger-breadths from that, one should draw a wrathful double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) made of red sandalwood, with wrathful deities emerging from its tip, extending twelve finger-breadths. In the southeast corner, having uttered the wrathful double-vajra, one should draw it with red sandalwood, with wrathful deities emerging from its needle-like tip. In this very manner, one should proceed to the south, southwest, west, northwest, north, and northeast. With all these materials, one should draw the wrathful double-vajras with needles, with wrathful deities emerging from their tips, using red sandalwood. Between the northeast and Indra, at a height of four finger-breadths, is *Oṃ Sau*. Between Indra and Agni, *Āgneyī*. Between Agni and Yama, *Yāmyā*. Between Yama and Nirṛti, *Nairṛtyā*. Between Nirṛti and Varuṇa, *Vāruṇyā*. Between Varuṇa and Vāyu, *Vāyavyā*. Between Vāyu and Soma, *Somyā*. Between Soma and Īśāna, in the northeast, is *Hūṃ Vā*. The conclusion is between Indra and the others, within the replica, *Hūṃ Te*. In the south, at the end of the replica, *Vāruṇyāṃ pratimasyāntare*. In the north, within the replica, *Somyāṃ pratimasyāntare Hūṃ Trāṃ*. The conclusion [2] is with all these: for oneself, the divine eye of ten million perfectly enlightened ones (*samyaksaṃbuddha*) is spoken; thereafter, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with a mixture of red sandalwood and camphor. With all these, the placement being completed, one should smear the hands with fragrant substances free from defects. Holding hands joined in the hollow of fragrant flowers, mutually perfumed with fragrant flowers, one should form the root mudrā of the Bhagavatī, utter the mantra, and apply it to the ten directions of oneself. Having applied the seat-mudrā to the seat, one should form the Great Casting Mudrā (*mahākṣepa*)—*Cakra Cakra Vikraca Cakra Svāni*—utter the mantra, and visualize each weapon on the accomplished cloth (*siddhapaṭa*) and employ them. Afterwards, behind the replica and facing the cloth, one should form the Great Casting Mudrā of the thirty-three gods who have descended, utter the mantra, and apply it seven times behind the replica with the wrathful deity, visualizing the "cutting of the wrathful wrath. Having formed the Stake Mudrā (*kīlamudrā*) and uttered the mantra, one should touch the stake placed in a copper vessel. With the vajra-peak (*kulisa*) and the vajra-fragment (*bharga*), while not releasing the seat, one should say: "I stake with the mantra the one who is assailed by such-and-such a wrathful deity. Taking the stake together from the copper vessel in front, while not releasing the seat, one should strike the stake whose essence is the wrathful double-vajra. Taking the second, placing it between the two thumbs and the two index fingers, forming the stake-mudrā and uttering the mantra, one should strike the stake whose essence is the southeast wrathful double-vajra. Taking the third stake situated in the copper vessel, placing it between the two thumbs and the two index fingers, forming the stake-mudrā and uttering the mantra, one should strike the stake whose essence is the southern wrathful double-vajra. While not releasing the seat, taking the fourth stake situated in the copper vessel, placing it between the two thumbs and the two index fingers, forming the stake-mudrā and uttering the mantra, one should strike the stake whose essence is the southwest wrathful double-vajra. While not releasing the seat, taking the fifth stake situated in the copper vessel, placing it between the two thumbs and the two index fingers, forming the stake-mudrā and uttering the mantra, one should strike the stake whose essence is the western wrathful double-vajra. While not releasing the seat, taking the sixth stake situated in the copper vessel, placing it between the two thumbs and the two index fingers, forming the stake-mudrā and uttering the mantra, one should strike the stake whose essence is the universal vajra (*viśvavajra*). Taking the seventh stake situated in the copper vessel, placing it between the two thumbs and the two index fingers, forming the stake-mudrā and uttering the mantra, one should strike the stake whose essence is the northern wrathful double-vajra. While not releasing the seat, taking the eighth stake situated in the copper vessel, placing it between the two thumbs and the two index fingers, forming the stake-mudrā and uttering the mantra, one should strike the stakes whose essence is the other wrathful double-vajras. Above the eight, taking the tenth from that same vessel and placing it between the two thumbs, forming the stake-mudrā and uttering the mantra, one should take them all and strike them in the aforementioned places against all the wrathful deities. With all these stake-wrathful deities, measuring six finger-breadths, they pierce the earth for sixty thousand yojanas and enter the seven underworlds (*pātāla*). How could there be a wrathful deity even beyond the thirty-three-fold world-system, which is six finger-breadths deep at both ends? Furthermore, having offered fragrance, flowers, and incense to the accomplished cloth, one should address the gods of the Four Great Kings: "O Siddha-Vajrapāśa, stand facing east toward the one who is assailed there."

Taking the previously mentioned *siddhapāśa* (accomplished noose), one should plant a stake in the western direction (*vāruṇī-diś*) and fix the *vajrapāśa* with its two ends four finger-breadths apart. Having wound and turned the right-hand *vajra* noose around the stake in the northern direction (*saumyā-diś*), one should bind it. At the end of the noose in the eastern direction (*aindrī-diś*), having wound and turned it around the stake with its two ends four finger-breadths apart on the left side of the *vajra*, one should bind it. In the southern direction (*yāmyā-diś*), having wound and turned it around the stake with its two ends four finger-breadths apart, one should bind it. From the eastern direction, using the left hand, one should place the second end of the noose at that very spot on the right side of the stake. With both *vajrapāśas* bound together, the practitioner should stand facing them. With all these [nooses], remaining in the *amuktāsana* posture, one should bind [the target] with five-colored threads. Having placed the *siddhapaṭa* (the accomplished cloth-painting) upon those [threads], which are situated in a copper vessel mixed with mustard seeds, and having offered perfumes, flowers, and incense to every part of the *siddhapaṭa*, one should take the fifty-six-finger-long five-colored noose in the right hand; standing in the northeastern direction (*aiśānī-diś*) with the noose in hand, one should remain there with the *kaṭakamudrā* at the tip of the stake. With the left hand, forming the *kururamudrā*, one should hold the *vajrapāśa* in the left hand toward the northwest direction (*vāyavyā-diś*). One should plant a white stake and bind [the noose] by winding it around both ends. In this very manner, one should bind [the target] in the four directions—southwest, southeast, northeast—and the others, according to the prescribed rule. Having touched the previously intended garment and filled both hands with handfuls of flowers, one should offer them to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni. Afterwards, having formed the *pañcamukhamahāmudrā* and recited the mantra, one should place [the flowers] one by one upon the *kulisa* (thunderbolt) of the *siddhapaṭa*. Then, having formed the *trayastriṃśāvigalitapriyadevamahākṣepa* mudrā and recited the mantra, one should direct a wrathful gaze toward the back of the previously mentioned image. While remaining in the *bandhasthitapadmāsana* posture, having pressed down and filled the hands with handfuls of flowers, one should contemplate the *siddhapaṭa* seven times with the left hand. The handful of flowers should be gently cast upon the back of the image while saying, "O so-and-so, stay facing east! As soon as this is said, the fruit of the mantra, which was being propitiated with great exertion, shall become fruitless.

If it is not extracted on the following day, then for a thousand years the fruit of the mantra—though propitiated like the fire of the mind—will go to waste. It must be carefully examined if the practitioner wishes to bring the fruit of the mantra forth from the mouth of [the deity]. This should be performed everywhere in this tantra, according to the prescribed ritual in the Great Maṇḍala of the Purification of Passion. If it is not extracted on the second day, fire will issue forth from his domain and his abode; his villages and cities will be burned, as will Indra, the thunderbolt, and the earth.

If the practitioner desires to perform various types of *pratyāyana* (revival), he shall cause [the deceased] to be released according to the prescribed rite in this very *Vajraśrīteja-mahāmaṇḍala*. If on the third day the person is not extracted, a drought shall occur for six years in the region where that person resided.

The mantra-holder, desiring to bring about the realization of the meaning for that world, causes [the victim] to be released according to the prescribed rite within the great maṇḍala of Vajraśrītejagarbha by means of the vidyā-dhara. [Curl] [2] If on the fourth day he does not cause [the victim] to be released and does not extract [the mantra], lightning immediately strikes his internal domain.

Desiring to bring [the deity] back, the practitioner should, according to the previously mentioned procedure, empower the Vajraśrītejagarbha maṇḍala and then cause it to be released. If it is not withdrawn on the fifth day, when the conflagration at the end of the eon arises in Jambūdvīpa, the gods—Harihara, Hiraṇyagarbha, and others—will cry out, "Alas! Alas! What a tragedy! What a tragedy! and with palms joined, they will say to the practitioner, "Jambūdvīpa has been consumed; our efforts have been in vain."

By the practitioner who desires to perform the rite of re-summoning, the conflagration at the end of the eon (kalpādāha) is to be pacified through the aforementioned ritual action within the maṇḍala of this mantra and its four mudrās.
The effigies of the Vidyādevis of the Tathāgata family—namely Prajñāpāramitā, Sarvabuddhadharmagaṇī, Āryakāpālī, [somebody], Sarvabuddhanetrī, Mahāmāyūrī, Maitryā, and Ānandā—are to be fashioned.

All sentient beings have been brought to peace by these knowledge goddesses (*vidyādevī*) within the family of the Tathāgata: Prajñāpāramitā, the source of all Buddha-qualities; Āryakāpālī, pierced by the arrow of praise; the guide of all Buddhas, Mahāmāyūrī; likewise Maitrī and Ānandā. These knowledge goddesses, who have attained the unsurpassed great state, appear in forms suited to those to be trained; they stand at his side as knowledge goddesses.

When a practitioner desires to perform various types of wrath against wrath, concentration against concentration, or the piercing, binding, and paralyzing of the mantra of a Vidyā-deity directed toward a single object, he should fashion an image of that Vidyā-deity out of black aloe-wood, twelve finger-breadths in size, with four arms and three eyes—the middle and smallest eyes being natural—and facing it eastward according to the previously described procedure.
The same applies to the Vidyā-devīs of the Vajra family: Vajraśṛṅkhalā, Vajragāndhārī, Vajramāṃsī, Vajrakelīkilā, Vajrāparājitā, Raktaṅgī, Vajrapraharaṇā, Vajratejā, and Vajragarbhi.

In this very manner, within the Vajra family, there are the Vidyādevis: Vajrasṛṅkhalā, Vajragāndhārī, Vajramāṃsī, Vajrakilikilā, Vajrāparājitā, Raktāṅgī, Vajrapraharaṇā, Vajratejā, and Vajragarbhi. These are the Vajra goddesses of the Vajra family who have attained the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and assume forms for the sake of those to be converted (*vaineya*). Beside him are the Vidyādevis, whose wrathful and peaceful aspects correspond to various meditative absorptions (*samādhi*). These supreme Vidyādevis are three-eyed and four-armed; their eyes may be of the middle or lowest type according to their natural state. When a practitioner desires to perform the binding, piercing, and immobilizing of mantras against one facing east, he should do so according to the previously mentioned procedure for one intent upon those respective tantras.
The same applies to the vidyā-devīs of the lotus family (*padmakula*):

The third is the Lotus Family (*padmakula*). The knowledge goddesses (*vidyādevī*) of the Lotus Family are Bhṛkuṭī, Aparājitā, Tārā, Śvetā, Mahāśvetā, Pāṇḍaravāsinī, Māmakī, and Gāndhārī; these are the knowledge goddesses of the Lotus Family. For one engaged in those various tantras, if the practitioner desires to perform the binding, paralyzing, or pinning of a mantra, or wishes to draw [the deity] facing eastward, he should consecrate them together with a single knowledge goddess using the previously mentioned woods. They should be fashioned according to the previously stated procedure, having four arms and three eyes, with the wrathful deities and their respective meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) and non-existent eyes positioned at the side of that knowledge goddess.

In the *Vidyotama-mahātantra*, within the *Vajrabhairavābhicāracakra* visualization, there are the mundane and supramundane tantras, the tantras, the yantras, and the vidyās—the supreme vidyās. This is a portion of the *Vajrapāśasādhana*, like the clarified butter from seven fires; it is the power and valor of emptiness, [describing] Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha according to their respective narratives. Om.

Having taken [the materials] according to the previously mentioned procedure and having consecrated them with well-constructed mechanical devices, one should perform the binding of the directions, intermediate directions, and the ten directions by means of stakes, enclosures, cages, and boundary-seals. Following the stated method, the deluded practitioner should join the two together and employ them. In that very place, the undeluded practitioner, having offered flowers, incense, perfumes, bali-offerings, blood, fish, and meat, along with mantras and mudrās, toward the ten directions, should thereafter wash his hands and feet, enter the house, and place the *siddhapaṭa* facing north. At that moment, having performed the "Great Casting" (*mahākṣepa*) of the Lord of the Wheel of Strides (*Cakravikrama*), he should recite the mantra and appoint the great wrathful deity named Vajravijṛmbhana in the east. In that same place, accompanied by the casting-mantra, he should appoint the great wrathful deity named Trailokyavidhvaṃsana in the south. In that same place, accompanied by the casting-mantra, he should appoint Vidyotamānadeva and Merukumbha in the west. Afterwards, for the sake of subduing [the opponent], he says, "I shall accomplish this for the purpose of restraining him," and prepares the excellent Vajramudgara. He should take a single piece of wood from a tree that has not fallen—either a nimba tree, a khadira tree, a vaṭa tree, an udumbara, or an aśvattha—and have it well-cut to a length of thirty-two finger-breadths, perfectly round, and possessing its own auspicious marks. The nimba-mudgara is for the summoning of yakṣas, rākṣasas, Brahmā, Kubera, and so forth. The second, the khadira-mudgara, is for the summoning of Hari, Hara, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Vināyaka. The third, the nyagrodha-vajramudgara, is for the summoning of kṣatriyas, kṣatriya women, and kṣatriya maidens. The fourth, the aśvattha-vajramudgara, is for the summoning of brahmins, brahmin women, and brahmin maidens. The fifth, the vajramudgara made from a tree with flowers, fruits, and leaves, is for the summoning of vaiśyas, vaiśya women, śūdras, śūdra women, or others of various castes; it is for the summoning of whomever the practitioner desires. The practitioner who wishes to accomplish the Vajramudgara for the purpose of summoning should establish a single Vajramudgara according to the previously mentioned procedure. On the tip of the mudgara, four finger-breadths deep, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the wrathful deity with five needles. [Recite: *Oṃ ghraḥ hrīḥ phreḥ phrīḥ phaṭ | Oṃ grī phaṭ | Oṃ hrī phaṭ | Oṃ hrī phaṭ | Oṃ hrī phaṭ | Oṃ hrī phaṭ | Oṃ hrī phaṭ | Oṃ hrī phaṭ | Oṃ hrīḥ phaṭ | Oṃ hrīḥ phaṭ*. This is the placement of the Vajramudgara in the four directions. When finished, it should be placed with fragrant flowers and scented water. Furthermore, it should be smeared with fragrant perfumes and placed before the *siddhapaṭa*. Having fashioned a single image out of clay, six finger-breadths in measure, and placed it in one spot, one should bind the Great Mudrā common to the three families and station oneself in the four directions. Having bound the "Great Casting" of the thirty-three gods who have dissolved [into the deity], one should empower the Vajramudgara. One should visualize the summoning of all yakṣas, rākṣasas, Hari, Hara, Hiraṇyagarbha, and humans into one place. Again, having offered perfumes, flowers, and incense to the Blessed One’s *siddhapaṭa*, one should remain seated in the lotus posture like one who is bound.
Various supernatural attainments (siddhis)

I shall explain the ritual manual for the root mudrā of the Blessed Lady, the Vidyā of Āryā. Om! Now, when meditated upon, the Blessed Lady performs all rites. On the eighth or fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having fasted for a full day and night, one should perform a great worship of the goddesses, stand facing south, and offer eight thousand oblations of sesame seeds mixed with the three sweets. Thereupon, she becomes accomplished; one performs the rites of accomplishment: the inciting of weapons, the inciting of all planetary spirits (*graha*), and the inciting of the entire world; the removal of the rain of stones, the removal of lightning, and the pacification of the trembling of deities and the expansion of space.
Having entered into the middle of water, one should recite [the mantra]. One causes [the enemy] to be impregnated.
[Further rites for killing, desiccation, and so forth, using human bone, including the sabotage of a brothel.]

Having fashioned a [charm] made of human bone measuring six finger-breadths and consecrated seven times, if one buries it in the middle of a house, [the inhabitants] become insane. If one buries it in the middle of a field, the crops are destroyed. If one buries it at the door of a house, [the household] is driven away. If one buries it in the middle of a cow-pen, there is no milk. If one buries it in the middle of a horse-stable, the horses die; the same applies to elephants. If one buries it at the door of a courtesan’s house, she becomes devoid of men. If one buries it in the house of a potter, his vessels cease to exist.
The same applies to the cremation ashes; furthermore, this is also directed against kings, ministers, and others.

Having fasted for a full day and night on either the eighth or the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, and having performed a great worship of the goddesses, one should take cemetery ash from an image situated in the south, consecrate it seven times with mantras, and cast it into the house of someone. That person will become deaf; no one can release them, except that they may release themselves. One should offer oblations to the goddesses; [the target] becomes paralyzed. Having taken the name of anyone whatsoever, one should kindle a fire with wood from a cremation ground and offer eight thousand oblations of charcoal mixed with ash and smeared with blood. Within seven days, either the king or the royal minister will die.

Now, wishing to banish kings: taking earth from the gate of a royal city, together with cremation-ground ashes, black mustard seeds, and the three sweets (*trimadhu*), one should offer eight thousand oblations while they are dyed red. Elephants and horses die; a plague (*māri*) breaks out among humans. Within seven nights it causes distress; within twenty-one nights, they die of their own accord. [To cause] the eclipses of the moon and sun... to attract.

Having fasted for a day and night, one should kindle a fire with *sammāna* wood in front of the goddesses and offer eight thousand oblations of large fruits, *guḍūcī*, honey, and *akṣa* seeds. If one offers these while reciting the name of a person—whether a woman or a man—and gives a flower, a fruit, or even a root consecrated seven times, that person arrives at that very moment. If one makes a powder by mixing cemetery ash, ashes from a cremation ground, and black mustard with salt, grinds it with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), and fashions an image from it, one should cut it with a thread and offer it eight hundred times; then that person becomes submissive. Or, having consecrated a flower or fruit with the name of a specific person or a root, and having recited the mantra over it seven times, one should recite it over the eyes; then he becomes beloved by all people in the royal court or at the city gate, and he will be victorious in legal disputes against the king. Having consecrated cemetery ash seven times, one should apply it as a triple mark (*tripuṇḍra*) on the forehead; then one becomes beloved by all people.

Furthermore, against marauding armies, or when there is fear of thieves: having consecrated seven times the ashes of a cremation ground and powdered bone, one should throw them into the enemy army; it causes them to fall. Having made a powder of the bones of a cow, a buffalo, or *darbha* grass, together with black mustard seeds, and having consecrated it eight times, one should offer it as an oblation (*juhuyāt*). Taking those ashes and consecrating them seven times, one should throw them into the enemy army while they are fighting; it destroys them.
To cause a person to be hated:

having taken hair, husks, and the wings of a crow and an owl, together with cremation-ground ashes, one should grind them into a single mass and cook them in oil. If one gives this to anyone—whether a woman or a man—on the head or on the body, that person becomes loathed by all people.
One should perform a propitiation, or cook an offering in milk; one should give the offering and offer a hundred oblations of milk. [The patient] becomes healthy.

To see the gods and receive their favor, one should recite [the mantra] seven times over [the materials]. Having spoken with the fruit of the cremation ground wood and the three sweets, one should offer oblations one hundred and eight times. One will see the gods face to face; they grant boons, and all activities are accomplished by the mere thought of the mind.
To subjugate a king and others:

having drawn a maṇḍala in a cremation ground (*śmaśāna*), one should place the Goddess in its center—mounted upon a corpse (*preta*), holding a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) as her weapon, and adorned with all ornaments. Having depicted her and offered a *bali* sacrifice consisting of all kinds of nourishing substances, one should offer into the fire a great *phalluṣa* (meat-offering) smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhura*) one hundred and eight times. A king together with his thousand-fold retinue will become submissive. For whomever one recites this, it shall act against all *grahas* and *bhūtas*. [To become invisible...]

By this very procedure, having taken the five limbs of a man and reduced them to powder, having fashioned a face out of *akula* wood, having lit a lamp with great oil (*mahātaila*), and having taken the soot, one should stir it with clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and recite the mantra eight hundred times over it. Then, one should apply it to the eyes; one becomes invisible. If one lights the face, one is seen. [Note: *Mahātaila* is used for invisibility;
the eye-ointment is for subjugation and for becoming invincible in gambling and the like.]

Having consecrated it seven times with mantras, whoever one looks upon becomes submissive; and for whomever one looks, all *grahas*, *bhūtas*, *piśācas*, *asuras*, *rākṣasas*, and humans—whether in legal disputes, in the royal court, or in gambling—become defeated. To whomsoever one gives it, whether to a woman or a man, they all become submissive. Whatever one desires, that one obtains. As long as this collyrium remains in the eyes, for that long one remains healthy; no weapon can prevail against one’s body.

With this very powder, together with the testicles and the female organ (*bhaga*), as well as gold—one should combine those powders, consecrate them seven times, and then apply them by drinking, smearing, or as an ointment; one should also sprinkle it upon food, edibles, flowers, and betel. She becomes subject to the previously mentioned hymn; whatever she does, she remains doing. Furthermore, having rubbed hand against hand, whoever one seizes becomes subject; whatever one seeks, that one obtains.

Desiring to bring a village or a city under one's control, one should take dust from the gate of the city, mix it with sesame seeds, *palālava* (chaff), and meat, and grind them into a powder. Having kindled a fire with wood from a cremation ground, one should offer oblations eight hundred times every day for seven nights. One will become beloved by all people.

One should offer eight hundred oblations mixed with powdered *rājikā* (black mustard), sesame, and salt. All sentient beings will come under one's influence. One should offer seven oblations every day; one will become beloved by all people, and they will not suffer harm.

Furthermore, for the protection of cattle, or for those desiring human beings, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of *dūrvā* grass smeared with salt and honey. Having kindled the fire with fuel-sticks of *palāśa*, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of *paramānna*; thus there is peace for the cattle. With milk, supreme peace is attained. Furthermore, for the purpose of subjugation:
One should offer oblations smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhura*); all people will become submissive to oneself or to another.

To counter possession, one should perform a *rājikā* (black mustard seed) homa. One should offer *nirguṇḍī* leaves together with *nīpa* leaves; this releases one seized by a planetary spirit (*graha*). With incense of *sarjarasa*, one causes them to speak; by means of speech, one causes them to release.
To instill madness:

one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of *dhūrta* seeds (*dhattūra*) together with black mustard (*rājikā*). Reciting the name of the person while using their footprint dust, that person will wander about insane, and no one at all can release them.

To destroy [an enemy], one should fashion a kīla (stake) made from the bone of a horse or a buffalo, six finger-breadths in length, and having consecrated it seven times with mantras, one should bury it together with the linga; [the enemy] will perish.
To cause a woman to bleed uncontrollably: [one should perform the rite as follows].

Having ground together the urine of a menstruating woman along with the dust from her footprint, black mustard seeds, and cremation-ground ashes, one should bind the powder in a cloth from a funeral pyre, consecrate it seven times with mantras, and bury it in a cremation ground; her blood will flow, and by digging it up, she is released.
The ritual manual (*kalpa*) for the Bhagavatī is completed. || O ||

Regarding the uses of a certain kind of medicinal plant (likely called *mahānīlā*):

[It is] Vidyujjvālā Karālī, Svedāmbujamahārākṣasī. It was known by the Omniscient One; it was created by the Omniscient One; it was favored, served, honored, and worshipped by all gods, nāgas, yakṣas, kinnaras, mahoragas, and humans. Then Vidyujjvālākarālī, whose great eyes were like sweat-drenched lotuses, spoke this:

there is a medicinal herb renowned throughout the world, which accomplishes all rites."
The goddess who has arisen, who bestows the peace of immortality, and whose names were spoken by the God of Gods— I shall proclaim them so that a human being may know her:

Raudrī is the beloved of the waking state; Raudrī is renowned as Kālī, the destroyer of enemies in battle. These names should be understood by those who have gathered [the knowledge]. the goddess residing in the *kaṇḍa* is seen, and the flower has a luster equal to gold.
One should recognize [the deity] by these signs as resembling the color of a ripe fruit;
likewise, during the conjunction with the Puṣya asterism,
one should offer oblations and give *tālī*, fresh *pañcamūlī*, at night when the proper time has arrived.
Then, having wrapped them with a thread spun by a maiden,

One should prepare equal portions of agarwood, guggulu, śrīvāsa, sandalwood, turmeric, white sugar, and musk;
having fumigated [the person] with this, a man may then go to the royal court.
In other houses of women as well as in the houses of enemies,
all those who smell that fragrance become his servants.
One should prepare fine powders in equal proportions from snake-skin, mantra-herbs, great-blue flowers, lotus-receptacles, and horse-tongue;
one should grind them with sesame oil and apply them to the soles of the feet.
This is the most excellent and supreme yoga, which brings together men and women.
The seeds and leaves of the udumbara tree, along with peacock feathers,
combined with mahānīla, karṇakārī, and elephant ichor,
should be administered as a fine powder with a serene mind.

A mixture of *naraṇa*, *nārī*, *rocana*, *mahānīla*, *vasamī*, *puṣpa*, and *priyaṅgu*— these should be made into a fine powder in equal proportions. Anointed with these, whatever one looks upon from all sides, [one gains mastery over it].

One should take nine *vacakīṭa* insects that have recently fallen from a tree, dried, ground smooth, and rubbed against the edge of a fine cloth; the wise man should drink one-eighth of a *pala* of this with ghee, milk, warm water, or freshly pressed oil. in stature like an elephant, in speed like a horse, in the excellence of his vision and hearing like gold, with thick hair whose ends are long and curled, and free from all impurities, he becomes beautiful and charming.

With a voice equal to that of a Gandharva or Vidyadhara, a man shall live for seven hundred years; there is no deficiency in food or drink, nor any affliction from heat, noise, or sexual intercourse. Enjoying whatever he desires as he pleases, he makes an old man young within a month.

The ritual procedure for Vairocana:

One should consume seven lumps of food with their tips intact. Having consecrated fine powder with the mantra and mixed it with honey, by consuming it for seven days, one becomes wise and a possessor of the power of retention (*śrutidhara*).

The previously mentioned powder, mixed with honey and consecrated seven times with the *Amṛtabhaiṣajyadhāraṇī*, should be taken; by doing so, a person will become healthy for seven days, and all diseases will be pacified. Through the application of the *yakṣas*, one becomes a possessor of a retentive memory (*śrutidhara*). Within a month, there will be a vision of the Tathāgata.
The *Amṛtabhaiṣajyadhāraṇī* is completed. Om.
The maṇḍala or icon of the Devī, possessing twelve heads, eighteen arms, and the articles of the cremation ground.

The circle named *Pretotkaṭa*, with its fierce seat, terrifying with the great eyes of perspiring lotuses and formidable with streaks of lightning-flames—this [circle], like a mass of fire, was surrounded by all the *rākṣasas*, *asuras*, *gandharvas*, *kinnaras*, and the most fierce humans and non-humans; by Virūḍhaka, Virūpākṣa, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Kuvera; and by Śakra, Brahmā, and the others from the thirty-three classes of gods, including Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha. Crying out, "Alas! Alas! What a tragedy for the host of gods! they meditated upon this name: "The Terrifying *Pretotkaṭa* of Lightning-Flame Fear."

Now, therefore, I shall explain the ritual procedure for the mandala of the Blessed Lady (*Bhagavatī*). On the eighth or the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should draw the mandala in a well-known great cremation ground, on a site of excellent ground. In the center of a mandala measuring three cubits in its interior, one should depict the Goddess. She stands upon two corpses with the soles of her feet pressing down upon them. She has twelve veins, eighteen arms, and so forth; she has tawny eyes, wears a garland of skulls, and her ornaments consist of black serpents coiled around her limbs. Her body is terrifying, fearsome, and a source of dread, causing terror even to the gods. Her hair is bound on each individual strand by the noose of every serpent, and the tongues of all the serpents loll out. In each pair of hands she holds a serpent-limb; she has sharp nails like the points of spikes, a protruding belly, and wears a lion-skin garment. Her weapons are fierce, sharp, and held with a grand, swelling posture.
In the upper right hand is a six-spoked wheel; in the second [right] hand is a discus;
with the third hand is the threatening gesture.
In the fourth hand is a mace,
in the fifth hand a trident,
and in the sixth hand a bell.
In a seven-cubit [space], a spear; in an eight-cubit [space], a banner; in a nine-cubit [space], a club.
In the upper left hand is an elephant goad, in the second [left] hand a water-pot,
and in the third [left] hand a skull-cup.
The fourth hand is in the boon-granting gesture (*varada*),
the fifth hand holds a spear (*śakti*), and the sixth hand holds a staff (*daṇḍa*).
The bow is seven cubits long, the thunderbolt is eight cubits,
and the index fingers are nine cubits.
With these weapons, one should cause [the deity] to grasp the vajra-fist at the tip of the flame; he should stand within the central mandala of the entire cloth painting.
Whether one desires sovereignty over kings, entry into a cave, or the state of a vidyādhara, one should stand facing the cloth [painting], or toward the northwest.
One who desires to perform the rites of killing, withering, burning, inciting enmity, pinning, cutting, splitting, yawning, paralyzing, deluding, or possession, should stand facing the south.
While the cloth painting is not yet finished, the heart-mantra of the Great Mudrā should be applied. In the four corners, four skull-cups filled with blood should be placed.
Within that cloth [painting], one should place a human skin filled with great flesh (*mahāmāṃsa*). If such is unavailable, it may be made of clay, wood, or lac.

One should drive four foundation-piles (*āśayakīla*) measuring eight finger-breadths, together with the roots of the *devīmūla*, *pāṭalī*, *vacā*, and *nirguṇṭhī* plants, into the four corners. These should be consecrated eight times with the Heart Mantra using a thread soaked in blood and mixed with mustard seeds. At a distance of twenty-eight finger-breadths from the center of the womb-maṇḍala, a square with four gates should be constructed.
The directions are assigned as follows: Indra, Agni, Yama, and Nirṛti in the south; Varuṇa in the west; Vāyu, Soma, Īśāna, and the abode of Brahmā in the north.

In the directions beginning with the southeast (Agnēya), there are four-armed [deities] of red color. One should draw the Yakṣiṇī named Vidyut, who has gone far away and is covered by a cloth, measuring one cubit. She has hair standing on end, knitted eyebrows, and Buddha-like eyes; her breasts are erect, she has a protruding belly, and she is clothed in human skin. On the north, she wears a sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*). She has distorted fangs, holds a sword in her right hand, and in her second right hand she holds the severed head of a king. In her upper left hand she holds her own heart, and in her second left hand a skull-cup filled with flesh and blood. A youth adorned with all ornaments should be depicted in this very manner.

Like Hārītī? In the south-western direction is the yakṣiṇī named Ulkā. She has a lean body, three tufts of hair standing erect, and is embraced by a black serpent. Her eyebrows are knit; her two ears are adorned with reddish-brown serpents as ear-ornaments. She wears a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) made of black mustard seeds and is clothed in human skin. She has four arms: in her first right hand is a goad (*aṅkuśa*), and in the second right hand is dried meat (*vallūra*). In her first left hand is a skull-cup filled with blood, and in the second left hand is a human head. One should depict her with the garments previously mentioned. She is to be placed in the south-western direction.

In the northwestern direction is the yakṣiṇī named Śvetaraudrī. She has hair standing on end, laughs with a loud roar (*aṭaṭṭahāsa*), has an erect body, and is pot-bellied. She is clothed in human skin and possesses four arms. In her first right hand she holds a trident; in the second right hand she holds a pregnant woman. In her first left hand she holds a skull-cup filled with blood; in the second left hand she holds a piece of great flesh (*mahāmāṃsa*) together with marrow. In this very manner, one should have her depicted on the previously mentioned cloth. She is to be stationed in the northwestern direction.

In the northeast direction, one should draw the Yakṣiṇī named Pradhurā. She is yellow in color, with hair standing erect, knitted eyebrows, and a distorted face; she is honey-brown, wrathful, with bared fangs, and her hair is bound with snakes. Her upper hand is raised, she has a protruding belly, wears a garland of skulls as a sacred thread, and is clothed in human skin. She should be depicted with four arms: in the upper right hand a battle-axe (*paraśu*), in the second right hand dried meat (*vallūra*); in the upper left hand a youth (*kumāra*) holding a vessel full of blood, and in the second left hand an elephant’s head. Having drawn her according to the previously mentioned procedure, she should be stationed in the northeast.

In this manner, it should be established in the four directions. One should place four vessels filled with blood, meat, and mustard seeds before the four Yakṣiṇīs. At the eastern gate, one should place the syllable *dhīḥ* using bone powder and the powder of a human corpse (*idgala*) mixed with this very liquid. Immediately following that, one should place the syllable *ṣṭrī*. Immediately after that, one should place the syllable *phaṭ*. Immediately after that, one should place the syllable *bhrū*. Immediately after that, one should place the syllable *svā*.

One should place a skull-cup in the southern direction. There, one should place the syllable *oṃ* in the north. Immediately after that, one should place the syllable *hūṃ*. In the space between those, one should place the syllable *āḥ*. Immediately after that, a vajra-lotus is situated. Immediately after that, an arrow.

In the western direction, one should place a lump of blood. Immediately after that, one should place a parasol. Immediately after that, one should place a banner. Immediately after that, one should place a lotus. Immediately after that, one should place a trident.

One should place the *śakti* in the north; immediately following that, one should place the *cakra*; immediately following that, one should place the *daṇḍa*; immediately following that, one should place the *vajra*; immediately following that, one should place the *kṣara*; immediately following that, one should place the *śrīvatsa*; and immediately following that, one should place the *paraśu*.

Having performed the *nyāsa* in a clockwise direction with all these materials—either colored powders smeared with blood from the cemetery garments—one should draw a red wheel measuring eight finger-breadths (*aṣṭāṅgula*). One should fashion four wooden stakes (*kīla*) measuring eight finger-breadths, wrap them with five-colored thread, empower them one hundred and eight times with mantras, and drive them into the four corners.

Four fire-pits (agnikuṇḍa) should be prepared at the four gates. At the eastern gate, one should stand with weapon in hand and arms raised, remaining unflinching. Immediately following that, situated upon a vajra-seat, one should kindle a fire in the southern pit using wood from a cremation ground and offer eight hundred thousand oblations of human flesh mixed with guggulu incense into the center. She will appear visibly, terrifying with flames like lightning, and say: "O practitioner, choose a boon; what do you desire? I shall grant you mercury, elixir, an underground cavern, a sword, the state of a Vidyadhara, mastery over the underworld, sovereignty over Jambudvipa, or the accomplishment of the twenty-eight sacred sites. [She continues: "O Goddess, I shall accept as much sesame-rice as I can take," until the fire-ritual in the four pits is completed. One should request her in this very manner. In the western pit, one should again offer eight hundred oblations. Once more she appears, and one should say: "O practitioner, grant me whatever I desire," until it is finished. By this same procedure, while performing the rite in the northern pit, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations. Then she must be asked: "O practitioner, is the Buddhahood you desire present or not?"

Having gone and bound the king of trees with the stride of the *paduka* [sandals], and having looked toward the eastern sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in the southern direction, one should offer red flowers, red sandalwood, and incense of *guggulu*, as well as a lamp of great fruit, *guḍa*, and human blood mixed with great oil, in the vicinity of the mandala. Standing before the pit, having focused the mind on the accomplishment of what was previously mentioned, one should kindle a fire with funeral-pyre wood (*śmaśāna-kāṣṭha*) and perform the supreme oblation (*parama-homa*). As soon as he casts [the offering] into the pit, he beholds the Goddess. When the oblation is completed, it should be said: "Upon the completion of the oblation, the tongue of the corpse emerges. Measuring eight finger-breadths and possessing a sharp nature, one should divide it into four pieces, take one portion, wrap it in the three metals (*triloha*), and place it within the central mandala. Having cast the pill (*guḍikā*) by means of the withdrawal [mantra], at the very moment it is thrown, the accomplished Vidyādharas tremble. Whether it be a human woman or not—having combined that powder, it should be used for killing, subduing, or causing division; one who desires to destroy a city or a kingdom should act with this powder.
