Then Vidyujjvālākarālī, whose great eyes were like sweat-lotuses, joined her palms in reverence and, prostrating at the feet of the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One: "Speak, Blessed One, Sugata!
The Blessed One replied: "The culmination of both is [attained]."
Does this mean that both are attained?
Listen, O Great Rākṣasī; it is a matter of ritual procedure (*upacāra*).
It may be in a cremation ground, or even in an empty house, and likewise under a solitary tree.
In a forest, on a mountain peak, or at a crossroads, one should perform the rite of malevolent sorcery (*abhicāra*).

Having dug a triangular pit with a four-finger-wide altar-edge, and having smeared it with clay, one should kindle a fire with four-finger-long sticks. Then, one should offer eight hundred oblations while reciting "Kill! (*māraya*), using human blood, mustard seeds, salt, and the previously mentioned powder, while reciting the mantra: *tatraḥ hūṃ aḥ phaṭ* (three times).

Having fashioned an effigy of the enemy out of *nimba* wood measuring eight finger-breadths, one should kindle a fire with jujube thorns. Having smeared the effigy with neem oil, poison, and the powder of *asurī*, one should offer oblations one hundred and eight times while reciting the previously mentioned mantra once for each oblation, saying: "I cause so-and-so to die."

Having fashioned an image out of flour and a wooden peg eight finger-breadths long made from human bone, one should take that image together with the previously mentioned powder, empower it by reciting the mantra eight times, and strike the head while uttering the name of the enemy; by the mere act of striking, the head falls off immediately.

"Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ! Kill so-and-so!"—thus it should be spoken. Having consecrated the previously mentioned powder seven times with the aforementioned mantra, one should place it in a silver vessel or a bronze vessel, or leave it in the house of the enemy or in an open space. As soon as it has been placed there, [the enemy] shall fall down instantly.

In this very manner, having kindled a fire with *jaṃbhāga* wood, one should offer oblations in the name of whomever one desires—whether it be a king or a royal minister—using oil from the *lavanāsurī* thorn-plant mixed with powder and consecrated eight hundred times. He, together with his retinue and the women of his inner apartments, shall die. This is a secret more secret than the secret; it must not be disclosed in any place whatsoever.

Having kindled a fire with thorny wood, one should again fashion an effigy out of thorny wood, smear it with poison-powder, and place it in a jar within the fire-pit. Standing over that, one should offer oblations into the fire with thorny wood seven times consecrated with mantras while uttering the name of the person [targeted]. That person’s body will be shattered.

Furthermore, there is pacification (*sānti*). Having examined the ground, one should perform the rite: having kindled a fire with thorny wood (*sūlakāṣṭha*), one should offer oblations with the name of the person targeted, using a powder of the roots of *mahānīla* and *indravāruṇī*. At the mere utterance of the name, they die; there is no bringing them back to life. Having kindled a fire with thorny wood, one should offer oblations with a powder of needles and salt. At the mere completion of the offering, within seven days, the enemies will perish.

Having fashioned an image of Mahādeva, one should smear that image with a powder mixed with poison and blood. Having empowered it seven times with the previously mentioned mantra, one should bury it in his temple. Merely by its being buried, the *liṅga* shall crumble into a hundred pieces. [In this case] the restoration of the *liṅga* must be performed; once it has been extracted, there is liberation.

That powder, together with *gorocana* and peacock’s eye-pigment (*mayūracandrikā*), should be tied in a pouch and hoisted at the top of a banner. Merely by its being hoisted, the enemy army falls away like worms.

Note: Regarding martial magic—one should grind together camphor, tagara, vacā, kuṣṭha, gorocanā, and the previously mentioned powder. One should then smear this upon one's own body and one's mount; no blows shall prevail against his body.

By this procedure, one should combine *gorocanā* with its powder, wrap it in gold, and place it in an uncountable [number of] locations; or one may wrap it in gold, silver, or copper. That uncountable [substance], when buried in the middle of the treasury-house, shall cause wealth, grain, and the goddess Śrī-Lakṣmī to increase within the house.

The secret named *Pretotkaṭa*, which is formidable with the flames of lightning and possesses great eyes like perspiring lotuses, should likewise be performed by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as by the mantra-holder through secrecy. For the great maṇḍala of *Pretotkaṭa*, there is the *Vidyut* named *Trakṣaṇā*, and likewise *Śvetā*, *Raudrī*, and *Pradhūrā*.

Now, therefore, I shall explain the ritual procedure for the Yakṣiṇī. One should take the previously mentioned Yakṣiṇī [image] onto a single cloth and have it drawn using human bone. Having consecrated it one hundred and eight times with mantras, one should bury it in a cremation ground by name. Then, if either a king or his minister dies, one should take that cloth and wrap it in grass and leather. If one buries it within the city, as soon as it is buried, the city will be seized by a great conflagration and disease. Upon its removal, there is liberation.
In this very manner, one should bury the cloth in an elephant's footprint; as soon as it has been buried, the person dies.

Having placed the cloth painting of the Yakṣi�ṇī in the position of the householder—with human flesh, two wings, and a skull held in her two hands—facing south, the mantra-holder should place it within a triangle. In the central mandala, one should smear a skull-cup with red sandalwood that has been consecrated eight times with wood from a cremation ground. Having placed that board before the Yakṣiṇī, one should say, "Kill so-and-so," while using royal mustard seeds consecrated eight times. As long as the sandalwood board does not dry up, the body of that person will die of a great disease; thereafter, peace is restored.
The fierce secret mandala of the preta, formidable with the blazing flames of lightning.
Now, therefore, follows the characteristics of the mudrās of the Blessed Lady.

Then, having smeared both hands with sandalwood paste, one should release the two hands from the *ciṭi* [gesture]. Having formed the *añjali* with both hands and placed them at the heart, one should interlace the thumbs. It should be stated that they are within the little fingers; the two ring fingers are in the shape of a coil (*kuṇḍala*), and likewise for the index fingers. One should extend the two middle fingers like needles. This should be viewed as being well-fashioned by the Omniscient Śākyamuni from the treasury of his *ūrṇā*. It should be asked: "The eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma. This mudrā should be viewed as being manifested directly by the seven guides of the Buddhas. The White Yawn-Vajrī, who performs all activities, is the mudrā named *Pretotkaṭa*. The mantra is: *hūṃ hūṃ hrīḥ phaṭ phaṭ | vajrī sattvakarmakarī svāhā*. One should employ the previously mentioned *Pretotkaṭa-vetāḍa* in the mandala and in all mandalas. By this very method and by means of this very seat, the binding of the boundary, the dhāraṇī, the stake, the enclosure wall, the cage, and the placement should be performed in the previously mentioned great *Pretotkaṭa* mandala using this mantra.

In this very manner, having formed the *añjali* with both hands, one should place the two thumbs in the secret location (*guhyasthāna*) in the shape of a hook (*aṅkuśa*). Upon them, one should firmly interlace the two middle fingers. At the tips of the two thumbs, the two little fingers should be shaped like earrings (*kuṇḍala*). Having extended the two ring fingers against each other, one should bind the two index fingers as needles upon the ring fingers. This is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) of the Wrathful Vajra-yawning (*vajravijṛmbhaṇa-krodha-utkaṭa*). The mantra for this is: *Oṃ raudrapracaṇḍavegadhara prahara 2 sarvaduṣṭān hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ 2 svāhā*. With this mudrā-mantra, one should employ it seven times in the eastern direction while facing east. By the mere employment of this, a great boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) of seven hundred *yojanas* is established. One should empower oneself seven times with this mantra and mudrā. In the same way, it should be performed in the south, west, and north using the previously mentioned mudrā-mantra.

Having formed the vajra-fists with both hands, one extends the two middle fingers like needles; this is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of the laughing vajra-fist. With this seal, one should employ this mantra: *oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Thus, one should apply it at the western gate. By applying it just seven times, a great boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) is established that remains concentrated for three hundred *yojanas*.

In this very manner, with both hands joined, one should press the two little fingers against the middle finger-pins from both sides. One should awaken the two index fingers and the two ring fingers. One should awaken the two middle finger-pins by moving them away from each other, and awaken the two index fingers and the two ring fingers in the four directions. This is the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) named Trailokyavikramavajravijṛmbhaṇa-ṣaṇmukhā. The mantra for this is: Oṃ aḥ hūṃ hūṃ sūṃ sūṃ nāṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā. One should employ it in the eastern direction of the gate. In the Pratotkaṭa Mahāmaṇḍala, one should perform all rites; it initiates the fierce oblation (raudrāhuti) and accomplishes all activities. It belongs to the Tathāgata family, yet it is common to the three families and may be employed in the location of every maṇḍala. || O ||
The chapter on mudrās is completed. || O ||

Now, therefore, I shall explain the chapter on the mantra of the Blessed Lady. It is as follows: Oṃ! O Raudrī! O bearer of fierce and agitated speed! O lightning-tongued one! O large-bellied one! O bearer of a garland of fierce skulls! O adorned with a crown of matted hair! O bearer of various weapons! Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ! Remember the samaya-mantra of the Tathāgata! Roar, roar! Hūṃ hūṃ! Crush all enemies! Drink their blood! O bearer of violent speed! Cook, cook! Boil, boil! Heat, heat! Hūṃ! Scatter, scatter! Hūṃ! Burn, burn! All enemies, all the wicked! Destroy them! Be gracious! Hūṃ! O you of great speed! Kill, kill! Hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ!
Whatever one wishes to say, this is the root mantra: Oṃ raudrini hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
With this mantra, one should recite it one hundred thousand times in front of the cloth painting (paṭa).

While burning *guggulu* incense, one should offer red oleanders (*karavīra*) and red wine, and give white [offerings]. [Recite: "Come, come, O Raudrī! Do not transgress the truth of the Buddha! Do not transgress the truth of the Saṅgha! Accept this offering of perfumes, flowers, incense, and bali; accomplish my purpose! This is the mantra for invocation. At the beginning of the sacrifice, one should assign the six-faced seat: "Oṃ prasphuṭa 2 hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ! O Jvālāvatī, O Mahorasya, go, go! O Great Rākṣasī, scatter the flowers and return again! This is the mantra for dispatching. "Oṃ hrīḥ hūṃ svāhā."
The flower mantra: Oṃ suru 2 hūṃ svāhā.
The incense mantra: Oṃ raudra pracaṇḍa hūṃ śrīḥ svāhā. The food offering mantra: Oṃ jvalita huru 2 hūṃ svāhā.
The lamp mantra: Oṃ hrīḥ kuru ravaiḥ hūṃ svāhā.

The mantra for renunciation by means of the powerful one is: *Oṃ namo bhagavati hilike tilike bhūtamāta paṭale hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. Whatever one desires should be spoken; for that very purpose, one should employ the Six-faced One (*Ṣaṇmukha*). *Oṃ raudrapracaṇḍavegadhari prahara 2 sarvaduṣṭāṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ 2 svāhā*. Whatever one desires should be spoken. In the southeast corner is the mantra of the Yakṣiṇī; her ritual service (*upacāra*) should be performed according to the previously stated procedure. Whether in the south, west, or north, it should be performed with this mantra.
The chapter on the mantra of the great rākṣasī Svedāmbujyā, who is formidable with flashes of lightning, is completed. || 0 ||

Now, having gone with both hands joined together, one should apply the two thumbs to the place of the hair-tuft (*maṇibandha*). Having rubbed the four fingers and the two palms with saffron and then again with sandalwood paste, one should form the *vajramuṣṭi* (diamond-fist) with the right hand and visualize the eighteen weapons. Having uttered the syllable *HŪṂ*, one should place the *vajramuṣṭi* itself upon the forehead. In that very same manner, one should place it on the right eye, the left eye, the right arm, the left arm, and likewise at the location of the heart. One should employ the Great *Vajramuṣṭi* Mudrā of the Blessed Lady in every situation. Having formed the *vajramuṣṭi* in that very same way, whether entering an empty house, or while reciting the mantra, or while standing up, one should whirl that fist seven times over the topknot (*śikhā*).

Now, therefore, follows the Akṣaya [mudrā]. The two hands, with their fingers interlaced, are extended upward and displayed like leaves, or else they are joined together; having stepped forward with the left foot and then whirling the right foot around, one steps forward again with both feet, crossing over the ten fingers. The two hands look at each other, and one should wrap them externally, placing two finger-breadths upon the forehead. One should hold them together with a single thread.

In the fourth position on the right, the dancer holds the *pallava* (bud) gesture; having clenched both fists tightly and placed them against the forehead, she holds the fourth *pallava*. Having contracted the two index fingers of the fists into a needle-point (*sūcī*) and extended them, she places them one above the other on the left side. With her head turned back, her face blooming, her eyes wide and gazing upward, and her lower lip bitten by her left canine tooth, she raises her eyebrows and brandishes [the weapon] without error. This is the *ākṣepa* (summoning) mantra: OṂ JVALANA HŪṂ HRĪḤ DAHA DAHANA HŪṂ HRĪḤ PACA PĀCANA RAUDRĀYUDHADHĀRIṆI HŪṂ PHAṬ 2 SVĀHĀ. Having bound this together with the *ākṣepa* mantra at every location of the maṇḍala, and having joined it to the ten directions along with white sesame and clarified butter, one should consecrate the ground. At that very spot, one should employ the recitation of the *ākṣepa* mantra at the beginning and end of the cloth-painting (*paṭa*). As soon as it is employed, the abode consisting of the seven jewels, extending for twenty thousand *yojanas*, becomes ablaze with flames and trembles. Together with the twenty thousand *yakṣiṇīs*, she quickly arrives. "Speak! says the practitioner. Whatever he desires must be stated. [She is] the one whose valor is like lightning, blazing, with blazing weapons, the great summoner (*mahākṣepa*).

With both hands joined in the añjali gesture, place the two wrists at the level of the forehead. According to the ritual, bend the right five-fingered hand into a fist while extending the arm; this is the *narttavarī* (dancing) gesture. With the right foot placed over both calves, extend the index finger (*tarjanī*) and perform the circular dance (*vṛttābhinaya*). Having recited the mantra, one should brandish it. Having stepped onto the position of the left foot with the right, and having stepped onto the position of the right foot with the left, form the open circle (*maṇḍali*) with both hands. Bend the *narttavarī* into a fist and extend the arm; placing it over the thigh at the position of the calf, perform the circular dance with the fingers not opened. Having recited the mantra, one should let it hang down. This is the brandishing of the eighteen weapons, the blazing, fierce, and great brandishing. The mantra for that brandishing is: *oṃ jvala hūṃ tapa tāpana hūṃ paca pācana hūṃ hana 2 hūṃ daha dāhana hūṃ hrīḥ dhṛṃ raṃ je svāhā*. Having bound this brandishing together with the mantra, whether on a cloth painting or during the installation of a maṇḍala, one should apply the aforementioned brandishing along with the mantra to each individual weapon. As soon as it is applied, the holder of the mantra becomes obedient to the command regarding each individual weapon. This very brandishing is of great supernatural power (*mahardhika*) and great majesty (*mahānubhāva*). Having bound that very brandishing together with the mantra, one intent upon the recitation of the great *rākṣasī* of the sweat-lotus should employ it before the Blessed Lady at the three junctions of the day within the previously mentioned *samaya*-maṇḍala. By performing the fierce oblation (*raudrāhuti*) in a triangular pit bounded by a vajra, one effects the shattering of the three worlds. Having bound the eighty-eight maṇḍalas together with the previously mentioned brandishing mantra, one employs them. Encircling the four directions and the intermediate points, one establishes the infinite and limitless world-systems. One accomplishes that success (*siddhi*).

The second *ākṣepa*: Placing both hands upon each other at the forehead, performing a salutation, stepping forward with the left foot first, then stepping forward with the right foot before it, rotating the two hands open like dancers, and extending them, one should utter the mantra and move the back [of the hands]. Likewise, for the face-to-face gaze, with the left [hand] raised above, one should clap there; this is the *cakravartti-cakravikrama-svāmimahākṣepa*. For that very [rite], the mantra is: *Oṃ namo bhagavati hūṃ hūṃ prajvalita hūṃ vara vara he hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This *ākṣepa*, together with the mantra, should be employed seven times along with the previously mentioned *saṃticakra*. By merely employing the *pauṣṭikacakra* in the same way, the King of Syllables (*akṣararāja*), when held by the mantra-practitioner, attains accomplishment without fail.

In this very manner, having performed the *ākṣepa* (the casting) as before, one should perform the great *vajra-jṛmbhana* (thunderbolt-yawning) seven times, bind the *mahākṣepa*, and gaze [upon the target]. This should be applied to the south, west, and north; it is to be employed according to the ritual procedure within the great mantras and yantras known as the *vidyotama*.

I shall now explain the fourth *ākṣepa*. Standing in the *utkuṭaka* posture, one should extend both shanks and feet. Joining the two thighs together at the secret place (*guhyasthāna*), one should place the two hands in the form of lotuses facing each other. One should place the right shank upon the left shank. There, the two thumbs and the two little fingers should likewise be joined; with the two thumbs, one should place [the mudrā] upon the forehead. Having recited the mantra, one should open the fourth finger (the ring finger) of the right hand. At the position of the binding of the dancer (*nartāyanī*), one should place the *sūlamudrā* formed by the little fingers. Again, having recited the mantra, one should contract the little fingers for the *sūlamudrā*. Extending them upward is the *Akṣaya-ākṣepa-mantra*: OṂ VIŚVA VIŚVAKE ŚRĪ HŪṂ ṢṬRAṂ VIŚVA VIŚVA HRĪḤ HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. This is the Great *Ākṣepa* of the Prowess of the Wind-god (*Vaiśvāsava*) of the Lightning and the Vidyuts.

Having first performed the previously mentioned *raudra* oblation into that *kuṇḍa*, one should form the *ākṣepa* [mudrā] and apply it twenty-four times. As soon as it is applied, Vaisvānara becomes manifest within that *kuṇḍa*. Having formed that *ākṣepa*, one should apply it to the four directions within the great *maṇḍala* of the fierce *preta*. One should know that there is the triangular *maṇḍala*, and likewise the fourth, the great *maṇḍala* named Mudrā, or the great *maṇḍala* named Vidyota. In the great mantra for pacifying (*śāntika*), enriching (*pauṣṭika*), or subjugating (*abhicāra*), this *kuṇḍalī* king of *ākṣepas* should be employed seven times each. As soon as it is applied, a fierce thunderbolt falls from the fire.
The Great Casting of the Lightning Bolt is completed. || 0 ||

Now, therefore, follows the characteristic of the root-mudrā (*mūlamudrā*) of the Blessed Lady. With both hands smeared with sandalwood paste, one should join the thumbs and perform the *mārayet* gesture; at the fourth [joint], one should say "ciṭi 2. Having extended the two arms, smeared them, and rubbed them together, one should rotate them. Again, having smeared them with perfume, one should fumigate them. Filling both palms with a handful of fragrant flowers and ten sprouts, one should first pay homage to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni and offer the fragrant flowers. Then, in that very place, one should offer the face-bearing and lotus-bearing [deities], and subsequently the Vidyotamā, who has a row of blazing flames, the great Rākṣasī Svedāmbuja, and the vajra-made mudrā by the mantra-holder. The knower of the pledge (*samayajña*), having clearly obtained the well-characterized instruction, should sit firmly in the lotus posture at the secret place before the cloth painting (*paṭa*). The wise one should then perform the ocean of the Bodhicitta-mudrā. Again, with both hands smeared with perfume, one should join the thumbs and perform the *mārayet* gesture, saying "Artti vicartti ciṭi ciṭi kā," which brings about liberation. Again, having smeared them with perfume, one should fumigate them. Placing the two palms joined together, containing fragrant flowers and ten sprouts, at the tip of the nose, one should interlace the two index fingers with a single thread. The two little fingers should be positioned likewise; the tips of the two little fingers should rest upon the two index fingers. The nails of the two ring fingers should touch each other on their backs. Extending the two middle fingers like needles, the nails of the two index fingers should touch each other on their backs. Extending the two forefingers, the nails should touch each other. Beyond the two middle fingers, the space between the two [forefingers] should be separated. The third finger (middle) should be separated from the two ring fingers. Having directed it toward the face and placed it on the forehead, one should likewise [place it] on the right arm, the left arm, and the heart. Having withdrawn it, and again having smeared [the hands] with perfume and bound the mudrā according to the previously stated rule, one should recite [the mantra]. One should recite one hundred thousand times over two days. This is the root-mudrā.
Having likewise formed the mudrā, having placed the two thumbs at the root joints, and having performed the salutation begun with the two little fingers [of the hands], it is released.

This is the *āvāhana-mudrā* (invocation gesture). Having consecrated both hands according to the previously stated procedure, one should form two fists and place the two thumbs against the middle joints of the two ring fingers (*aṃ*). Extending the two index fingers like needles in the shape of a coil, one should extend the right little fingers of each hand and grasp them with the two thumbs, then touch the two index fingers. This is the salutation for the commencement of the ritual circle.

This is the *preṣamudrā*. Having formed that same mudrā, one should bend the two middle fingers inward; with the two index fingers, one should place the two middle-finger needles against each other in the shape of a hook (*aṅkuśa*) at the sides of the two thumbs. When the two [thumbs] are bent in a gesture of salutation, it is the *gandhamudrā*. With both hands, having extended the two index fingers against each other, one should press the two middle-finger needles against each other at the back in the shape of a hook, and having extended the two little fingers, they are joined in mutual salutation.

This is the Flower Mudrā. In the same manner, form a fist; place the two thumbs and the two index fingers in the shape of a hook. Extending the two middle fingers like needles, and keeping the two little fingers separated from one another, perform a prostration for the sake of awakening.

This is the *nivedya-mudrā* (offering mudrā). Having formed two fists with both hands, place the right fist around the left fist; there, extend the right thumb and likewise the left thumb. Extend both index fingers so that their nails touch each other in a mutual salutation. With both hands in the *añjali* gesture, draw the two thumbs inward, extend the two index fingers, and form two needle-like middle fingers. Place the two middle finger joints upon the two index fingers. [The right thumb touches] the left nostril; with the left little finger and the right little finger, they perform a mutual salutation by circling one another.

This is the Lamp Mudrā (*pradīpamudrā*). With the backs of the two hands joined, the back of the left little finger is placed against the right little finger. The right ring finger and the left little finger are interlocked at their tips. One should place the right thumb and little finger upon them. The left ring finger and the right middle finger should be interlocked like needles. Extending the left middle finger like a needle, one should press the left index finger down with the right index finger and touch it to the tip of the thumb. One should place the right index finger on the first joint of the left middle finger’s needle-like tip. This is from the second cycle of salutations.

This is the bali-mudrā. In every direction, intermediate direction, and sub-direction—whether finite, infinite, or boundless—one should perform the offering of the bali at all locations within the maṇḍala, accompanied by this mudrā and mantra, while reciting the great vidyā-mantra Vidyujjvālākarālī-svedāmbuja-mahārākṣasī. The chapter on mudrās is completed. Oṃ.

Learn the characteristics of the second mudrā: first is the enclosure wall, second is the binding of the directions, third is the cage, fourth is the ritual pinning, and fifth is the seat, each according to its proper manner.

First, one should purify the hand smeared with fragrance by means of the wall-seal (*prākāramudrā*). Joining the two thumbs at their joints, the backs of the two hands should face each other. One should bind them together with the two little fingers; likewise, one should bind the two ring fingers with the two middle fingers acting as needles. The two thumbs should be positioned in the same way. This is the Great Seal for Binding the Directions (*disābandhamahāmudrā*). The mantra is: *oṃ vegavighna kula 2 hūṃ hūṃ ra hūṃ ra hūṃ bandha bandha sarvadisāṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This mantra, accompanied by this seal, should be employed in all maṇḍala recitations and applied to the ten directions at the place of the burnt offering (*āhuti*).

Forming a mutual wrist-lock with the two hands, extend the five fingers of the right hand to the right and the five fingers of the left hand to the left; then, contracting both the thumbs and both the little fingers, rotate them over the crown of the head. This is the *Sīmābandha-mahāmudrā*. The mantra for this is: *Oṃ śruṃ śrūṃ huṃ hūṃ dhruṃ dhruṃ hana hana daha daha paca hūṃ mahāsīmāṃ bandhāmi svāhā*. One should employ this mudrā together with this mantra—the *Vidyottama* great mantra—at all maṇḍalas, during fire offerings (*āhuti*), at the site of recitation (*japa*), and for the binding of the boundary (*sīmābandha*).

In the same way, having formed two fists at the position of the wrists with the hands facing one another, one should extend the right index finger with the right hand and the left index finger with the left hand. Having placed the two thumbs upon the middle joints of the two index fingers, one should place the two fists beneath the palate and beneath the neck. One should rotate [the hands] to the right of oneself while reciting the mantra, placing the right index finger on the right ear and the left index finger on the left ear respectively. Again, having recited the mantra and visualized a wall made of vajras, one should rotate them once more. This is the mantra and mudrā for this wall: *Oṃ prasphoṭa 2 jvala 2 nāga hūṃ khaḍgāṅgī hūṃ prakvalitaprākāra svāhā*. This mantra, together with the mudrā, should be applied there; at the site of the maṇḍala offerings and recitation, one should employ the previously mentioned mudrā and mantra for the wall.

Placing the two hands in a form that conceals one from the other at the base joints, the index, middle, and ring fingers of the right hand form a needle and rest upon the back of the left hand; the index, middle, and ring fingers of the left hand form a needle and rest upon the back of the right hand; the thumb of the right hand and the forefinger of the left hand are placed against each other on the respective opposite arms; the two palms are extended toward one another and then brought to the head and rotated. This is the Pañjara-mudrā.

In that very context, the concealment (*gopanā*) is as follows: for the *jeṣṭhā* [mudrā], one extends the two index fingers of both palms against each other, binding the middle joints of the two index fingers together in the shape of a leech's neck; this is the *kīla-mudrā*. OṂ ŚRŪṂ ŚRUṂ HŪṂ PRA JUṂ HŪṂ VIDYU-PAÑJARA SVĀHĀ. This is the *pañjara-mudrā*. One should employ this *vidyotama* great mantra along with the *pañjara-mudrā* at the place of offering and recitation for all maṇḍalas. OṂ PRASPHURA PHUṬ HŪṂ HANA PRARA DHRU SPHAṬA RAUDRA VAJRA-KĪLANA SVĀHĀ. This is accompanied by the *kīlana-mantra*.

*Śāntika*. *Abhicāra* (2). *Śāntika*, the *śāntika* stake, the *pauṣṭhika* stake: *oṃ dūbarā stha ttha*. With *vaṭa*, *khadira*, *palāśa*, *arjuna*, *kadaṃba*, *aśoka*, and *nāga* trees one makes the stake; with human, elephant, horse, buffalo, cow, donkey, tiger, deer, and cat [skins/feathers], one makes the stake, together with the previously mentioned auspicious mudrā and mantra. [2] Afterwards, at some time, one should perform or drive in the stake.

Having formed fists with both hands, one should extend the two middle fingers like needles and place them against each other; then, with the two thumbs, one should press upon the backs of the ring fingers in the space between the two middle-finger needles. The two index fingers should be bent in the shape of a hook and placed upon the middle joints of the two middle fingers. This is the *āsana-mudrā*. The mantra for this is: *oṃ kāla hūṃ kṣiti vajrī hūṃ vajragarbha niṣīṃ hūṃ phaṭ 2*. One should employ this *āsana-mudrā* together with its mantra at the beginning of the place for offerings and recitation. As soon as it is employed, it holds his seat like the *vajrāsana* upon his head.

Having bound the previously mentioned mudrā together with its mantra, one should bind the earth situated at the place of sound. Then, no affliction shall prevail from any species of living beings, such as all types of nāgas, scorpions, *goṇasa* snakes, serpents, *kusarvas*, or camels.
This concludes the Great Rākṣasī of the Sweating Lotus, Terrifying with Blazing Lightning, together with the mantras and mudrās for the subsequent ritual. || O ||

Now, therefore, [the worship] of the four Yakṣiṇīs: Vidyunmālā, who is terrifying with flashes of lightning, is on the forehead; the great Rākṣasī Svedāmbujā is likewise; Ulkā is on the right eye; and Śvetaraudrī is on the left eye; Pradhurā is on the heart. This is the ritual service (upacāra).

First, one should draw the yakṣiṇī named Vidyut according to the previously mentioned procedure, using red sandalwood and red karavīra flowers. While burning guggulu incense, one should recite [the mantra] together with the yakṣiṇī’s root mudrā until it is completed. Then, taking the cloth-painting (paṭa), having again offered perfumes, flowers, and incense, one should go to one's dwelling. Having smeared the ground to the depth of a knee with clay, having set up the yantra, and having loosened the top-knot (śikhā), one should perform the rite of fanning (pavana). If the wind does not arise, then with the top-knot loosened, wearing bark garments or carrying mineral pigments, one should proceed toward the quarters.
Smudged, barely legible, with many uncertain readings.

[In a place] free from the presence of outcastes, those who drink intoxicants, and heretics, and devoid of those who transgress [the law], one should, O Brahmin, at the proper time, seek alms while looking only a yoke’s length ahead. Having bathed, one should perform the rites for the sake of the next world. At the conclusion of the recitation (*japa*), having prepared food—whether it be made of earth or otherwise—one should contemplate the womb of the Sugata as being like a reflection. Likewise, one should [place] seven volumes of the scriptures... [as previously described]. [The altar] should face south, west, or north; for rites of pacification (*śāntika*), enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), or subjugation (*abhicāra*), [the deity] faces one direction, while for elixirs, rejuvenation, sovereignty, and power, [the deity] faces two directions. One should visualize even the solitary [deity] as accomplished.

First, for the sake of pacification (*sāntika*), having kindled a fire with *asoka* wood, one should offer a thousand oblations of mustard seeds smeared with the "three sweets" (*trimadhura*). When the oblations are completed, one should enter within, face the cloth painting (*paṭa*), form the root mudrā, and recite the mantra. Again, having gone outside, one should perform the ritual in the east, south, west, and north. One should take unblemished *gorocanā*, the ghee of a tawny cow (*kapilā*), and the three types of collyrium (*añjana*); placing these three upon three leaves of the *aśvattha* tree and covering them with a third leaf, they should be set before the yakṣiṇī. (Note: This refers to an archaic method of leaf-manipulation.)

Having offered incense, flowers, incense-sticks, and food offerings, as well as my equal—human flesh and blood—one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times. At the conclusion of the recitation, one should examine the substance for signs of success or failure. If it emits smoke, one should employ the Yakṣiṇī together with the mantra. As soon as it has been employed seven times, the cloth-painting will tremble. (Note: Archaic signs of accomplishment include the emission of smoke and the movement of the painting; meat, fish, and blood are offered.)

Having approached the one worthy of offerings with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), the practitioner should say: "Grant me a boon. Whether it be a wife, a sister, a daughter, a mother, or a daughter-in-law—the practitioner must not speak of such things as these again. Having offered perfume, flowers, incense, bali-offerings, and blood, he should recite the root mantra of the Yakṣiṇī together with her root mudrā ten thousand times (*ayuta*). At the conclusion of the recitation, he should employ the Yakṣiṇī seven times together with the six-faced mantra (*ṣaṇmukha-mantra*). As soon as it is employed, an army consisting of non-human forms will appear. The practitioner should say: "Grant me a boon. Having examined whether it is real or unreal—whether it is real or unreal—if it is unreal, he should display the six-faced mudrā and mantra; having examined it even by a mere glance at the teeth... [text fragmentary].

[The text is] smudged; there are many uncertain readings: *traḥ*? *?*? (*brāhmaṇa*?). Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas go for three thousand *yojanas*, crying out "Alas! Alas! They remain with their palms joined in a gesture of salutation, as if forming an artificial seal. The practitioner should say, "Excellent, O Yakṣiṇī, sister! [Then] he should fashion a noose.

Taking the three substances previously mentioned and mixing them together, one should offer them to the Yakṣiṇī. Then, taking *gorocanā*, collyrium, and the ghee of a tawny cow (*kapilā*) with her hand, one should smear a noose made of flower-metal (*puṣpaloha*), measuring two finger-breadths in length and consisting of two strands, and bind it around the crest-jewel (*śikhāvajra*) of the Yakṣiṇī. Wherever she is dispatched—whether for the extraction of flowers, the extraction of fruits, or even gold-dust; whether for a kingdom, an elixir (*rasa*), an alchemical potion (*rasāyana*), a subterranean cave, or whatever desired object—the practitioner shall achieve success. At the time of the shadow’s heat (midday), having taken food, drink, and the hundred-fold meal, as well as the eighteen kinds of edibles, wherever you are sent, go there and return quickly.

Now, therefore, follows the mudrā and mantra of the Yakṣiṇī: Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ prasphuṭa śru śru hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā. This is the root mantra (mūlamantra). Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ ru hūṃ ru pradhura pradhura vidu āgaccha āgaccha vidyujjvālākarālī! Svedāmbujamahārākṣasī commands you: do not transgress her command! If you transgress her command, I shall fix you upon the point of a stake. This is the striking mantra (āhananamantra). Oṃ vara vara oṃ hūṃ aṭaha aṭaha gaccha vana vana vidyuvatī! Be strewn with flowers; come back again! Svāhā. This is the dispatching mantra (preṣaṇamantra).

Oṃ pra ṣṭrīḥ hūṃ hraḥ ṭaḥ sugandhaḥ. This is the incense mantra (*gandhamantra*). Oṃ aḥ traiḥ praṃ supuṣpe svāhā. The flower mantra (*puṣpamantra*). Oṃ pāṭanai hyaṃ sudhūpa svāhā. The incense mantra (*dhūpamantra*). Oṃ prasphuṭ vipralānyaṃ hūṃ svāhā. The mantra for the offering of food (*nivedyanivedanamantra*). Oṃ kāla 2 dhuru 2 hūṃ su kṣitipati sudīpa svāhā. This is the lamp mantra (*dīpamantra*). Oṃ ṣuru 2 guhye svāsa sphu hūṃ prasparddhasurīḥ svāhā. The bali mantra (*balimantra*).

Now, therefore, follows the description of the mudrās for the Yakṣiṇī. First, there are two. With one hand, having smeared the other hand with sandalwood paste, one should offer a flower at the position of the wrist with the thumbs interlocked. Afterwards, one should bind the mudrā at the secret place, on the edge of the cloth, or on the back. Both hands should be placed at the position of the head; likewise, having extended them over the right arm, one should hold the left middle finger like a needle against the right ear with the right hand. One should step forward with the left foot and hold the sole of the right foot with a single thread (?). One should hold the thumb and fingers upon both shanks. With all eyes directed upward, one should strike the left foot. This is the *vidyuvikrama-ākṣepa-mantra*: Oṃ ṭha ṭha ṭha ṭha ṭha ṭha hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. This *ākṣepa* [mudrā] of the Yakṣiṇī should be employed in all places. With both hands, one should join the two thumbs and the backs of the two little fingers at the root joints. The left ring finger and the right index finger, and the right ring finger and the left index finger, should be interlocked. Having extended the two middle fingers like needles, they should be separated by the measure of a split barley grain. This is the *mūla-mudrā*. Binding the mudrā in that same way, one should cause the two thumbs to lean toward each other (*ālīḍha*). The invocation (*āvāhana*) is performed in that very same way. Having stepped forward twice, one should release it in the *prālīḍha* posture. By this very method, having contracted the two middle fingers inward like needles, one should press the middle joints of the two middle fingers with the two thumbs. The right index finger should rest on the back of the left thumb, and the left index finger on the right thumb. The two needle-like ring fingers should be placed upon the middle joints of the two ring fingers by means of the two little fingers interlocked. This is the *gandha-mudrā*. With both hands joined back-to-back, one should hook the two little fingers like a hook (*aṅkuśa*), and the needle-like ring and middle fingers. In that same way, with the two thumbs, the two index fingers should be joined. This is likewise the *puṣpa-mudrā*. Binding that same mudrā, one should touch the tips of the two thumbs with the two index fingers. Having extended the two needle-like middle fingers against each other, this is the *nivedana-mudrā*. Having formed two fists, one should cross the two thumbs and the two little fingers of both hands like needles. The two index fingers should be shaped like earrings (*kuṇḍala*), and one should step into the middle of the bent right thumb. This is the *pradīpa-mudrā*. In this same manner, having formed two fists, one should touch the tips of the two thumbs with the two ring fingers. One should extend the two index fingers against each other. This is the *bali-mudrā*. The *gandha-mudrā* should be combined with the *gandha-mantra*, the *puṣpa-mudrā* with the *puṣpa-mantra*, and likewise the offering (*nivedya*) and the lamp (*pradīpa*) should be combined in the same way. A practitioner who desires accomplishment with an undeluded mind will attain happiness in this world and have no fear in the next.
The chapter on the mudrās of the yakṣiṇīs is completed. || 0 ||

Now, therefore, follows the ritual for the mandala of Yakṣiṇī. One should draw a two-cubit square mandala with eight corners, surrounded by seven tiers of altars, upon the cloth previously described. It should be positioned facing north within the central mandala. A stake made of human bone, eight finger-breadths long, should be wrapped with a five-colored thread. Having consecrated it one hundred and eight times with the Heart Mantra, it should be driven into the eight corners along with the stake. Around the entire cloth, one should display, as before, a mass of flames emerging from black and red powder. On the first tier is a young boy of black form; on the second tier, a black *preta*; on the third tier, an *aṅkuśa*; on the fourth tier, Vināyaka; on the fifth tier, Mahākāla; on the sixth tier, Garuḍa as a vehicle; and on the seventh tier, Indra with a thunderbolt in his hand. All of these are black in color and have their palms joined together. On the back of the cloth, on the southern tier is a skull; on the second tier, a head; on the third, a sword; on the fourth, an arrow; on the fifth tier, three black serpents held in the hands; on the sixth tier, a tortoise; and on the seventh tier, the staff of Yama. With all these, he describes the binding of the cloth. On the western side, on the first tier is a Vajra; on the second tier, a *preta* emitting breath; on the third tier, Paśupati; on the fourth tier, the staff of Yama; on the fifth tier, a noose; on the sixth tier, the destroyer of the *ajagara* snake; and on the seventh tier, a black jar. Facing the cloth, on the first tier is a vajra-axe; on the second tier, a vajra-noose; on the third tier, a Vetāḍa; on the fourth tier, a vajra-hook; on the fifth tier, three black serpents held as before; on the sixth, a peacock; and on the seventh, Hārītī together with Priyaṃkara. With all these installations (*nyāsa*) performed according to the rite, the mandala should be installed without confusion.

Having offered perfumes, flowers, incense, bali-offerings, lamps, garlands, and other gifts according to the previously described procedure, one should empower oneself seven times with the three dhārmika-sattva root mudrās and mantras around the entire mandala. Facing the cloth painting, having bound the previously mentioned [mudrā], with eyes fixed and gazing upward, one should contemplate the cloth. As soon as it is contemplated, the cloth rises; the back bows down while the front rises.

Again, having formed the *ākṣepa* (seizing) mudrā, one should likewise gaze at the cloth [painting]. With the mind’s vision directed toward the east and west, and north and south, one should recite the root mantra ten million times (*nayuta*) while remaining firm in the terrifying *bandha* posture facing the miraculous face of the cloth. At the end of the recitation, having bound the mudrā, a servant-maid (*ceṭī*) will immediately arrive and say, "Choose a boon. The practitioner must not speak. The servant-maid sent by the Yakṣiṇī may be either real or artificial, and she speaks sweet words from the mudrā. If she is a real great demoness (*mahāmāmi*), the practitioner must not speak; he should address her as "Mother," "Sister," or "Aunt. The practitioner should say to the servant-maid, "I shall do whatever you desire. Whether it be a cave, the entrance to an *asura*, a treasure (*nidhi*), an elixir (*rasarasāyaṇa*), the curing of all beings' diseases, the summoning of beings, cutting, piercing, binding, striking, or causing hatred—wherever you send me, I shall take that and return quickly. If I am to be among those who lack compassion for beings, then swear an oath! If she is terrified, the practitioner should not speak with the Vidyādhara or the Yakṣiṇī unless they have been tested. He should present the *sūla-mudrā* together with the mantra seven times, and show the six-faced mantra directly to the Yakṣiṇī. As soon as it is shown, the artificial servant-maid falls down instantly.
Note: A fabricated subordinate is sent ahead to test the *sādhaka*!

The Yakṣiṇī Akṛtimā, her mouth sealed by the practitioner, circumambulates him three times and stands before him. The practitioner, having offered her a seat, stands respectfully to her right. The practitioner, having consecrated an iron hook made of *puṣpaloha* seven times with the heart-mantra of the Great Rākṣasī Svedāmbujā, should embrace the Yakṣiṇī and bind her with the Great Vow (*mahāvasena*). Thereafter, the mantra-holder should say: "Sister, I wish to perform service for the Three Jewels. She replies: "What kind of service does the practitioner wish to perform? [He says: "Sister, give me the elixir (*rasa*). Without exceeding that very moment, she goes to where the elixir is refined, takes it, and returns quickly. As she arrives, he says, "Welcome. The practitioner, having taken the elixir, should rub one *karṣa* of it [into gold]; it becomes one thousand pieces of gold. One thousand becomes two thousand; two thousand becomes six thousand; six thousand [remains] as long as life lasts, undiminished for the Three Jewels. Living upon this supreme servant, he lives happily through the power of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) until the arising of a Buddha, the Blessed One. He fulfills the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) and must avoid the mortal state. For as long as three eons, free from old age and disease, endowed with the perfections of generosity, morality, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom, and the ten paths of wholesome action, he will become a Bodhisattva. He shall reach the end of existence (*bhavānta*).

Thus, the *Vidyut*—terrible with streaks of lightning, fashioned upon the broad forehead of the great *rākṣasī* Svedāmbuja—for the sake of subduing all malevolent beings and for the sake of favoring all commitments (*samaya*), wherever the *yakṣiṇī* named Vidyut is dispatched, there success (*siddhi*) is achieved.
The ritual manual (*kalpa*) of the *yakṣiṇī* named Vidyut is completed. ||o||

Now, therefore, regarding the second yakṣiṇī, the great yakṣiṇī named Kṣitiulkā: having drawn her according to the previously described procedure for the great maṇḍala of the *preta* Utkata, either on a board of *vaṭa* wood or on a board of *śāla* wood, according to the aforementioned method; while burning incense of red oleander flowers, red sandalwood, and *guggulu*, and having completed the ritual, one should take hold of her. Then, having again offered perfumes, flowers, and incense, one should resort to an empty house, a cave, a stream, or a place surrounded by trees or a magnificent site dedicated to the Jina, and recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, subsisting either on alms-food or on a diet of tubers, roots, and fruits. At the conclusion of the recitation, having kindled a fire with *nāga*-wood, one should offer eight thousand oblations mixed with *buka* flowers and *sarja* resin. Thus the yakṣiṇī becomes accomplished.
Some dietary austerity and seclusion during *japa*.

Now, therefore, I shall again proclaim the mudrās and mantras by means of the mantra-holder: Oṃ vidyuṃ dhruṃ 2 uṭ 2 hūṃ 2 hūṃ 2 sphuṭa sphoṭaya svāhā. This is the root mantra (mūlamantra). Oṃ ūrṇṇa ru ūrṇṇa ru hūṃ [5] āgaccha ūrṇṇa ru | O great rākṣasī of the sweat-lotus, do not transgress my command; accomplish my task, svāhā. This is the invocation mantra (āvāhanamantra). Oṃ dhuna 2 dhuna 2 ūrṇṇa śrut || hūṃ gaccha gaccha mahāyakṣiṇī jvālāvatī puṣpāvakīrṇṇa punarāgamanaṃ kuru svāhā. This is the dismissal mantra (preṣaṇamantra). For the dismissal, it is the bliss of blossoming; for the invocation, it is the face of the pressing [of the offering]; for all yakṣiṇīs: oṃ dhūṃ hūṃ svāhā. The scent mantra (gandhamantra): oṃ sraṃ [54v] jriṃ huṃ hūṃ svāhā. The flower mantra (puṣpamantra): oṃ kuru kuṃje kuru anyaṃ hūṃ svāhā. The mantra for the presentation of the food offering (nivedyanivedanamantra): oṃ khuṃ khuṃ jrīḥ duḥ hūṃ svāhā. The incense mantra (dhūpamantra): oṃ puṣpa vi hūṃ svāhā. This is the lamp mantra (pradīpamantra): oṃ ṣuṭ 2 vajrīḥ i hūṃ svāhā. The bali mantra (balimantra): [as above].

Now, therefore, follows the description of the *ākṣepa* (the casting/throwing) gesture. First, for the *ākṣepa*: having crossed the two hands over one another at the ends of the fingers, both hands form fists. The right fist remains in that same position at the ear, with the middle finger extended like a needle. The left fist rests upon the three shanks of the left leg. Having formed this *ākṣepa*, with eyes fixed on the target and gaze directed upward, one should perform the binding in front of the Yakṣiṇī while reciting the mantra: *oṃ ghraṃ ghruṃ kṣuṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. This is the *ākṣepa-mantra*. With the hand smeared with perfume, saying "ciṭi 2 kā," one releases the bond by forming two fists and extending the two middle fingers against each other, placing the tips of the two index fingers and the two thumbs in the shape of a hook (*aṅkuśa*). At a crossroads, this is the *vajra*-form. This is the root-mudrā (*mūlamudrā*). Bending the two index fingers and pressing them back with the two thumbs behind the backs of the index fingers—this is the summoning mudrā (*āvāhanamudrā*) for the desired goal. Extending the two index fingers, bending the two middle fingers inward against each other, and joining the tips of the two thumbs—this is the dispatching mudrā (*preṣaṇamudrā*). In that same fist, bending the two index fingers inward, one should awaken the two thumbs and the two little fingers. This is the perfume mudrā (*gandhamudrā*). Likewise, in the fist, bending the thumbs and little fingers inward, extending the right index finger, and extending the left ring finger and the right index finger against each other—this is the flower mudrā (*puṣpamudrā*). Making a double *añjali* with both hands, one should place the two thumbs upon the first joints of the two index fingers. This is the incense mudrā (*dhūpamudrā*). In that same *añjali*, the two thumbs are in the shape of a hook and the two index fingers likewise; this is the offering mudrā (*nivedyamudrā*). In the same way, making the *añjali*, one should place the two middle fingers against the middle fingers of the two thumbs. This is the lamp mudrā (*pradīpamudrā*). In this very manner, making a double *añjali* with both hands, bending the two thumbs inward and likewise the two little fingers—this is the food-offering mudrā (*balimudrā*).

A Vidyādhara who wishes to accomplish the previously mentioned Yakṣiṇī should take the cloth-painting (*paṭa*) of the Yakṣiṇī and, having gone to a solitary place according to the previously stated procedure, draw a circular maṇḍala one cubit in size with four corners and a western gate using yellow ochre (*suvarṇagairika*). He should drive stakes made of *puṣpaloha* metal, measuring eight finger-breadths in length, into the four corners after consecrating them eight times with the root-mantra and mustard seeds. At the western gate, there is a fire-pit (*agnikuṇḍa*). On the first altar to the east, he should place a *śrīvatsa*; on the third, a *nandyāvarta*. On the first altar to the right (south), a jar (*kuṃbha*); on the second, a lotus (*padma*); and on the third altar, a hook (*aṅkuśa*). On the altar at the western gate, he should place a vajra resting upon a lotus; on the second, a noose (*pāśa*); and on the third, a vajra-bell (*vajraghaṇṭā*). On the northern altar, first a vajra-jar (*vajrakuṃbha*), and on the second, the syllables *haṃ* and *laṃ*. He should place conch shells in three of the four corners, following a clockwise direction. All these should be installed using yellow ochre as previously described. The previously mentioned cloth-painting of the Yakṣiṇī should be placed facing west. Having offered scents, flowers, and incense, and having performed the previously mentioned invocation, he should gaze upon the painting. He should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to the previously stated procedure; success is achieved during the dark fortnight for one intent upon it. Day by day, he should perform seven oblations (*āhuti*). At the conclusion of the oblations, he should perform one recitation of the *Mahāsamāja* and offer a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into a Sugata-caitya containing relics.
What is a *mahāsamāja*? Also [discussed] above in the blurred passage!

At the time when success is near, those who are full of passion or full of hatred approach the mantra-holder. Form is opposed by form; likewise, there is the grasping of sound, taste, and touch. At that very moment, a maidservant is sent forth: "O practitioner, choose a boon; I shall grant it. The practitioner, whose senses are skilled in the five objects of sense, should examine the maidservant’s abode. If she is a great *rākṣasī*, she will have perspiration on her lotus-like face. Having formed the root-mudrā, one should show it to the *yakṣiṇī* face-to-face. If the maidservant is artificial, she will weep. Thus one understands. If she is a real *yakṣiṇī*, she will circumambulate and say: "Choose a boon, O practitioner! Whatever you desire, I shall do it. [I shall provide] elixirs, alchemy, sovereignty over Jambūdvīpa, the eighty-four thousand [inner] accomplishments—whether superior, middling, or inferior. Whichever you send forth, I shall bring that accomplishment to pass. The practitioner should say, "Excellent, sister! and may enjoy the *yakṣiṇī* for as long as he lives. One should avoid mortal women; a good life is well-attained, for they fulfill the perfection of generosity in this world. Indeed, a good life is attained where there is no fear of elephants, cattle, or foreign armies.
% NB This is the maidservant again; the grades of *siddhi* are said to be eighty-four thousand in total!
The ritual manual for the second *yakṣiṇī* in the great mandala of the fierce *preta*, the great *rākṣasī* Svedāmbuja, who is formidable with streaks of lightning-flames, is completed. || o ||
Now, therefore, I shall explain the ritual service for the yakṣiṇī Raudrī, who is renowned by the name Tṛtīyasvetaraudrī.

[2] Having drawn the Yakṣiṇī according to the previously mentioned procedure, while burning *pāribhadra* flowers, red sandalwood, and *guggulu* incense, one should draw a single-hasta triangular mandala with a single altar and a northern gate using yellow orpiment (*haritāla*). Within the central mandala, one should place the Yakṣiṇī named Śvetaraudrī. Having offered the previously mentioned perfumes, flowers, and incense, one should place skull-cups (*kapāla*) containing blood and mustard powder in the three corners. A lamp placed in a skull-cup filled with oil should be set in the triangle. In the center of the fourth mandala, a six-finger-long stake made of human bone, consecrated seven times with this mantra, should be driven into the southern corner. In front of the cloth painting, having fashioned an effigy of the enemy with charcoals from a cremation ground—one with loose hair, a round face, hanging arms, and feet falling into bubbles of blood—one should drive the image at the heart-center with mustard seeds consecrated eight hundred times with this mantra: *Oṃ śveta mahāśveta śvetaraudrī hana 2 pata 2 phaṭ*. This is what Māra must say. A stake made of human bone, four fingers long and consecrated eight hundred times with the previously mentioned mantra, should be taken from the body of the enemy; pressing the palm against the foot, one should drive the first stake into the heart-center with "hrīḥ phaṭ," the second stake into the left hand with "hrīḥ phaṭ," the third stake into the left thigh at the Brahma-spot (the head) by uttering the name with "hrīḥ phaṭ," and the fourth stake into the right thigh at the Brahma-spot with "I nail down so-and-so, hrīḥ phaṭ. While pressing with the knee, he shakes his hand; the enemy is nailed down in the four directions by Māra. If the practitioner does not wish for his recovery, he should quickly perform the withdrawal. On the second night, when smoke issues from the enemy's body, a great pestilence spreads for three hundred *yojanas* on all sides. By extracting the stake, there is liberation. One should smear that effigy with clay mixed with iron filings, combine it with the previously mentioned *pāribhadra* flowers and earth, and fashion a pill (*guḷikā*). Taking one pill and consecrating it eight hundred times with the previously mentioned mantra, it should be driven into the base of the door of the enemy's house; it will cause him to collapse. By extracting it, there is liberation. One should throw into the fire the root of *utpāda* (madder), the root of *upodakī*, and the fat of a frog, together with the previously mentioned pill. Even if burned for a thousand years, it will not be consumed. That is the powder of a white frog soaked in blood. Having combined the previously mentioned pill with the white *utpāda* stake and anointed one's limbs, one may enter the fire. One is not burned by the fire. This is the mantra for paralyzing fire. Having combined the previously mentioned pill with the testicles of a *susumāra* fish and the juice of a lotus leaf, and having anointed one's own body, one may enter the water. One sees the aquatic creatures; this is the supreme method for paralyzing water.
% [Folio slightly worm-eaten/torn] % Entering into fire or flood! Unusual *siddhis*.
The ritual manual (*kalpa*) of Śvetaraudrīyakṣiṇī is completed. || o ||

Now, therefore, I shall explain the fourth ritual manual for the great yakṣiṇī Pradhura, who is the great king of the maṇḍalas of the fierce pretas, the great rākṣasī Svedāmbujā, who is formidable with the blazing flames of lightning.

On the eighth or the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, having fasted for a full day and night, O mantra-holder, one should draw [the image] according to the previously described procedure for the great maṇḍala of the fierce *preta*. While burning *kokilākṣa* flowers, red sandalwood, and *guggulu* incense for the *yakṣiṇī*, one should recite the heart-mantra of the *yakṣiṇī* ten thousand times: *oṃ pradhura phuṭa huru 2 hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ amukaṃ vaśam ānaya svāhā*. Having fashioned an image of a girl out of cane (*vetralatā*), and having consecrated it eight hundred times with the previously mentioned mantra, one should strike the new cane image [saying], "The girl named so-and-so must be brought! As soon as it is struck, she will be seized by a great illness; no one can release her. One should bathe her with milk mixed with mustard seeds and water, consecrated eight hundred times with the previously mentioned mantra; she will be liberated. One should offer perfumes, flowers, and incense to the *yakṣiṇī*. Having fashioned an image of a girl made of lac on the palm of the right hand and consecrated it seven hundred times, one should strike its reflection with mustard seeds in front of the cloth painting (*paṭa*). At that very moment, the girl will be summoned. Having drawn the previously mentioned *yakṣiṇī* on the palm of the right hand with yellow orpiment (*haritāla*), one should strike it with mustard seeds consecrated eight hundred times with the root-mantra of the great *rākṣasī* Svedāmbuja. Flowers, fruits, leaves, other drinks, clothing, or women, men, boys, or girls will be summoned. If she is not summoned, one should bind the root-mudrā and rub the palm of the hand; at that very moment she arrives and is summoned.
The rite for the yakṣiṇī must be performed in secret; if one reveals it, the yakṣiṇī will turn her face away and depart from the mantra-holder.

The ritual manual (*kalpa*) for the Four-Eyed One within the vast mandala of the fierce preta, the great rākṣasī of the lotus who is terrifying with flashes of lightning and perspiration, is completed. || O || *Note: The necessity for secrecy is required.*
The *Tantrarāja* as obtained from the Blessed Lady Svedā is completed. || O ||

Final Colophon: In the year [indicated by] a-p-ta 4 (i.e., 574), on the second day of the bright fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, during the victorious reign of the Mahārājādhirāja Parameśvara, the illustrious Lakṣmīkāmadeva Parameśvara. This manuscript was written by Kyaraṇākara Datta, a resident of Śrī-Gāṅkuṭalāṅga. The measure of this work is one thousand eight hundred [verses], namely 1800. Maṅgalam. Oṃ.
